discharging. The Vessel is not to be obliged to force ice, nor to follow
icebreakers when inward bound. If on account of ice the Master
considers it dangerous to remain at the loading or discharging place
for fear of the Vessel being frozen in and/or damaged, he has liberty
to sail to a convenient open place and await the Charterers' fresh

Charterers' account.
If the contemplated employment of the ship entails voyages to
ports where these conditions may be encountered, the terms and
conditions under which that activity will be performed must be
negotiated and set forth in minute detail in the charter-party.

The owner invoked the "ice clause" when his ice-strengthened bulk car
rier encountered these conditions. Photo: A/S Hydraulik Brattvaag.
Any charterer who takes ships for a period of time becomes
involved, as has been indicated, in considerations related to the
expenditure of large sums of money (as for fuel) or the actual
scheduling of voyages and the unavoidable responsibility for loss of
time resulting from impaired performance of the ship. To protect
the charterer in both these typical instances, there must be agree
ment before the contract is signed as to the amount of fuel the ship's
power plant will consume in twenty-four hours at normal service
speed in calm seas, and this statement must be contained in the
charter-party. The speed of the ship and her carrying capacity,
expressed both in cubic feet of enclosed space and in deadweight
tons, are stipulated by the owner, along with numerous other
details of the ship's physical characteristics, in what are called the
"warranties." These are statements of fact which are expected to be
borne out by the performance of the vessel. Failure to live up to the
warranties can make the owner liable for breach of contract.

Most of the warranties are provable without difficulty, but
speed and fuel consumption are affected noticeably by weather
conditions. Should a dispute arise over either or both of these
stipulations, there will be discussions between the contracting par
ties until a satisfactory adjustment is made. Should no compromise
be reached in these areas or in any other part of the charter-party,
the dispute may be referred to arbitrators. Their decision will have
the same force as a judgment handed down by a court of law.
The charterer always stipulates the port in which the ship is to
be made available to him-or, in the terms of the trade, "tendered"
by the owner. The charterer also sets forth the beginning and the
ending of the period of days during which tender (or delivery) of
the ship may be made. This period is known as "lay days." The
charterer also states the date beyond which he reserves the right to
cancel the agreement and to refuse to accept the tender of the
vessel. The owner protects himself from arbitrary action by includ
ing this clause in the charter-party:
I f the vessel cannot be delivered by the cancelling date, the Charter
ers, if required [by the owners], are to declare within 48 hours (Sun
days and holidays excluded) after receiving notice thereof whether
they cancel or will take delivery of the Vessel.
Should the contract be for a single voyage, the exact commodity
to be carried and the charter hire payable per ton of that commod
ity actually loaded, are designated, as are the ports of loading and
discharge. These details are important to the owner not only for the
obvious reasons but also because they permit him to look ahead for
other employment following the completion of the present charter.
Experience and knowledge will guide him in estimating the num
ber of days the ship will need to carry out the contract; a judicious
guess must be made as to the possible delays, and long-range
commitments thereafter can be consummated. During those peri
ods when there is reasonably good demand for ships, an astute
owner may be able to keep his vessel profitably employed for a full
year with hardly any movements in ballast.

allowed for loading and discharge (also known as "lay days")9, the
penalty for holding the ship in port

be made as to the possible delays, and long-range
commitments thereafter can be consummated. During those peri
ods when there is reasonably good demand for ships, an astute
owner may be able to keep his vessel profitably employed for a full
year with hardly any movements in ballast.
Among provisions of the voyage charter are the number of days
allowed for loading and discharge (also known as "lay days")9, the
penalty for holding the ship in port beyond the allowed period for
working cargo ("demurrage"), and the premium for reducing the

time spent in port ("dispatch"). For instance, a 20,000-ton tanker is
fixed for a load of petroleum from a Caribbean port to a range of
ports on the Atlantic coast of the United States north of Cape
Hatteras (generally referred to by the initials USNH); alternatively,
it may be assigned specific ports such as Aruba and New York. The
ship is allowed a certain number of hours for loading and discharg
ing; demurrage is set at $2,200 per day and dispatch at half that
rate, prorated to the actual hours.
Because the voyage charter imposes the least operational re
sponsibility upon the charterer and is convenient for the movement
of bulk commodities, it has become the most common form of
contract. The owner of the ship, under the "gross" form, pays for
every item of expense, including loading, discharging, port fees,
and all expenses in connection with the cargo, as well as the operat
ing charges such as crew wages, subsistence, and fuel. 10 Under the
"net" form, the owner pays all normal ship operating costs, and the
charterer is responsible for charges accrued for loading and dis
charging the cargo as well as for port fees (except those related
directly and solely to the crew) exacted against ship and cargo. The
owner retains the full burden of managing the ship.
A voyage charter, as has been pointed out, is concerned with
moving a particular cargo between designated ports. It is under
stood that the charterer will provide sufficient cargo to fill the entire
ship unless the contract stipulates otherwise. The master must
assure tnat the loading of the vessel is correct and seaworthy; almost
always he has authority to decrease or increase the quantity of cargo
offered by the shipper, as may be required to give the ship proper
trim and stability.
The charterer, for his part, must pay the agreed sum for each
ton of the commodity he has contracted to ship; ifheloads less than
the ship's capacity, he is liable for the difference between what
should have been loaded and what actually was put into the hull
("dead freight"). The owner intends for the master to accept as
much as the safety of the ship will permit, in order to obtain the
maximum revenue from the voyage. It is expected that the

charterer, for his part, must pay the agreed sum for each
ton of the commodity he has contracted to ship; ifheloads less than
the ship's capacity, he is liable for the difference between what
should have been loaded and what actually was put into the hull
("dead freight"). The owner intends for the master to accept as
much as the safety of the ship will permit, in order to obtain the
maximum revenue from the voyage. It is expected that the charter
er, having set the date when he will be ready to receive the ship, will
have the cargo waiting so that no time will be lost once the ship has
been tendered. Any delay on the charterer's part subjects him to the
possibility of paying demurrage.

Unlike the revenue earned under the voyage charter, which is
based on the payment per ton of cargo loaded, the time charter hire
is predicated upon the carrying capacity of the ship. That is to say,
the ship has a deadweight capacity, always determined at the sum
mer load line, and so much enclosed cargo space. The charterer has
the full use of that capacity and space for the duration of the
charter. He may load any cargoes not prohibited by the charter
party, and may direct the ship to proceed wherever he desires
within the limits fixed by the contract. The charterer has no connec
tion with the navigation and operation of the vessel; he provides
cargoes for the ship, keeps her busy, and pays the owner at the
agreed rate per deadweight ton per month. If he fails to find
employment for the vessel, he still must pay the owner the stipulat
ed hire. The owner provides the crew, stores, and all necessary
equipment for the vessel; pays all port charges incurred for and in
behalf of the crew; and is responsible in all respects for the naviga
tion and maintenance of the vessel, and the stowage, care, and
safety of the cargo. The charterer provides the fuel; pays port
entry, clearance, and agency fees; pilotage charges, tug hire, costs
of loading and discharging cargo, including wharfage and dock
age; and arranges for appropriate representation in the ports dur
ing voyages. 11
To illustrate the theory of the time charter, here is a simplified
form of agreement for the use of a ship:

Register of Shipping, and of about 711,000 cubic feet grain capacity,

of 30 feet, with a service speed of 16J;2 knots on a consumption for all
purposes of about 25 tons of best grade fuel oil), now in service and
trading. These particulars are not guaranteed, but are supplied in
good faith and are believed to be correct.
It is agreed that the vessel is tight, staunch, and strong, and in every
way fitted for the contemplated service. She is to be delivered to the
charterers in Galveston, Texas, not earlier than October 13, 1981, and
not later than October 30, 1981, and redelivered to the owners in a

safe United States Atlantic port north of Cape Hatteras but not east of

Should the vessel not be delivered by October 30, 1981, the charter
ers have the option to cancel. If the vessel cannot be delivered by the
cancelling date, the charterers are to declare, within 48 hours (Sun
days and holidays excluded) of receiving notice from the owners,
whether they will cancel or take delivery of the vessel.
The vessel is to be employed in lawful trades to carry only lawful
merchandise, excluding explosives, livestock, sulphur, and phos

2. The charterers shall pay all dock, harbor, light, and tonnage dues

4. The whole reach and burden of the vessel's holds, decks, and

5. The master shall prosecute his voyages with all reasonable speed,
and all vessel logs shall be shown to the charterers on demand. The

5. The master shall prosecute his voyages with all reasonable speed,

7. The owners shall have a lien upon all cargoes and subfreights

8. The vessel is to work day and night if required. The owners shall

9. Any dispute arising under this charter is to be referred to arbitra

10. A commission of 2 Y2 percent is payable by the owners to the

The bareboat charter is similar to the time charter in that the use
of the ship is acquired for a period of time, but the full responsibil
ity of operation is transferred from owner to charterer. Obviously,
a heavy burden is placed upon any person taking a ship under such
an agreement. Few deals of this sort are consummated; for the most
part they are the result of complex financing transactions in which
the legal owner is not a ship-operating organization but a bank or
similar institution. The charterer must have a complete staff in
existence to assume the duties of running the ship. Nearly always
steamship companies which charter ships on a bareboat basis do so
to augment their fleet capabilities either for a short period of peak
cargoes, or over the long term in lieu of purchasing a ship.
Perusal of the different charter-parties is rewarding, for the
numerous provisions of the documents reflect the experience of
shipowners and charterers through the years. Drawn by practical
shipping men working alongside experts in maritime and commer
cial law, the charter-parties represent a working compromise be
tween the demands of the shipowners and the insistent require
ments of the charterers. Negotiations for a particular

or over the long term in lieu of purchasing a ship.
Perusal of the different charter-parties is rewarding, for the
numerous provisions of the documents reflect the experience of
shipowners and charterers through the years. Drawn by practical
shipping men working alongside experts in maritime and commer
cial law, the charter-parties represent a working compromise be
tween the demands of the shipowners and the insistent require
ments of the charterers. Negotiations for a particular transaction
usually start with one of these standardized, preprinted forms, with

appropriate insertions of agreed terms. If necessary, the clauses are
modified to fit the circumstances of the proposed charter.
"Working the market" requires that both charterer and ship
owner be alert to many factors. The charterer needs to know a great
deal about the availability of ships and the consequent fluctuations
of the freight and charter markets. He must note how rates change
for the same commodity on different trade routes and at varying
times of the year. The operator has to be aware of practically
everything the charterer should know while keeping at his fin
gertips a wide assortment of facts and details which are part and
parcel of his business life. He must be cognizant of conditions in
ports around the world, the charges made for handling his ships,
the efficiency of longshoremen, and the availability of cargo-work
ing equipment. He has to be alert to the peculiarities of harbors
their depths, tides and winds, ice and fog anchorages, and local
customs concerning the use of pilots and tugs. He is wise also to be
informed of ship repair facilities in those ports. He needs contacts
in anticipated ports of call which will furnish current, reliable, and
prompt reports of all developments affecting shipping in those
waters. Where to procure fuel is a never-ending cause of concern,
especially as the quality of that which is offered today is subject to
wide variation.
When it comes to cargoes, the tramp shipowner must be inti
mately acquainted with the characteristics of practically every com
modity in the world that moves in bulk, so that when he sets a rate it
will be fairly certain to earn a reasonable revenue from each ton
carried. Finally, he must know how these bulk commodities are
handled, for in some ports everything is mechanized and therefore
assures fast loading or unloading, while in other ports the process is
altogether by hand.
It is small wonder that mastering the intricacies of the tramp
shipping business is a full-time career!

section_path_text: CHAPTER 3 - The Management of Tramp Shipping
text:
To
PROVIDE timely and efficient transportation
from a producing area separated from a consuming region by
thousands of miles of ocean is both a highly complex business and a
very severe test of the business judgment and skill of those responsi
ble for the effective employment of tramp ships. Not every vessel is
adapted to carry every cargo, and not every port has a constant
stream of ships entering and leaving. Some commodities are sea
sonal in their movements, while others provide a steady flow month
after month and year after year. Some items are easy to load and
discharge, and cause no structural damage, whereas others are
troublesome and dangerous. On some routes, competition between
tramps is intense, which means that the margins of profit are
narrow, if they exist at all. Other routes, for a variety of reasons,
offer more acceptable rates of compensation, but fewer opportuni
ties. Certain ports are renowned for prompt dispatch, while others
seem to be afflicted with insoluble problems of delays and the
resulting congestion. Matching ships to cargoes, selecting the most
advantageous routings, ascertaining accurately the costs of per
formance under different types of contracts, and balancing present
opportunities against future prospects, are a few of the areas of
concern in the profitable and effective management of tramp ships.
As is true in any form of commercial enterprise, the motivating
purpose must dominate the decision-making process. In tramp
shipping, the purpose is to transport cargoes at the most profitable
level of compensation. The commodities that move in greatest
quantity, and therefore offer the best opportunities for employ
ment of ships, are ores, grains, and coal. Of these, grain is the most
likely to experience fluctuations in demand, and therefore to have a
significant impact upon the tramp shipping industry. This fact
helps to explain why grain-a term which includes a wide variety of

cereals such as wheat, corn, oats, barley, rye, sorghums, and soyas
has been called "the great leveler" of the shipping business. As a
basic requirement in feeding the population of the world, grain is in
constant demand. It is grown in many regions, but only the United
States, Canada, Argentina, and Australia (in that descending order
of magnitude) have significant quantites for export.! As a cargo,
grain can be carried in many different types of ships, and because it
moves almost exclusively in bulk, it is susceptible to mechanized
handling, with resultant short loading and discharging times. Until
the advent of containerships and the introduction of the very large
bulk carriers, grain was an attractive "filler" cargo for ships in the
liner service, and therefore became the target of intense competi
tion between "regular traders" and tramps.
A different aspect of competition became manifest when the
large, fast, specialized containerships were introduced to these
routes and, at about the same time, the tankers and bulkers of at
least 50,000 tons deadweight capacity began actively to seek grain
cargoes. Both these types were able to offer freight rates which,
because of economies of scale, were significantly below those which
the conventional 12,000- to 16,000-ton tramp could accept. It is
worthy of note that the movement of grain on the North Atlantic
trade route is dominated by large-capacity vessels.
The tramp ship, however, has not been eliminated from the
North Atlantic. Despite rigorous competition, the versatility ofthis
vessel, with the advantage of being able to enter ports too shallow
for the deep draft bulkers, has made possible satisfactory employ
ment in a variety of cargo movements. Grain continues to be a
commodity which these smaller ships can and do transport as they

It is not surprising, therefore, to discover that both the users of
tramp ships and the owners of those hard-working carriers become
avid readers of the daily news, with special emphasis upon accounts
of weather in different areas, economic conditions, political events,
and crop reports. A sudden flood in midsummer, when crops are
ripening, and only minor quantities of rainfall are needed, may
have devastating effects on the final harvest. Not only is the farmer
involved immediately, but the sellers and importers will have to
begin to make adjustments in their marketing plans. Carriers
both land and oceangoing-may discover that the tonnage requir
ing their services is reduced to a trickle. The worldwide patterns of
tramp ship operations may be altered drastically as a result of this
untimely excess of water in the growing region. The ability to relate
news events to transportation activities is a prime requisite for those
who would participate in this fascinating and ever changing activity.

For the owner and operator of tramp-type shipping, the goal
toward which all efforts are directed is the most effective employ
ment of the units of the fleet. The ultimate criterion of success is the
profit or loss sustained from the voyages undertaken during a given
accounting period. Whether the color of the ink used by the book
keeper is black, announcing a profit, or red, admitting a loss,
depends upon the ability of the managers of the fleet to reduce
nonrevenue-producing voyages in ballast to an acceptable mini
mum, to control the number of idle days between active voyages, to
find the most suitable cargoes for the ships, and to obtain the best
freight rates and the most favorable terms. Unquestionably, the
burdens placed upon the persons who must make the final deci
sions are very great, but so are the rewards when the results show
that the decisions were sound.
To be able to arrange for a series of charter commitments which
will follow one upon another with little or no intervening time
during which the ships do not earn any revenue is the ambition of
every manager. Should the policy of the owner be to keep the fleet

in the market for voyage charters, where the returns are higher but
the risks of finding continuous employment are greater than in the
longer term time charter activity, it is necessary to be extremely
selective in the commitments made. For example, a high rate may
be offered to carry a cargo of grain from New Orleans to Calcutta,
but unless there is some assurance that a load can be found within a
comparatively short distance from Calcutta, the business may be a
money loser because of the high cost of sending the ship to the area
of her next employment. Ideally, as each voyage charter is ended
and the ship is redelivered to the owner, a new assignment is
waiting, and the time between revenue-producing voyages is re
duced to the absolute minimum. In practice, this happens only
occasionally; all too often, it is necessary to send the ship on a trip of
several thousand miles to pick up the next load. The profits, if any,
from the first voyage may be absorbed in the cost of repositioning.
To illustrate the various possibilities for employment of a tramp
ship, this hypothetical example is offered: A 15,OOO-ton general
purpose vessel was assigned to lift grain from New Orleans to India.
By the time she had completed discharge at the port of destination,
these were the possibilities under consideration by the owner:
1. To proceed in ballast to Australia to pick up wheat for
delivery in either the United Kingdom or the Bordeaux-Hamburg
range of the European continent; or
2. To proceed in ballast from India to Mauritius to load a full
cargo of sugar for a port on the Atlantic coast of either Canada or
the northern range of the United States; or
3. To proceed to Murmugao, India, to take on a load of ore for
Japan. From Japan, there were these potential opportunities for em
ployment: (a) to sail in ballast to the Philippines to load copra for Eu
rope; (b) to go to the Philippines for a cargo of sugar for a United
States port on the Gulf of Mexico or the Atlantic coast; or (c) to pro
ceed in ballast to British Columbia for either a cargo of grain for Eu
rope, or a full load oflumber for the Atlantic coast of the United States.

In the real world of tramp shipping, there must be assurance
that the terms and conditions demanded by the charterer are fair
and reasonable from the viewpoint of the shipowner. What at first

may seem to be a very profitable rate may turn out to be a guarantee
of a heavy loss if there is no protection against excessive delays
incident to port congestion. For instance, if a cargo of grain is
offered from Churchill, a Canadian port on Hudson Bay where the
weather is notoriously uncertain and often shuts down the port
altogether for several consecutive days, the owner should insist
upon the charterer agreeing to compensate him for time lost in
such an eventuality. Otherwise, despite a very attractive rate, the
voyage might result in a deficit. This is especially true in the case of
the modern large-capacity ships which have operating expenses
amounting to many thousands of dollars each day.
As a tool with which to formulate decisions relating to the future
employment of a tramp steamer, the electronic computer is of great
value, gaining greater recognition year by year. In no way, how
ever, does it supersede the commercial wisdom which tramp ship
managers have acquired through years of experience in their pro
fession. The machine is only as good as the programs by which it is
governed, and the programs of greatest utility are those which
reflect the realities of tramp shipping. Combining electronic wiz
ardry with business experience in this computer age makes it possi
ble to obtain quickly a wide variety of almost unbelievably detailed
calculations. From these products of the machine the owner can
determine which of the various choices available to him will result in
the most efficient employment of his ship.
Despite the great amount of data which the computer can
provide, the final decision as to the type of charter to accept de
pends upon the owner's ability to evaluate the calculations and to
foresee the future demands for ships of the type he controls. If it is
likely that there will be a significant increase in cargo movements in
the near future, relatively short-term voyage charters are prefer
able in order to have the ships available when the expected higher
rates are being paid. Should the indications point to a long period
when rates will be held at the current level, a series of voyage
charters of moderate length might be desirable-provided the
ships will be kept busy. If, however, the forecast is for a severely
depressed market during which freights will be reduced, it would
be prudent to accept time charters paying enough

Although any forecasts regarding the trend of the world freight
market contain a high degree of conjecture, there are certain
developments that serve, when they occur, as guideposts on which
considerable reliance may be placed. As soon as prominent grain
trading organizations begin to charter ships for some months in the
future, or to accept ships under long-term time charter, it is an
almost assured indication that freight rates will remain at their
current levels; if they do drop, the new rates will be very close to
those prevailing on the current market. Major importers of grain
who are informed about future deals are very likely to attempt to
cover their requirements before the news is made public. Their
actions therefore are the subject of constant scrutiny in the never
ending effort to see into the future. Similar comments might be
made about Chinese charterers; the perspicacity and long-range
views of these businessmen are almost legendary, and have been
proved to be amazingly accurate.
The necessity to make comparisons between the advantages of a
voyage charter and a time charter is part of the daily routine of the
tramp ship owner. In the normal course of business, there fre
quently are occasions when the owner must decide between two
offers, one to place the ship under a voyage charter, in which the
compensation is payable for the actual tonnage of cargo loaded,
and the other to commit her to a time charter on which the return is
predicated upon a sum paid per deadweight ton, summer draft,
per month. An example of this sort of comparative computation
will explain the process.

The owner, in deciding whether to accept a voyage or a time
charter, must take into account the advantages and the risks inher
ent in each type of charter.
A ship under voyage charter is always under the total control of
her owner. The contract calls for transporting an agreed quantity
of a certain cargo between named ports, is limited to the time
required to load, to travel from port to port, and to discharge, and is
fulfilled when delivery of the cargo is completed. Should the voyage
be lengthened by unexpected heavy weather, the added expense is
borne by the owner. Unless otherwise provided by the contract,
interruptions to cargo-working operations attributable to adverse
weather conditions such as heavy rains, snow, or exceptionally high
winds are charged to the owner. Notwithstanding the aforemen
tioned hazards, which are not all-inclusive, the great inducement
for an owner to offer his ship for a voyage charter is that the hire
usually is greater than would be that of a time charter, and the
opportunity remains with the owner to take advantage of increases
in freight rates.
The owner of a vessel who is working the voyage charter market
must be always on the alert for new opportunities. Ideally, as one
charter is terminated, another is waiting for the ship, and the ports
in which the ship discharges and loads are separated by very short
distances, so that little time is lost between assignments. The reality
is far removed from this ideal, and quite often an interval of several
days elapses between completion of one charter and commence
ment of the next. This time of idleness is almost unavoidable
because of the necessity to allow for possible (but not inevitable)
contingencies. If they do not materialize, the ship lies idle.

A frequent experience in tramp shipping is the necessity to send
the ship on a fairly long voyage (as in this case, when the Scandic
Wasa went to Detroit) at the owner's expense to reach the port
where the next charter becomes effective. Sometimes the charterer
can be induced to pay a "ballast bonus" to assist in meeting the cost
of the voyage to the loading port. This desirable circumstance
normally occurs, however, only when there is an existing or antic
ipated shortage of ships at the loading point, or the voyage is to
commence at a place off the normal routes.
A time charter has the advantage that, once the ship is delivered
to the charterer, the costs of fuel, port fees, canal tolls, and steve
doring, as well as all ship time, are for the charterer's account.

This self-unloading collier can top off a deep-draft bulk carrier at the

Delays that can make the difference between profit and loss for the
owner under a voyage charter are allocated to the charterer; only in
the event of a breakdown and consequent inability to perform
under the charter would the owner be held responsible for ship
time. Variations in fuel prices also are the concern of the charterer,
a consideration of significant importance since the drastic price
increases that began in 1973. The ship is assured of employment
for the period stipulated in the charter-party, which protects the
owner in times of reduced demand for ships, but at the same time
precludes the possibility of capitalizing on a rising market.
Owners of tramp ships must be alert at all times to the direction
in which the charter market is going. If freight rates are believed to
be at or near the peak, it is the proper time to fix as many ships as
possible for the longest periods to which charterers are agreeable.
If, however, charter rates are low, but the owners are optimistic that

there will be a marked improvement in the near future, they would
seek short-term contracts in order to take advantage of the higher
rates when they become effective. Owners also must watch develop
ments worldwide to position their ships for the best opportunities.
If, for example, in one geographic area the principal export com
mands a small market, and numerous ships are vying for the
available business, the competition will drive the rates down. In
another part of the world, at this same time, shippers of a commod
ity that moves in very large quantities are unable to attract as many
ships as they need, and are paying premium freight rates. The
astute tramp owner will send his ship to the second region, hoping
to be among the early arrivals who will get the highest payments.
It is true, however, that there are many periods when all tramp
trades are depressed, freight rates are extremely low, and many
ships are unable to find employment. When this situation arises, the
oldest and least competitive ships are withdrawn from service and
placed in what the owners hope will be temporary lay-up. This
action is taken only after careful consideration because the cost of
returning a ship to full commission can be very great. It is a melan
choly fact of shipping that never are all the laid-up ships put back
into service. When circumstances do justify bringing ships out of
lay-up, at least some of the oldest, slowest, smallest, and, therefore,
the most expensive, ships are sold to ship-breakers, because reacti
vation is found then to be too costly.
Whereas the liner service operator has a regular route and
carries a predictable variety of cargoes offered, in the main, by a
comparatively small number of shippers who use his vessels re
peatedly, the tramp shipowner is required to find new clients for
almost every voyage.2 Given the world-ranging nature of tramp
ship employment, this would be an impossible task for an individual
owner acting by himself. The difficulty is resolved, as has been
described in another chapter, by the brokers who are found in
almost every port of commercial importance.
In the complex world of tramp shipping, there are brokers who
have principals whose ships are engaged in many different trades,
and therefore must have an extensive knowledge of the entire field
of marine transportation. In

In the complex world of tramp shipping, there are brokers who
have principals whose ships are engaged in many different trades,
and therefore must have an extensive knowledge of the entire field
of marine transportation. Inevitably, there also are individuals who
handle one type of business more and more frequently, and who
find themselves becoming specialists in a particular trade. In this

manner evolved those experts in the movement ofliquid petroleum
cargoes or in finding charters for tankers; similarly, concentrating
upon fixing ships to handle full loads of grain led other experts to
devote their attention exclusively to ships seeking grain cargoes, or
the reciprocal relationship. There are, as might be expected, many
large ship brokerage houses which serve the entire industry but
have subdivided their activities and assigned specialists appropri
ately so that the greatest efficiency in negotiating charters can be
attained.
Most chartering procedures commence with discussion of the
acceptability of the standard charter-party for the particular trade
to which the ship is to be committed. These standard agreements
have been drawn up, primarily by shipowners' groups such as the
Baltic and International Maritime Council, a multinational associa
tion of many tramp ship owners with headquarters in Copenhagen,
and incorporate the experience gained from hundreds of voyages
in individual trades. While they are revised and brought up to date
as frequently as possible, it is true that often circumstances prevail
ing at a particular moment will make it desirable for one or
the other party to the negotiation to suggest minor modifications in
some clauses, changes of substance in other clauses, and even
deletion of inapplicable or unwanted terms. Great care must be
exercised in these circumstances to assure that the changes do not
run counter to court rulings, established practices of the trade, or
other clauses in the contract. The burden assumed by the broker to
safeguard the interests of his principal is obvious.
Not only must brokers be well informed on those practices of
the trade which are reflected in the terms and conditions of the
charter-party, but they also must be aware of the level of freight
rates prevailing day by day in the trades in which their principals
desire to participate. Fortunately for all concerned, the great ma
jority of fixtures of ships under charters is published daily in bulle
tins compiled by large brokerage houses or in trade journals. Al
though the specific terms which may have influenced the accepta
bility of a particular rate may not be known, the experience of the
broker will permit him to make extremely accurate guesses about
these matters. Constant and careful analyses of these reports are an
integral part of the broker's daily routine.

possibility for desiring to keep the deal out of the news is that
neither party wishes to reveal the figures-the charterer for fear it
will indicate his profit, and the shipowner because he does not want
to disclose how low the rate was. Complete secrecy rarely is main

information about the market which occurs between brokers will
serve, willy-nilly, as the medium of communication about these
private deals.
Some mention already has been made of the fact that there are
standard charter-parties in existence covering a great number of
trades. These documents have been criticized occasionally by char
terers as being the exclusive handiwork of the shipowners, and
therefore they do not provide adequate protection for the interests
of the parties contracting to use the ships. The explanation of this
criticism lies in the fact that the shipowning and ship brokerage
professions are rather closely knit and are engaged in constant
interchange of ideas and information. Basically concerned with the
problems of operating ships in a great variety of circumstances, the
owners have in common the need to find solutions and to protect
their financial positions. Shipowner organizations have been
formed as a result, and these groups draw up contracts acceptable
to the operators.
The users of tramp ships, on the other hand, are not organized,
nor is it likely that the wide disparity of their interests can be
reconciled to the extent that a particular position can be taken and
held against opposition. This is not to disparage attempts which
have been made to bring charterers together to form proposals to
present to the shipowners; in a number of instances , they have been
successful and better relations between the two interests have come
about. The limited successes, however, emphasize the fact that
individual charterers often have problems that can be solved only
by paying attention to those acknowledged difficulties. Frequently,
what is satisfactory for one charterer is not, and cannot be, accept
able in any form to another charterer.

Every clause must be examined to be sure that it applies in its
entirety to the contemplated use of the ship; if it does not, it is
common practice for the principals, advised by their brokers, to
make mutually acceptable adjustments. In the case of one grain
charter which was used for many years for exports from Argentina,
a large number of substitute clauses was drawn up to reflect
changes in business practices. These typewritten changes were
pasted routinely in all the preprinted forms. Eventually, these
amendments were incorporated in a completely new contract, to
the relief of all concerned.
This vignette of shipping history is cited to show that shipown
ers, by choice, operate under charter-parties which are well known
and have withstood the analyses and interpretations of courts oflaw
and decisions of arbitrators. They believe, with considerable rea
son, that it is better to make a few changes, as each employment
requires, in the familiar contract, than to draw up a completely new
document which invites interpretation by a court if a dispute should
arise. When new charter-parties are proposed, they receive the
most careful and searching examination on the part of the owners,
their lawyers, and the brokerage profession, to be sure that, insofar
as possible, the interests of the shipowners are safeguarded. It is a
highly commendable fact, therefore, that new, rewritten, or sub
stantially revised charter-parties emanate from many sources on a
fairly regular basis. The tramp-shipping industry may be called
conservative, but is not stagnant.

Tramp shipping can be highly remunerative to owners when
there is a brisk demand for transportation of cargoes moving in
bulk, and can be disastrous when, for reasons beyond any possibility
of control by the owner, there is a sudden reduction in require
ments. Inherent in this situation is the fact that ships normally
working in a certain trade will be reassigned to different routes

whenever the need for carriers diminishes. In such circumstances,
the competition becomes very intense, freight rates drop precipi
tately, and the older, less efficient ships may have to be laid up
because of no employment.
In a sense, the tramp ship's owner nearly always is at a disad
vantage in the market place, because only very rarely is there so
small a supply of ships that owners can set their prices on a "take or
leave" basis. In the words of one economist, the shipowner is a
"price-taker," which means that the charterer usually dictates the
maximum for ocean freights. Even granting that the bold and
venturesome carrier may send his ship to new geographical re
gions, or reassign her to a different trade, he will find that for the
most part his freedom to demand high rates is circumscribed by a
variety of limitations.
Despite the problems which the owner of tramp ships must face,
it remains true that it is an enterprise in which the rewards can be
extremely good, and therefore it attracts both individuals and
corporations to invest their capital. Whereas in the years before
World War II it was possible to purchase a ship for a sum not
beyond the capability of one man (or a small group of investors) to
raise, the great increase in the cost of ships resulting from their
larger size, higher speed, more elaborate and hence more expen
sive accommodations for the officers and crew, and often the provi
sion of costly cargo-working gear such as deck cranes, mechanically
operated hatch covers, and better cargo ventilating equipment,
have combined to reduce the number of individual adventurers.
The actual number of ships has been diminished in the postwar
years, but total carrying capacity has been increased as vessel sizes
have been magnified and speeds have been augmented in the
ceaseless effort to achieve greater efficiency and therefore greater
profit.
The emergence, in the decades following the second world war,
of the large bulk carrier has had a profound impact upon the tramp
shipping business. Formerly iron ore, coal, grain, and lumber
moved in comparatively small ships which were interchangeable
between trades. When demand for steel suddenly exploded, the
limited capacities of the general-purpose tramp, even though this
ship had grown by almost one hundred percent in its dead

ports because they have no cargo-handling gear installed. Some of
these big ships are designed to carry alternate cargoes of com

A further handicap which the conventional tramp must over
come is the invasion of the grain trade by tankers. It was only after
the conclusion of hostilities in 1945 that it became practical to
transport wheat in the cargo spaces of a tanker. This eventuated
from the perfecting of a portable suction device which would re
move wheat and other grain by pneumatic action rather than
having to rely upon the conventional discharging equipment of the
"marine leg" with its endless chain of buckets and a conveyor belt
leading to the shoreside receptacles. Once the "vacuveyors" had
demonstrated their effectiveness, literally scores of tankers were

assigned to carrying grain. They were attractive to shippers because
the cargo tanks were comparatively small, the hatches were of
minimum size, and neither shifting boards nor feeders were need
ed. These advantages were translated into actual cash savings not
only in the cost of these fittings, but also in ship time. Modern
dry-cargo bulkers have compromised by installing quickly portable
shifting boards which are part of the ship's outfit, and can be set up
or removed in a short time, usually by the ship's crew.
Between the loss of iron ore and the keen competition for grain
cargoes, the owner of the conventional tramp has found it more
difficult to keep his ships employed, but has earned higher profits
during those times when the demand has been strong for the type
of tonnage he controls. It remains true that most ports of the world
have a limiting depth of between thirty and thirty-five feet, and it is
to these shallow harbors that the modern, efficient, and economical
tramps make their voyages.
Tramp shipping today requires, as does the entire steamship
industry, a higher degree of managerial skill than formerly, as well
as the tools of good management such as the computer, the satellite
relayed telephone, and the complex automation found more and

more aboard ships as owners seek to enhance their profit-making
capability by the use of sleepless and tireless monitoring devices.
This sophisticated type of supervision permits more effective con
trol of ship use, more accurate cost determination, and overall
superior performance. The essential requirement remains for a
keen awareness of where the business can be found and when the
freight rates are favorable for time charters rather than for voyage
charters, and only the skilled and careful owner is able to place his
ship where it will meet the demands of the industrial world. There
is now, and there always will be, a vital role for the tramp ship to play
in the continuing drama of the commercial community.

MORE than one maritime country, tramp ship
ping provides a substantial portion of national income. This is
especially true of Great Britain, the Scandinavian countries,
Greece, Italy, and Japan. No single country today dominates the
world's shipping trade as did England before 1914, but the British,
Norwegians, and Greeks are still among the leaders. To these
nations, sea carriage is an important source of foreign credits, and
seafaring a traditional occupation for their people.
This tradition of life at sea helps to explain how men-and
increasingly women, as careers at sea become available to them
can face patiently, courageously, and with spiritual satisfaction the
labors involved in tramp ship operation. A typical voyage is marked
by hard work and prolonged absence from the home port as the
ship finds employment in the "cross trades," i.e., on routes that
cross the oceans without touching the shores of home. In fact, it is
rather exceptional when the vessel is assigned a voyage back to the
land of her registry.
That protracted voyages are anything but unusual gives rise to a
variety of problems in management. There are, for instance, the
ever present necessities of fueling, provisioning, and putting the
ship into ports never before visited. The master must cope with
personnel changes occurring by reason of death, desertion, or
illness; if crews are repatriated periodically, there are significant
alterations in the composition of the ship's company. Although
what is carried nearly always is one of the commodities moving in
bulk, there still are cargo-loading problems to be solved. Port
entrance and clearance routines for remote or infrequently visited
places must be envisioned and anticipated. While some of these
details may be handled from the owner's office in the distant home
land, many of them inevitably are delegated to the master of the
the master of the

ship. Throughout the voyage, he must serve as the representative
of the owner, and thus becomes to a measurable extent the custo
dian of that often shadowy figure's fortunes.
The competitive nature of the tramp trade, previously de
scribed in some detail, is such that no permanent system of govern
ment subsidy has been developed in any country. A very interesting
and quite successful venture into this field was made by the British
government in 1935 when world shipping was critically depressed.
A law was passed setting up a fund of two million pounds sterling to
help British tramp operators, on condition that the industry devise
the means to administer the scheme. A Tramp Shipping Adminis
trative Committee was formed to work toward the goals of minimiz
ing domestic competition, improving freight rates and chartering
conditions, and promoting the fullest employment of British ships
in competition with vessels which received some form of govern
mental assistance. British tramps were rationed to prevent uneco
nomic competition, and through the efforts of cooperating owners
the rates of charter hire were fixed at levels which prevailed in
1934. These were sufficient only to keep the ship in operation,
without allowance for depreciation or interest. The stability that
resulted did improve market rates about fifteen percent in the first
year, even though the volume of cargo moving remained un
changed. The scheme was continued until 1938. No similar com
prehensive plan has been instituted in the post-World War II
decades.l
No undisguised subsidy is paid to tramp ships today; there are
no regulations governing where the ships shall go, or how many
voyages must be completed each year. Fleets vary in size from one
to many ships, depending upon the financial status of the individual
owners. In the Baltic region, small operators sometimes form an
association and empower a single manager to handle the ships as
though they belonged to one corporation.
Inasmuch as tramps spend most of their economic lives far away
from their ports of registry, owners do not maintain large offices,
crowded with hurrying clerks and noisy with business machines. It
is more likely that the typical tramp operator will have a small
headquarters where a few persons handle the details of ship move
ment and arrange future commitments. Although it is not precisely
applicable today, the old maxim of the Golden Age does indicate

The home office of the tramp relies upon brokers around the
world for representation in the constant search for cargoes. Daily,
and sometimes hourly, cables come from many regions with infor
mation or offers of business. Decisions are made and shipmasters,
agents, brokers, and governments are informed of what the owner
deems best in a wide variety of circumstances. Modern communica
tions have changed the trade to the extent that owners now make all
the major decisions, and the master no longer is expected to find
employment for his ship when a charter expires. The master,
however, must be a shrewd businessman as well as an excellent
seaman, a good administrator, an expert in personnel manage
ment, and a conscientious representative of his owners.

The competition mentioned earlier in the analysis of tramp
shipping manifests itself principally in the rates charged by dif
ferent shipowners for transporting the same commodities. A su
perficial glance at the reports of ship fixtures suggests that these
rates are established in a casual fashion. To the contrary, much
thought and skill are required in developing the rates of charter
hire. Fluctuations reflect the circumstances facing both owners and
charterers at the precise moment that a decision must be reached.
The first step in determining the price is to estimate the cost of
performing under the charter. Success or failure-both in the
sense of obtaining the business and in turning a profit from the
transaction-may hinge upon the difference of a few cents a ton.
The importance of the computer in establishing an acceptable rate
of charter hire has been mentioned already but deserves repeated
emphasis.
Of the numerous factors influencing the formation of freight
rates, it is generally acknowledged that the value of the commodity
has the greatest significance. In theory, the shipper of a ton of gold
is able to pay $1,000 for its transportation, while the exporter of
coal, which has a value at the mine of only $10 a ton, often cannot
accept a rate of $3 a ton. The economic reason for tramp shipping is
to provide the transportation required by those articles oflow value
exemplified by coal. To do this requires that daily the tramp ship
owner set freight rates which are low enough to encourage the
movement of goods yet high enough to cover the expense of
operating his ship, and ideally to yield at least a small profit.
Knowing his costs down to the smallest detail is one way in which
the owner attempts to achieve this objective. "Costs," in this connec
tion, means more than simply the obvious out-of-pocket expenses
involved in ship operation; also included must be the less conspicu
ous items such as amortization, interest, and overhead. For exam
ple, a general-purpose tramp with operating costs of $200 an hour
is chartered to carry a load of 15,000 tons of coal. Loading at the
rate of 500 tons an hour will take 30 hours. Only 200 tons are
discharged per

Some owners develop comprehensive tables of ship costs per
deadweight ton which include crew wages and subsistence, vessel
maintenance and repair, insurance, amortization, interest, and a
contribution toward overhead. Whether the ship is lying in port
waiting for assignment or steaming across the ocean, these items do
not vary substantially. The costs that do change with the employ
ment of the vessel are fuel, port fees, pilotage, towage, dockage and
wharfage, and cargo handling. When all costs are computed, the
owner should add a sum sufficient to cover unforeseen contin
gencies and to provide a profit. If the market is "strong," meaning
that there are many cargoes and few ships, these cost figures can be
used without trimming when negotiating for a charter. On the
other hand, if there are many ships and few cargoes, and the
market therefore is considered to be "weak," the owner must exer
cise the most exquisite judgment in cutting his estimates of cost to
meet the figures quoted by his competitors. Sometimes it is neces
sary to accept business at an actual loss rather than to incur the
expense oflaying up the ship.
Under a gross form voyage charter, for example, the owner of a
50,000-ton vessel chartered to carry coal from Hampton Roads to
Rotterdam for $14.00 a ton pays all costs out of that sum. Expenses
for loading and discharging the coal are $5.00 per ton. Actual ship
operating costs, including port time, are $7.00 per ton, so that on
the $14.00 rate, the owner's profit is $2.00, or $100,000 for the
voyage. Vessel costs are $12,000 per day; any delays in the ship's
passage, or unexpected increase in the cost of fuel or cargo han
dling reduce the margin of profit significantly.

cost and potential profit involved in a proposed voyage. Each ele

For instance, the speed of the ship can be related to the smoothness
of her hull and to the cost of fuel when purchased in various
bunkering ports. The rapidity with which the proposed cargo can
be handled in the ports of loading and discharge can have a major
bearing on the determination of the length of the voyage. The
actual number of tons of a given commodity which can be stowed
below decks is related to the amount of space needed to accommo
date one weight ton. Detentions may be individually unimportant,

but cumulatively can be disastrous. The willingness of longshore
men to work overtime or on holidays and religious festivals, delays
in putting the ship alongside the cargo-working berth, loss of time
from shortages of pilots or tugs in the harbor, and hours needed to
prepare the ship to accept the proposed load, can have a profound
effect on the profitability of the voyage. Providing this kind of
detailed information, set forth in terms of so much money per
hour, is justification for using the computer in making voyage
estimates.
In working out the finances of the voyage or voyages, the
computer can develop in any desired detail such things as these:
costs of the ship lying in port at anchor and at the berth working
cargo; costs of the ship steaming fully loaded at designed speed;
fuel consumption at different speeds and drafts; costs of fuel when
purchased at different points along the route, compared with the
time needed for refueling; port and harbor charges, with particular
reference to harbor dues on entering the port and accrued day by
day until departure; costs of loading and discharging the cargoes
contemplated for the complete voyage; and the costs of overtime
when cargo is being worked.
Once these data have been made available, it is possible to
develop a program by which the computer will determine facts of
this type concerning the proposed employment of the vessel: the
itinerary of the ship, showing for each port the arrival time, waiting
time, predictable lost time, and anticipated departure time; costs
for each port where cargo is worked, including stevedoring and
overtime expenses; and total costs of harbor dues and fees. Using
these basic figures, the computer can be programmed to provide
management with summaries of the cost to transport one ton or a
full shipload of cargo, the total revenue to be earned on the contem
plated voyage, and an analysis of the financial results of the planned
employment. This last presentation would include depreciation,
interest, overhead, ship operating costs, port charges, cargo-han
dling expense, and the net profit (or loss) at the offered rate of
compensation.

TANKER CHARTERING
At first glance, the process by which tankers are chartered
appears to be identical with that followed for dry cargo ships. That
is to say, rates, terms, and conditions are negotiated among the
interested parties, and when there is a meeting of minds, the deal is
closed. The pressures exerted by the availability of cargoes and
ships undeniably are the same, and therefore charter hire rates
fluctuate from day to day. Likewise, the ship operators must be
concerned with overall earnings if they are to cover out of pocket as
well as capital and overhead expenses.
When the actual practice of ship brokers specializing in tanker
chartering is examined, some interesting variations in the proce
dure emerge. The first, and by all odds the most conspicuous, is that
the ship fixture reports rarely, if ever, specify the rate in monetary
terms. Instead, the reports will read somewhat as follows:

nese flag, built 1979, WS 82.5.
Chiriqui Grande, Panama, to U. S. Gulf, May, 77,000 tons, dirty
(Tanker Copper Mountain), American flag, built 1964, AR 97.5.

for voyages between ports, as for instance from Houston to Rot

has been calculated to return $1,800 per voyage day for a standard
vessel, defined as a tanker of 19,500 deadweight tons, traveling at
14 knots and consuming 28 tons of high viscosity fuel oil per day at
sea. The $1,

The principle on which the resultant schedules of rates was erected

would receive the same net return per day after making allowances
for voyage expenses such as port charges, canal dues, and fuel costs.

The convenience of the system, as contrasted with the prewar
problem of negotiating each and every voyage individually, includ

Using the schedule, which applied to a standard T-2 tanker of
16,500 tons, with a speed of 14.5 knots and burning 30 tons of

heavy fuel oil per day, was much more efficient and a great time
saver. As ships increased in deadweight tonnage and in perform

The tanker trade between American ports is restricted by law to
ships built, owned, and registered in the United States. The con
venience of the rate scale in international movements was sufficient
to justify developing a similar system for the domestic trade. When
it was introduced in 1956, the compendium was known as the
American Tanker Rate Schedule (ATRS). With periodic updating
and appropriate modifications, including shortening the name to
American Rates (AR), the schedule is still in use. (Worldscale does
include many American coastwise voyages, but is rarely invoked by
brokers.)
In practice, therefore, brokers for cargo interests and the ship
owner will negotiate from the Worldscale or the American sched
ules, and, depending upon market conditions, will agree upon a
rate which is either the published figure or a deviation, upward or
downward, from that level. Variations from the base rate reflect the
demand for ships, the availability of cargoes, the particular voyage
proposed, the ships to be used, and any unusual charges the ship
owner may be called upon to defray.
Because of the demonstrated economy of using a single large
ship to carry a load as compared with assigning the cargo to two or
more smaller ships, it is not uncommon in tanker chartering for the

recession of 1975-1980, these big vessels were fixed at WS 18 and
WS 25, meaning that the owners were accepting reductions of 82

When the negotiating parties have agreed, the rate is set in

It should be noted that it is not feasible to prepare similar rate

Although tramp ship operation continues today as an indis
pensable adjunct of international oceanborne commerce, the ships
which carry the cargoes are very different indeed from the plod
ding coal-burners of that fabled Golden Age of Steam which ended
in 1914. Today not only are the vessels larger and faster, but they
are superior in every way to their progenitors. They also are very
much more costly, and therefore management of these ships is
more exacting and requires the support of the finest managerial
tools. No matter how much the design and supervision of the ships
may have changed, however, the burden of performance rests
today, as it always has rested, upon the hard working personnel
who take the ships across the seas and assure that the terms of the
charter-parties are carried out efficiently and effectively. Although
the salt-rimed and sea-weary tramp described so eloquently by
Joseph Conrad, William McFee, and H. M. Tomlinson has disap
peared into the mists of history, the seamen who make tramp
shipping possible are still of that same heroic and honorable cast
which these great writers so justly celebrated.

A Liner-Service Company
EVERY steamship company, regardless of nationali
ty or location of corporate headquarters, is organized to meet its
own particular needs and its own specialized functions, and there
fore no uniform pattern of organization exists in the workaday
world of shipping. Nevertheless, the functions of the different
officials, by whatever title they may be known, and however they
may fit into their individual companies, are sufficiently similar to
permit their identification within the corporate structure.
At the top of the pyramid is the Board ofD irectors, usually made
up of persons who have a financial or managerial interest in the
company. The board may consist of from five to twenty or more
people elected by the stockholders and responsible to them for
proper management of the business. Always included as a voting
member of this board is the chairman. Increasingly, in American
corporate practice, this person also is the chief executive officer,
meaning that he takes an active part in the affairs of the company
and makes major decisions within the authority conferred upon
him by the board. The president of the company, who in modern
American business also serves as the chief operating officer, is
exactly what that descriptive title indicates, and therefore is a mem
ber of the board. The treasurer, as the financial advisor, and the
secretary, who keeps the minutes of the meetings and authenticates
all official documents, very often serve as members of the board. In
all matters of magnitude, especially those involving massive ex
penditures (as, for instance, the purchase or construction of ships,
or entering into or withdrawing from a trade route) and the selec
tion of senior executives, the board makes the final decisions.
The President, as the chief operating officer, is responsible to the
board for the proper functioning of the entire organization. He
may have come up through the ranks of the company, or he may
may

have been brought in at or near the top. Because he is the supervi
sor of all activities, he does not become involved for any protracted
period of time in the working of any specific division, although his
advice in those areas where he has specialized knowledge may be
sought by the staff. As ships and their supporting operations have
become more expensive through the years, the office of the presi
dent inexorably has been concerned primarily with the financial
aspects of the company, and a primary consideration in the choice
of a president is the soundness of financial judgments he has made
in difficult circumstances.
The demands upon his time imposed by these fiscal burdens
have resulted in the president delegating much of the supervision
of daily activity to the Executive Vice-President, who may be described
accurately as the chief of staff. It is his responsibility to see that the
policies promulgated by the board and the president are carried
out. Within the scope of his authority, he makes all appropriate
decisions and sends to the president's desk only those matters
requiring special consideration. He is able to assume the duties of
the president whenever that official is absent from his office, and in
this capacity as "alternate president" must be as well informed as
the president about the affairs of the company.
The Secretary maintains the official records of the corporation,
supervises transfers and issuance of stock certificates (if the com
pany is publicly held), accepts service oflegal papers drawn against
the corporation, and can represent it in any court when identifica
tion of records or other similar data is an issue. He also is responsi
ble for preparing the annual report to the stockholders, usually in
conjunction with the treasurer and the executive vice-president.
Many of the secretary's duties involve legal matters, and conse
quently it is not unusual that he (or she) is a lawyer. Should it be
consistent with company policy, the legal section (sometimes known
as the house counsel) may be placed under his (or her) supervision.
This important segment of the organization usually consists of one
or more lawyers who provide legal advice, comment on the signifi
cance of court decisions and the impact of new laws, assist trial
attorneys in preparing court cases, and take part in negotiations
where interpretation of contract terms may be needed.

Analyzing the significance of accounts and supervising the op

today recognize the need for qualified specialists in this area, and
have established the office of Comptroller to handle all aspects of
fiscal control. This officer is assisted by the auditors, who oversee
accounting procedures and inspect financial records. In general
terms, the comptroller supervises expenditures in accordance with
the budget while overseeing routines of fiscal administration. In
smaller companies, the treasurer performs the duties of the comp

endeavor, and in those organizations where it occurs with some
frequency, full responsibility for this activity, with authority to
make final commitments, is assigned to a vice-president. Regardless
of title or location within the corporate structure, the official han
dling charters must keep abreast of the employment of the com
pany fleet and the potential demand for additional tonnage or the
development of a surplus. As circumstances warrant, he provides
extra ships or finds charters for those which are temporarily
redundant.

Aside from chartering, the functions of the officials described
above are those of the senior executives of any corporation. Essen
tial to their success are high moral character, inspiring leadership,
and sound business judgment. It is an advantage if these officials
have the widest possible familiarity with the maritime industry,
since this will assure them of respect in the business community
while providing a sound foundation for their decisions.
Maritime transportation is a business with specialized aspects,
but is neither unique as an economic enterprise nor is it without a
commercial counterpart. It exists to make a profit, and must sell its
product (transportation) to the public in precisely the same way that
the tire manufacturing industry must find markets for automobile
and truck tires. Terminology differs, of course, but the realities of
competition, cost, plant modernization, and promotion are as clear
ly defined in the shipping firm as in any manufacturing company.
The techniques of management are, in their essentials, the same as
in other forms of business. Circumstances and factors influencing
the activities of a steamship company often are remote from, and
completely beyond the control of, the maritime community, but
even here there are similarities with other types of commercial
enterprise.
As a case in point, the traffic department of the liner-service
company has the same goals as the sales division of a tire man
ufacturer. Both must sell their respective products, transportation
and tires. The techniques of salesmanship, adapted to the maritime
industry, can be applied successfully to "merchandizing" transpor
tation. The vice-president, traffic, is responsible for keeping a
constant flow of cargo coming to the ships just as the director of
sales must find buyers for the tires.
The operating department of a shipowning corporation should
be viewed in a similar manner, for it bears striking resemblance to
the production division of a manufacturing concern. Just as the
production vice-president is required to oversee all details relating
to the manufacture of the rubber tires previously mentioned, and
must adjust output to meet the requirements of the sales force, so
the vice-president in charge of marine operations must insure that
the ships are kept in good condition, on schedule, and in all respects
able to provide the service promised by the salesmen to the shippers.

must adjust output to meet the requirements of the sales force, so
the vice-president in charge of marine operations must insure that
the ships are kept in good condition, on schedule, and in all respects

In shipping as in manufaturing, the traffic (sales) and operating

(production) departments are mutually complementary and inter
dependent. The transportation salesmen must be assured that
ships will be available to lift the cargoes they procure; the operating
department must have the cargoes to fill the ships they have
brought into port. As one executive explained: "The best traffic
department in the world cannot survive without a good operating
department; the finest operating group has no reason for existence
unless it is supported by a good sales force."
TRAFFIC DEPARTMENT
The Vice-President, Traffic, directs the department
charged with generating the cargo to fill the company ships. He
reports to the president through the executive vice-president,
keeping both these officials informed on all matters related to both
outbound and inbound cargo. Within his department, the vice
president, traffic, sets policies to achieve the goals assigned by the
president and the board of directors. As an expert on traffic, he
may be called upon to work with carriers to solve matters of mutual
concern, or to consult with important shippers whose problems are
of magnitude so great that they merit attention from an executive
of his stature.
It is difficult to describe completely the responsibilities of the
vice-president, traffic. He must spend much time conferring with
his fellow executives, especially from the operating and chartering
departments, as to the proper scheduling of ships, seasonal changes
in demand for shipping space, better employment of the fleet,
improvements in design for projected new or modernized tonnage,
plans for the acquisition or disposition of vessels, and ways and
means of minimizing stevedoring expense. He also deals with the
claims agent, the insurance manager, and the financial managers to
develop better ways to handle claims for compensation for dam
aged or lost cargo. From time to time he will confer with the
terminal manager and the stevedore to consider techniques of
cargo handling which might lead to fewer claims. Now and again he
will be involved in formulating, with the comptroller, freight cash
ier, and vice-president for finance a policy dealing with the collec

that access to the terminal is satisfactory, that control procedures

company promises to shippers and consignees. As the patterns of
business place greater emphasis on intermodal transportation, he
must devote time to the development of this aspect, especially in
establishing freight rates payable to railroad and motor carriers.
Outside of the company, the vice-president, traffic, may serve as
a member of an industry group studying ways to improve packag
ing of goods or to standardize practices of booking full container
loads of cargo. Making rates which will cover the costs of inland
transportation, and which therefore must be acceptable to rail
roads, trucking contractors, and the government regulatory
bodies, consumes much of his time.
There are occasions when the vice-president, traffic, will be part
of a group from the steamship industry seeking ways to prevent a
disastrous freight rate war. Perhaps a new set of freight charges is
under discussion, and the need to increase revenue must be con
sidered in the light of pronouncements that higher rates will result
in these commodities being priced out of the market.
If the company belongs to an association of steamship lines
which regulates competition and sets uniform freight rates, the
vice-president, traffic, may represent his organization at times
when a firm commitment to a certain principle or policy is required.
He also may be part of a special committee of the association
responsible for adjustment of freight rates to meet changing condi
tions and shippers' requests. In addition to these "troubleshooting"
assignments, the vice-president must always be alert to better ways
to carry out his mission, to gain larger shares of the available
business, and to augment company profits.
The Freight Traffic Manager is the deputy to the vice-president,
traffic, and is qualified to substitute for that executive when he is
absent for any reason. He is the supervisor of the freight traffic
department and assures that departmental policies are carried out
in the most effective manner. He considers shippers' requests for
special calls at ports not on the regular schedule or to transport
large quantities of unusual cargo, and makes appropriate recom
mendations to higher authority when necessary. Troublesome
bookings, as, for example, unexpectedly large offerings for a ship

in the most effective manner. He considers shippers' requests for
special calls at ports not on the regular schedule or to transport
large quantities of unusual cargo, and makes appropriate recom
mendations to higher authority when necessary. Troublesome
bookings, as, for example, unexpectedly large offerings for a ship

already almost filled, or proposals to delay a ship's sailing to accom
modate a customer, also are referred to him.
Immediately under the freight traffic manager is the General
Freight Agent, who directs the salesmen (sometimes called solicitors)
and handles departmental administration. Salesmen are the con
tacts between the carrier and the shipping public; upon their ability
to convince these clients that the company deserves their patronage
depends its prosperity. The coordination of their efforts, and the
establishment of policies with regard to sales, are of great impor
tance, and represent a major part of the general freight agent's
work. He supervises the day-to-day visitations made by the sales
men, suggests approaches to difficult customers, and makes sure
that the capabilities of the company are set forth correctly. When
his subordinates make suggestions which have merit, but which
involve changes in departmental or company policy, he transmits
these suggestions, together with his recommendations, to the ap
propriate executives. As he obtains information which may be
useful in selling the services of the company, he calls in his sales staff
and develops with them ways to use this knowledge to induce
shippers to give their business to the company. Clients who benefit
by this effort may become supporters of the line since they ap
preciate that these salesmen often bring suggestions which, if ac
cepted, can be financially advantageous to that shipper.
In addition to these responsibilities, the general freight agent
directs the keeping of records which show the business received
from individual shippers, the seasonal variations in the volume of
cargo offered by shippers and in the tonnage carried by the ships,
and also comparisons between voyages and calendar periods.
These records have many uses. They may furnish data for some
governmental agency concerned with international shipping. Per
haps the president has directed that certain aspects of traffic activity
be analyzed; the most readily available information would be in
these statistical records. Should a traffic study (a forecast of future
business trends, based on past experience and present practice) be
in progress, the data from these records could be of major impor
tance. They also may suggest to the reviewing official trends in
traffic which have not been obvious to the less diligent examiner,
and which have great potential for increasing business.

The statistical section's reports show the volume of business
handled, revenue earned, demands for service to named ports, the
desirability of certain commodities in the light of the cost of han
dling them, and the frequency with which claims for damage are
made. These reports are circulated to the senior executives, the
comptroller, the operating department, and any other officials who
may require them, and are useful as the basis for judgments relat
ing to all aspects of freight traffic.
An important activity of the general freight agent is to maintain
close contact with the claims division to learn what commodities and
what shippers are involved in claims for damages and the probable
causes of the alleged damage as well as the validity of the claims.
As the departmental administrative officer, the general freight
agent makes routine and special assignments, sets up training pro
grams for new members of the department, transfers persons
within the department for most efficient use of their capabilities,
recommends promotions when earned, and dismissals when neces
sary. Incidental to these supervisory functions, the general freight
agent maintains appropriate personnel records.
The freight traffic department is divided into two major seg
ments, the Outward Freight Department and the Inward Freight Depart
ment, of which the outward is by far the larger. The chief of each
branch usually holds the rank of assistant freight traffic manager,
and reports to the freight traffic manager.
The Booking Clerk is a senior member of the outward depart
ment and controls the space in a break-bulk cargo ship, allocating
that space to individual shippers as they make their requests. He
obtains his basic information from the operating department which
informs him of the amount of fuel, water, stores, and equipment to
be aboard the ship on the proposed voyage, and the actual space, in
cubic feet, and capacity, in tons, available for cargo. As reservations
for space in a break-bulk vessel are received, the booking clerk
computes the stowage factors and allots the required number of
cubic feet. The salesmen work closely with the booking clerk to
assure that customers are extended the treatment they have been
promised. Conversely, when the booking clerk finds that he needs
either high-revenue or dense cargo, he often appeals to the sales
men to assist him in making a balanced load by arranging visits to
