Beside the cruise director, other "supernumeraries" in the
ship's complement include musicians, professional entertainers (of
ten hired directly from well-known nightclubs or variety shows, and
at the same compensation they receive for shoreside engagements),
lecturers, photographers, and in some ships a clergyman who
serves as the ship's chaplain. Lecturers and chaplains normally
travel as guests of the ship, exchanging their professional services
for the cruise.

More and more, as other opportunities to experience the plea
sure of a sea voyage as part of international travel become less
available, cruises are gaining in popularity. Not only do they carry
the passenger to overseas points, but they offer a completely dif
ferent style of life for the duration of the voyage. As floating
vacations, cruises demand specialized management, and to meet
this demand corporations have been formed for the express pur
pose of designing, building, owning, and running ships that cater to
that fortunate group of people who find a way to make a cruise and
to enjoy the "thrill of a lifetime."27

IN
C L U D ED in the thousands of vessels that collective
ly compose the mercantile marine of the world are many fleets
which, because of highly individualistic employment or very spe
cialized design, belong to one of two categories of shipping. The
first of these, the industrial carriers, serve the needs of particular
industrial enterprises, while the second, the special carriers, meet the
demands peculiar to certain types of cargo.
Industrial carriers are those ships that exist as part of the plant
and transportation properties oflarge industrial organizations and
are operated exclusively for them. The huge fleet of tankers main
tained by Exxon Corporation, the largest oil company in the world,
typifies this category. The only purpose of this globe-girdling ag
gregation of ships is to provide the transoceanic transportation
essential to the life of the parent concern. There are no other users
to be considered by the owners, and no obligations to be met except
those laid down by Exxon Corporation, which has full responsibil
ity and control.
Other ships, like the refrigerated fruit carriers or the auto
mobile transporters, are owned by steamship companies that are
not affiliated with any industrial activity but are built to carry a
certain cargo with greatest efficiency and economy. These ships are
the special carriers; they are made available, either under charter
or in regular berth service, to those users who must send their
goods across the oceans. For reasons of their own, these users do
not desire to become owners and operators of ships and are satis
fied to benefit from the capability without having to accept the
responsibilities and burdens of ownership.
It is apparent that many ships appropriately designated as in
dustrial carriers are designed to transport a single commodity and
therefore may be considered as both special and industrial carriers.

There is nothing contradictory in this finding, so long as the princi
ples underlying the reasons for the existence of these ships are
understood.
INDUSTRIAL CARRIERS
The industrial carrier is defined as the marine transpor
tation link in the process of manufacture or distribution (or both) of
the materials used or produced by an industrial organization. Some
carriers handle nothing but raw materials, and others transport
only the finished goods, while still others may be used
interchangeably.
It must be pointed out that some industrial carriers serve a
one-way trade, and as a consequence the parent concern may place
the ship in berth service, or on voyage charter, for the return trip.
The economic reason for this action is to reduce the cost of ship
operation, and to eliminate, if possible, the need to sail ships in
ballast on nonrevenue producing voyages.
The Broken Hill Proprietary, of Australia, operates a fleet of
eighteen bulk carriers and two specialized roll-on/roll-off steel car
riers. The bulkers haul raw materials to company steelworks; occa
sionally they are dispatched to Southeast Asia. The roll-on/roll-off
ships move semifinished and finished steel products from plants to
customers in Australia and across the Tasman Sea. An understand
ing of the magnitude of this operation is derived from the fact that
the annual cost thereof exceeds one hundred and fifty million
dollars.l
Crown-Zellerbach Corporation, the paper manufacturing and
distributing organization based in San Francisco, California, has
two specialized ships under long-term charter to haul newsprint
from Scandinavia and Canada to California ports. Serving only the
charterers, these ships are classified correctly as industrial carriers.
Exxon Corporation, already mentioned, at the end of 1984
operated a fleet of 104 ships of its own and about fifty additional
units chartered from other sources. Ranging in size from 3,800 tons
to 516,423 tons deadweight, this is one of the largest tanker fleets in
the world. A complete vessel operating department exists within
the Exxon corporate structure to control and administer this fleet.
United Brands, the banana-growing and distributing company
domiciled in the United States, owns a fleet of eleven refrigerated

units chartered from other sources. Ranging in size from 3,800 tons
to 516,423 tons deadweight, this is one of the largest tanker fleets in
the world. A complete vessel operating department exists within
the Exxon corporate structure to control and administer this fleet.
United Brands, the banana-growing and distributing company
domiciled in the United States, owns a fleet of eleven refrigerated

ships for the sole purpose of providing the transportation required
to serve its markets.
The principal purposes served by the industrial carrier are:
1. To control delivery schedules of raw materials or finished
products (or both) handled by the parent concern.
2. To reduce the cost of ocean transportation by elimination of
the "middleman's" profit.
3. To provide efficient transportation to the destinations re
quired by the parent company for the type of cargo of particular
interest to it.
There is a heavy burden of expense and responsibility inherent
in the ownership and operation of a fleet of oceangoing vessels.
Only those corporations with a continuing need for transportation
of goods in shipload lots, or between ports not served by common
carriers, have found it profitable to establish and maintain indus
trial carrier service. The large investment of capital may deter some
companies from buying their own ships; instead, they resort to
-

A lumber carrier, Star Columbia depends upon her own gantry cranes for
fast dispatch. Photo: Munck International.

Top left: Mel-(lin H. Baker, a self-unloading bulk carrier. The port for the
conveyor is at the stern. Top right: Discharging conveyor extended
through stern port. Bottom left: Discharging coal to inland waterways
barges. Bottom right: Conveyor systems below cargo compartments. Pho-
tos: Nordstroms Marine Systems.
long-term chartering. It is the use to which the ship is put, rather
than the design or the ownership, which determines the classifica
tion of a vessel as an industrial carrier.
It is worth repeating that industrial carriers may be of a special
ized design, but only when this suits the needs of the industry they
serve. The fleet of Broken Hill Proprietary is an excellent exponent
of this principle. The roll-on/roll-off ships were designed for the
express purpose of transporting the long lengths and prefabricated
pieces of steel sold by the parent company to purchasers in differ
ent parts of Australia. No other ships could perform this task so well
or so economically.

The Rondeggen carried rolls of newsprint in her holds and packaged
lumber on deck. Three traveling gantry cranes assured fast cargo han
dling. Photo: Brenner, courtesy Crown Zellerbach.
Considerations of cost also may influence a company initially to
charter one or more ships of either conventional or specialized
type, depending upon what is required and what is available on the
market that is satisfactory for the intended purpose. As experience
is gained, and the economics of the situation may justify, ships of
appropriately specialized character may be acquired.
It has been noted above that one advantage of the industrial
carrier is that it gives to the parent company control over delivery
schedules. Vessels are dispatched in accordance with the needs of
the industry; there is no concern for possible customers who might
be upset by sudden changes in sailing times, ports of call, or space
allocations within the ship. To companies like Exxon, United
Brands, Crown Zellerbach, and Broken Hill, which must depend
upon ships to bring in materials indispensable to their operations,
this factor alone justifies the maintenance of controlled fleets. The
fruit company also has flexibility in routing its ships to those ports
where the demand for bananas is at the maximum. In this way, it
satisfies the demands of its retail merchant-customers as well as
capitalizing on opportunities to sell the bananas at the highest
pnces.
Two other advantages accrue to the owner of an industrial
carrier. One is the lower cost arising from elimination of the profit
seeking shipping organization, while the other is the independence
of the ship charter market conferred upon the parent industry by
having a fleet already under its control. The aggregate savings from

Gantry crane with specialized lifting device and clear plastic overhead
panels handles newsprint safely in any weather. Photo: Munck
International.
these factors, tangible and otherwise, often outweigh the cost of
owning and managing the fleet.
Finally, it was noted that an advantage to the parent concern of
the industrial carrier is that it provides efficient and careful trans
portation for the proprietary cargoes. As experience is gained by
the operator of an industrial carrier in handling one or more
commodities, many cost-saving and profit-producing techniques

The diesel-powered ore-bulk-oil carrier Furness Bridge (built 1971) had a
deadweight of 166,064 tons and a speed of 15.5 knots. Piping for oil
cargoes lies outboard ofthe hatches with their thwartships sliding covers.
Photo: Ralston, courtesy Furness Withy Group.

are certain to be developed, eventually culminating in highly effec
tive, efficient, and economical methods.
For these reasons, industrial carriers are justified. The princi
ples are not violated by using chartered ships, so long as the charter
er maintains the same complete control over the ships' activities as if
he had title to those vessels.
SPECIALIZED CARRIERS
One of the more interesting, and certainly significant,
trends in mercantile shipping during the twentieth century has
been the development of specialized carriers, which are found
today on practically all sea routes. Their numbers and variety
increase annually, and bear witness to their ever growing
importance.
The specialized ship is one designed for the express purpose of
carrying, usually in shipload lots, a particular type of cargo, either
in bulk or in containers of stipulated size. A specialized ship thus
may be constructed for the exclusive carriage of alumina; a com
pletely different design would be needed for a vessel hauling auto
mobiles and trucks.
Among the many types of specialized carriers are ships built to
transport bauxite, bulk cement, chemicals in liquid form, coal, iron
ore, liquefied natural gas, newsprint and other paper products,
petroleum and its by-products, refrigerated fruits and meats, wood
chips, and wood pulp.
The significant feature, by which a ship employed in this man
ner is assigned to the category of a specialized ship, is the design, as
distinguished from the industrial carrier, which is classified accord
ing to the use to which it is put.
Although transportation by water is the most economical means
of movement ever devised by man, there is no single commodity for
which the individual cost of carriage does not constitute, in some
measure, a barrier to its ready sale in the markets of the world. The
carrier is entitled to be compensated for his services, but the ship
per demands that this compensation be kept at the lowest possible
level. To satisfy this requirement has called for the exercise of
amazing ingenuity on the part of the shipowner, the naval architect,
and the shipbuilder. Particularly in the second half of the twentieth

the ship
per demands that this compensation be kept at the lowest possible
level. To satisfy this requirement has called for the exercise of
amazing ingenuity on the part of the shipowner, the naval architect,
and the shipbuilder. Particularly in the second half of the twentieth

The starkly utilitarian design of the Japanese automobile/truck carrier
Nada V is her dominant characteristic. Photo: Moran Towing Co.
century have the fruits of these endeavors become important in a
wide range of shipping operations, as one specialized design after
another has been created to transport commodities once consid
ered immovable, or to reduce the costs of carriage to levels previ
ously believed not to be feasible. Extraordinarily complex ships
have been built to provide safe and efficient, as well as economical,
transportation. Paralleling these achievements, and often contrib
uting to the success of the project, have been the successful attacks
on that age-old problem of the shipowner: to reduce the time
required to work the ship in port and send her back to sea.
Designed as she is to transport most efficiently a single commod
ity in shipload lots, the specialized carrier often succeeds in areas
where the conventional ship would be totally unsatisfactory. An
interesting demonstration of this thesis may be found in the trans
oceanic movement of liquefied natural and petroleum gas. Efforts
to transport these by-products of the oil fields which were then, and
still are, in great demand, began in the 1950s, but it was not until
1960 that a commercially practicable method of handling these

cargoes was brought to perfection. The first full scale experiments
involved the shipment of methane, which becomes liquid when
cooled to -162° Celsius (-265° Fahrenheit). One of the many
distinctive features of liquefied gas, insofar as its carriage by ship is
concerned, is its bulkiness; one naval architect estimated that it
occupied about four times the space of an equivalent tonnage of
petroleum. Special ballast tanks to bring the ship down to her
normal draft were needed.2
A small dry-cargo ship was converted into a liquid methane
carrier in 1958. The Methane Pioneer used a "wool" made from balsa
wood as the principal insulation for the cargo tanks. The experi
ment was so successful that about two years later the Bridgestone
Maru, a tanker of 25,626 tons deadweight, was built particularly to
haul liquefied gas. She was assigned to the supply route from
Indonesia to Japan. Her performance validated many theories
relating to the technique of moving liquefied gases.3
As experience was gained with the pioneering ships, significant
advances were made in the design, metallurgy, and insulation of the
tanks in which these cargoes were carried. Beginning in 1962, a
succession of improved and enlarged gas carriers was put into
service. As if to prove that the movement of liquefied gas could
become an entirely routine and uneventful activity, the Polar Alaska
and the Arctic Tokyo, each with a capacity of 71,645 cubic meters of
liquid gas, completed more than 110 round trips between Alaska
and Yokohama in the six years that ended on May 31, 1976.4
In September 1975, the 125, OOO-cubic meter E l Paso Paul Kayser
was delivered by her builders, Chantiers de France - Dunkerque.
This twenty-knot, turbine-driven vessel was 280.62 meters long,
41.60 meters in beam, and had a draft of 11 meters. The six cargo
tanks were encased with heavy insulation to hold the cargo at -165°
Celsius. Boilers supplying steam to the 45,000-horsepower turbines
were equipped not only to burn oil but also to accept the gas that
"boiled off

Chantiers de France - Dunkerque.
This twenty-knot, turbine-driven vessel was 280.62 meters long,
41.60 meters in beam, and had a draft of 11 meters. The six cargo
tanks were encased with heavy insulation to hold the cargo at -165°
Celsius. Boilers supplying steam to the 45,000-horsepower turbines
were equipped not only to burn oil but also to accept the gas that
"boiled off' from the cargo. To provide maximum safety, each
cargo tank was isolated by cofferdams at the forward and after
ends, by wing tanks on each side, and by a double bottom. The wing
tanks could be used for ballast water, and provision was made to
heat this water in the event of cargo leakage to prevent the exces
sively cold gas from damaging the intrinsic properties of the steel in
the hull structure.5

text:
The packaged-lumber carrier Emma Johanna was equipped with six cen
terline cranes to assure rapid cargo-handling. Photo: Jeff Blinn, courtesy
Moran Towing Co.
Considered to be among the most complex of ship designs,
these liquefied natural gas carriers were enormously expensive to
build. The contracts for the first vessels of this type to be built in the
United States were signed in 1972, and the price was just over 100
million dollars for each of three. By the fall of 1980, the price had
risen to approximately 155 million dollars. There was sufficient
demand for the gas, however, to justify construction worldwide of a
fleet which, at the end of 1980, numbered 65 liquefied natural gas
carriers of 5,400,000 cubic meters total capacity, and 568 liquefied
petroleum gas carriers, with an aggregate of 6,500,000 cubic me
ters of cargo tank space.
An example, although somewhat old, of developing a special
type of ship to meet the peculiar demands of an industry was
presented in 1956 with the entry into service of the Duncan Bay.
This 20,000-ton deadweight capacity tanker was built to carry wood
pulp which had been loaded in a wet state (approximately one-third
pulp to two-thirds water), and after the water was pumped out of
the tanks, was transported from British Columbia to California.
There the pulp was resaturated to a consistency of 98 percent water

To assure uncontaminated handling of many different types of chemicals
at one time, an intricate web of cargo pipes is essential. Photo: Moss
Rosenberg Shipbuilders.
and 2 percent pulp, so that it could be pumped into "desaturation"
tanks before being stored. The ultimate paper product was im
proved through elimination of the process by which the pulp was
dried at the mill before shipping. At the same time, the cost of
handling was reduced by the mechanized loading and discharging
arrangement. Special features incorporated into the ship's design
were turbine-driven pumps for the dilution water, agitators to
blend and keep the pulp in solution during the unloading opera
tion, and nine high capacity pumps to transfer the pulp from the
twelve cargo tanks.6
In the construction and long-term charter of the Norwegian
motors hips Besseggen and Rondeggen are seen examples of the pro
cedure by which an industrial shipper will obtain the use of a
specialized ship without investing a substantial amount of his own
capital or establishing a marine department to operate the ships.
Crown Zellerbach Company wanted a ship to carry 5,500 tons of

This modern chemical tanker has thirty-five piping arrangements. Four
deck-mounted tanks accommodate small lots of specialized cargo. Photo:
Stolt-Nielsen, Inc.
newsprint in rolls stowed below decks and 1,000 tons of packaged
lumber on deck. High-speed loading and discharging in any kind
of weather was required. A Norwegian shipowner agreed to build
the ships with the stipulation that they be time chartered for a major
part of the anticipated life of the vessels.
Acting in concert, the charterer, owner, designer, and builder
produced a noteworthy solution to the problem. The engine and
bridge were located at the after end of the ship, to provide the deck
space for the packaged lumber and to facilitate operation of three
gantry cranes installed on rails extending the length of the weather
deck. The cranes were equipped with hydraulically operated,
hinged jibs to provide long outreach over the ship's sides when
loading or discharging. A rack-and-pinion driven trolley traveled
athwartships on rails welded to the main girders and jibs, and could
function despite noticeable list or tilt of the ship. A permanent,

The chemical tanker has a complex piping system, double bottom, double
skin, and cofferdams separating the numerous cargo tanks. Photo: Stolt
Nielsen, Inc.
semitranslucc::nt weather cover over the main girders provided the
mandatory protection against rain and snow, and the sides of the
cranes had curtains to complete the "all weather" protection. The
cranes weighed 126 tons each, and had a lifting capacity of 30,000
pounds. Special yokes were devised to accommodate eight rolls of
newsprint simultaneously, and another attachment was developed
to handle the lumber. The cyclic rate of cargo work was 1,000 tons
per hour; experience showed that about 750 tons per hour rep
resented the practical maximum. A minimum number of long
shoremen was required for the cargo-handling operation.
These two highly specialized ships proved to be both economi
cal and efficient. Much of their success could be attributed to the
cranes, which were of unique design and utility, very heavy, and
quite expensive. It was reported that they cost $196,000 apiece
when the ships were delivered at the end of 1962; an investment

which would make the general service carrier look critically at any
benefits which were expected to redound to him?
In many parts of the world, there is a continuing demand for
cement in very large quantities. For decades, it was impossible to
ship this commodity in bulk and to discharge it with the self-unload
ing equipment installed in coal and ore carriers. Cement is ex
tremely fine and powdery in its composition, packs easily, and has a
very high angle of repose. Mechanical discharge required that the
cement flow to the conveyors, a movement eventually achieved by
pumping compressed air into the mass. Using this principle, en
gineers developed several self-unloading mechanisms by which
ships carrying cement in bulk could discharge their cargoes effi
ciently and economically.
When she was delivered to her owners in 1981, the Castillo de
Javier was the largest self-unloading bulk cement carrier in the
world. She was a vessel of 44,000 metric tons deadweight, and had
six holds. Two of these holds were exceptionally large and were
intended for the cement cargoes. Transverse screw conveyors
moved the cargo to each side of the hold where the cement fell
through valve-operated trap doors into pipeways laid in the double
bottoms. Vacuum pumps sucked the cement out of the ship in two
cycles, one from the hold to a reloader chamber, and the other from
that chamber to the shoreside silo. By means of this system, the ship
could be emptied at the rate of 600 tons an hour. The builders
claimed that the mechanism they devised made it possible to carry
not only bulk cement but also low density commodities like flour or
any granular or pulverized material. A further advantage of the
pipeway system was that the tank tops were flat and easy to clean,
thereby making it feasible to carry different types of cargo on the
return voyage. The ship's utility was enhanced by the three twenty
ton cranes so mounted that they served all six hatches.8

One of the reasons that cargo liner operators put specialized
ships into their services is that it assures them of a segment of the
business which, but for this capability, would be denied to them
altogether. Often the special capability applies to cargo moving
only in one direction, as in the case of meats, bananas, and other
perishable fruits, and vegetables brought to consuming countries in
ever increasing quantities. On the return passage, these specialized
carriers offer to carry any kind of general cargo that will not
damage the expensive equipment of the vessel or interfere unduly
with the schedules of the homebound perishables. It must be noted,
in passing, that the stipulation by the owner or operator that only
the specialized cargo will be accepted does not change the common
carrier status of the line.
A large fleet of refrigerated ships has been built since the end of
World War II, both by liner companies and by independent owners
who seek long-term charters from importers of refrigerated goods.
Most of the independent (tramp) "reefers" are owned by Euro
pean, and particularly by Scandinavian, operators. The liner com
panies running reefers are of many nationalities and are found on
numerous trade routes.

RANGING in size from enormous to almost tiny,
transporting more tons of cargo of direct concern to more people
in more parts of the world than any other type of ship afloat,
tankers have become indispensable to the modern international
industrial economy. As vital components of the merchant marine,
tankers require many of the same managerial skills needed by any
other type of ships engaged in moving cargoes across the seas.
Dedicated to the movement of liquid commodities in bulk, how
ever, these vessels demand specialized knowledge and techniques
both from the personnel who take them to sea and those on shore
who supervise their activities.
In the age-old history of shipping, transporting oil in bulk is a
relatively new enterprise. The first steamship designed and built to
carry petroleum in bulk, rather than in wooden barrels or metal
drums was put into service in 1886.1 This was the Glilckauf ("Good
Luck"), built in England to the order of Wilhelm A. Riedemann, a
merchant of Hamburg, to serve the German-American Petroleum
Company.2 She was a small ship, 300 feet long with a deadweight of
3,020 tons-hardly noticeable alongside today's gigantic crude oil
carriers. Her place in history, however, derives from the fact that
she was the prototype of the world's tankers, with steam driven
pumps segregated from the cargo tanks by steel bulkheads, and
engine-room at the after end, separated from the cargo tank area
by a cofferdam formed by twin bulkheads. This pattern of con
struction, it is appropriate to note, has not altered significantly over
the years.

Since the GlUckauf was launched, bulk oil carriers have multi
plied in numbers, increased in speed and, most conspicuously,
grown enormously in size. Change was slow at first; as late as 1920,
the standard tanker had a deadweight of only some 12,000 tons,
although there were a few vessels of about 20,000 tons.3 In 1939, a
small group of 16,000-tonners was in operation, but the majority of
tanker-owning companies still leaned toward the "handy-sized"
ships of 12,000 tons. It is a minor footnote to history that the
average speed of all these ships was about eleven knots, compared
to the GlUckaufs ten.
The demands for transportation of petroleum during World
War II greatly exceeded the capability of the prewar fleet and called
forth new standards for tankers. Bigger and faster ships were
essential, and the United States built 532 oil carriers of the T-2 class.
With a deadweight of about 16,750 tons and a speed of 14.5 knots,
these ships proved incontrovertibly that large, fast oil carriers were
economical, efficient, and as versatile as the handy-sized tankers of
12,000 tons.4
Once the utility of the T-2 had been demonstrated, growth
became characteristic of the tanker-operating industry. In 1947,
the first of the really big ships were built. These "colossal" vessels of
25,000 to 27,000 tons deadweight were relegated quickly to lesser
positions by the prompt advent of tankers of 32,000 tons and, very
shortly thereafter, of 45,000 tons. By 1979, the peak had been
reached with the completion of the Seawise Giant, a crude oil carrier
of 569,783 tons deadweight owned by the C. Y. Tung interests of
Hong Kong. Owing to a reduction in consumption of oil world
wide, the demand for the very large crude carriers decreased
markedly, and no building programs including ships as large as the
Seawise Giant have been initiated since then.5

As the size of ships increased, tanker owners showed more
interest in obtaining optimum performance, but had to wait for the
acceptance of computers as standard tools of management before
realizing significant progress. To illustrate how the capabilities of
the computer might be used by an operator, a study was conducted
in 1970 of the hypothetical employment under time charter of a
20-knot, 500,000-tons deadweight tanker making a round voyage
from the Arabian Gulf to Northwest Europe, a total distance of
22,614 miles. Fuel consumption for the big ship varied from 200
tons per day at a cruising speed of 14 knots to 790 tons per day at
the maximum of 20 knots. The cost of fuel oil, at the time the
computation was made, was $17.50 per ton. At the slowest speed,
the round voyage would take 67 days and would require 13,460
tons of fuel. At maximum speed, twenty days would be saved, but
fuel consumption would jump to 37,209 tons. Calculating the pos
sibilities for different cruising speeds, the computer showed that
ordering the ship to travel at 16.5 knots for the round voyage of 57
days, with a total consumption of 20,355 tons of oil would be the
most effective employment of the tanker. Assuming that the ship
were registered under a flag of convenience and had a crew paid
minimum wages, the owner could cover all expenses and have a
profit equal to 10 percent on the investment if charter hire were
fixed at $1.15 per deadweight ton per month. This equated to a
freight rate of $3.05 per ton of oil delivered.7

Maintaining the ships to the highest standards is essential if

discharging ports to accomplish the necessary work.

Another facet of the practice of installing machinery to permit
fewer personnel to operate the tanker is that a great deal of what
formerly was classified as "ship's work" to be performed only by
experienced seamen now is done by computer-controlled devices
or is transferred to shore-based artificers. The challenge and ro

took pride in the skills they had mastered over a period of time are
finding that the work they are assigned aboard ship no longer is
interesting or demanding. This means that the crews' morale is of
much greater significance to management than in former years,
and supervisors must make more opportunities for personal con
tact with the mariners who, in the final analysis, are the indispens
able element in the operation of tankers. I I
The problems of tanker management listed above bear witness
that operation of these ships has become more complex through
the years. It would be wrong, however, to conclude that these
problems make the transportation of petroleum and its derivatives
a unique type of shipping. It is specialized, but it is only one aspect
of the whole business of moving goods across the seas. The follow
ing facts support this premise.
Tankers, like other ships, must be built, maintained, and re
paired. Seamen must be obtained from the ranks of available sea
farers, and in competition with other ships which may offer more
attractive inducements to crewmen. Sailing, bunkering, and dry
docking schedules are based on the same fundamentals as for any
other merchant vessels. As tankers have become larger and faster
and have been equipped with more complicated machines and
control devices, there has been a corresponding increase in the
demand for better-trained seamen. Dry-cargo ships, especially con
tainer carriers, have concurrently been built with the same types of
complex mechanical installations, and they have just as much need
for the best and the most competent mariners they can hire. Ship
yards, especially those with repair docks able to accommodate the
enormous tankers of today, are available only in a comparatively
few ports of the world and are equally in demand by huge dry bulk
carriers and very large containerships.12 Time is money to the

It cannot be denied, however, that there are some aspects of
ship management which are peculiar to the tanker business.
Among these distinctive characteristics may be cited the nature and
inherent properties of petroleum and its derivatives, the specialized
terminals required for loading and discharging the ships, the nor
mally one-directional flow of traffic, and the integration of the
schedules of operation of refineries, distribution centers, and
tankers.
The fact that petroleum traffic flows only in one direction is of
major economic importance in analyzing the operation of tankers.
Except in unusual circumstances, the ships are engaged for a sig
nificant portion of their lives in expensive and genuinely nonpro
ductive voyages in ballast back to their loading ports. Various
expedients have been examined in the search for ways in which to
reduce the cost, both in time and in the usefulness of the ship. One
of the more successful was the combination carrier that could haul
dry bulk or ore or oil, depending upon the demand for transporta
tion of these commodities. The theory was that, by judicious sched
uling, after delivering a cargo of oil the ship could be chartered to
lift a cargo of grain or iron ore to a port not far from the oil loading
point, thereby virtually eliminating the ballast leg. The San Juan
Pioneer was one of the first ships of this type to be employed in
alternate trades. A typical voyage involved carrying oil from Suma
tra to Los Angeles; sailing in ballast to San Juan, Peru, to pick up a
full load of iron ore for Japan; and then proceeding in ballast to
Sumatra to start the cycle again. The passages from Los Angeles to
Sanjuan and from Japan to Sumatra were relatively short, and the
revenue from the ore cargoes improved the ship's annual profit
making capability. 13

The primary reason for an oil company to own its tankers

rather than to depend upon chartered tonnage is to assure that
transportation for its petroleum will be available when needed. A
secondary, and equally important, reason is to exert a moderating
influence upon the charter market in times of ship shortages, and to
prevent exploitation by the independents of a producer's obliga
tions to meet delivery schedules at all costs. Experience has shown
that an oil company can satisfy requirements if its proprietary fleet
can lift approximately 60 percent of the petroleum tonnage that
must move in one year. The third reason to own ships is to provide
transportation for special cargoes such as many grades oflubricat
ing oils, petrochemicals, and numerous small lots of a variety of
fuels, or to make deliveries to shallow draft ports. These sometimes
unusual assignments often cannot be met by the vessels available on
the charter market, and therefore owning the appropriate types of
tankers is the only solution for the oil company.

the oil company to design its tankers. It is true that, in the years
immediately following World War II, the ready availability ofT-2

to operate these ships. With the passage of time, the T-2 was
superseded by newer designs that met company needs more effec

loaded; capacity of pumps; number of pumping systems necessary
to deliver several grades of petroleum at the same time; numbers
and capacities of cargo tanks; limitations on length and breadth of
hull imposed by certain ports, canals, or berths at refineries; and
economical cruising speeds. Size has varied from 20,000 tons to

As previously noted, oil companies look to the independents to
augment the capabilities of their proprietary fleets. Sound econom·
ic justification exists for this. The demands for capital to support
activities related directly to the production of oil have become so
great that little money is available for either construction or pur
chase of ships. If there is need for one or more ships of a design
especially well adapted to meet the oil company's requirements,
often a long-term time charter equal to the anticipated life of the
tanker will be negotiated with an independent. The charter-party
serves as collateral for the independent to borrow the funds with
which to build the ship. This financial arrangement was devised just
after World War II and has proved satisfactory to all concerned.
Chartered tankers, regardless of whether they are on time
charter or on single or consecutive voyage charter, are integrated

into the operation of the proprietary fleet, and their movements are
controlled by the marine traffic department.
Short-term, single voyage, or consecutive voyage charters are
used to meet immediate requirements which exceed the capability
of the ships either owned or on long-term contracts. "Spot" cover
age is a vital, but marginal, activity arising out of the need for one or
more ships for a voyage or two to provide transportation demand
ed by the producing or marketing divisions. If a temporary surplus
of cargo exists, or a shortage of company-controlled ships develops,
the prompt chartering of one or more tankers will ease the crisis
without taking on the obligation to keep the ship employed once the
pressing need has been met. Even though the price of the voyage
chartered ship may be comparatively high when measured against
the company's average time charter rate, the convenience of having
a tanker at the time required, and only for that period, is worth a
great deal to the oil company. The independent operator tries to
anticipate these demands and to position his ships to take max
imum advantage of the situation.
Some independents have built their fleets entirely on the basis
of medium to long-term time charters. While the return is not so
great as it would be if all the ships were chartered on the spot
market, the stability of the longer contracts has proven, in many
cases, to be more profitable than the earnings on the highly volatile
spot market. Regardless of what type of charter is being sought, the
reputation of the independent tanker owner is of paramount im
portance in determining whether he will be favored with the
commitment.
Tankers generally are engaged in one of two distinct types of
service, distinguished as "clean" and "black" (sometimes also called
"dark oil" or "dirty") trades. Ships in the latter trade carry only
crude, residual, and darker oils up to the diesel grade. Many of the
very heavy crude oils require heating to reduce viscosity before they
can be pumped ashore.
The clean trade, as the name implies, demands that the ship be
very carefully prepared before any cargo oil is pumped into the
tanks. Certain jet engine fuels must be carried only in tanks coated
with inorganic, nonferrous compounds to eliminate contamination
through corrosion of the tank walls. Lubricating oil may be emulsi

The clean trade, as the name implies, demands that the ship be
very carefully prepared before any cargo oil is pumped into the
tanks. Certain jet engine fuels must be carried only in tanks coated
with inorganic, nonferrous compounds to eliminate contamination
through corrosion of the tank walls. Lubricating oil may be emulsi
fied if any water is left on the tank walls, and therefore all these

surfaces must be wiped by hand to assure that no trace of moisture
remains to pollute the cargo. It is customary to fill ("press up") the
tanks to capacity so that there is no void space in which condensa
tion can form. In those instances where several grades of lubricat
ing oil, varying in color from grade to grade, must be pumped
through the same piping system, the lightest colored oil is pumped
first. This assures against contamination from any residue encoun
tered in the pipes.
Black oils are heavier than clean products, and therefore fewer
barrels of the former may be loaded for a given deadweight ton
nage. This fact is important in planning the load of the ship,
inasmuch as distribution of the load must be made in appreciation
of the stresses imposed by filled and void tanks. It also has a bearing
on the number and size of ships needed to move a given quantity of
oil. Normally, the capacity of a tanker is computed in terms of
barrels of gasoline and total deadweight tonnage. The T-2 tanker,
for instance, had a nominal barrel capacity of 140,000 and a dead
weight of 16,750 tons. Fully loaded, fueled, and stored for a voyage
from Port Arthur, Texas, to New York, the T-2 was able to lift
140,000 barrels of aviation gasoline but only 90,000 to 110,000
barrels of the heavier black oils.
Safety is another managerial responsibility of paramount im
portance not only on board ship but around terminals where tank
ers load and discharge. At sea, in the approaches to ports, at berth
when handling cargo as well as when waiting for orders, and
throughout the normal routines of cleaning tanks, performing
maintenance work, and standing watches, the utmost vigilance
must be exercised by all personnel if accidents are to be avoided.
Fire, obviously, is the ever present hazard, and elaborate precau
tions habitually are taken to reduce this danger. Terminals also
must be supervised continuously to assure that safe practices are
followed. Most tanker operating companies devote considerable
attention to the study of work practices and the analysis of accidents
to use in training programs for both seafaring and shoreside em
ployees. Closely related to these aspects of safety are the provisions
for safe navigation of the vessel:

To reduce the possibility of explosions set off by static electricity

in the enormous cargo tanks of the very large crude carriers,
installation of inert gas systems has been made mandatory in ships
of 40,000 tons deadweight or larger; this requirement will be ex
tended in the near future to vessels exceeding 20,000 tons. The
inert gas may consist of treated flue gas from main or auxiliary
boilers, gas from a gas turbine's exhaust, or gas from a separate
inert gas generator. Oxygen content of the gas must not exceed 5
percent by volume. In essence, this system pipes an inert gas into.
the tanks as the cargo is pumped out, thereby avoiding the mixture
of air and petroleum vapor which can become critical and subject to
explosion from a single spark.
Concurrent with the inert gas system has come the development
of crude oil washing of cargo tanks, which has been found safer
than the time-honored method of washing tank walls with streams
of water under high pressure. One of the benefits of the crude oil
washing system is that cargoes are delivered with less contamina
tion, at the same time that ballast water is clean and nonpolluting.
The new techniques necessitated the establishment of training
centers to instruct ships' personnel in the proper use of the inert gas
installation and the approved methods of washing tanks with crude
oil. This program fitted well into the existing effort of major tanker
operators to assure that their seafaring employees were able to cope
with the problems of managing (in all its varied aspects) the large
ships which are part of the world's tanker fleets. Simulators, using
computers and elaborate scenic effects, are providing extensive
training in ship handling in crowded channels and other demand
ing circumstances. The latest methods of fighting shipboard fires, a
constant threat, are under unending study. Seafarers are sent to
highly specialized fire-fighting schools on a periodic basis to assure
that they have the most up-to-date knowledge of this essential skill.
Victualing, storing, scheduling, repairing, and bunkering a
fleet of tankers in worldwide service are other aspects of manage
ment responsibility. Few tankers are employed in repetitious voy
ages between designated ports, and therefore long absences from
the home port often occur. To provide adequate supplies of food
and stores of good quality, and to procure these at reasonable prices
for scores of ships

fleet of tankers in worldwide service are other aspects of manage

ages between designated ports, and therefore long absences from
the home port often occur. To provide adequate supplies of food
and stores of good quality, and to procure these at reasonable prices
for scores of ships in oil-handling ports around the world, is an
activity of impressive dimensions. Full appreciation of the princi
ples of bunkering is mandatory for management of a globe-gir-

dling fleet of tankers if maximum capability of the ships is to be
attained. Management never is a routine matter when voyages are
subject to unforeseen deviations, reroutings on short notice, and
unexpected delays beyond control of either the ship or her owners.
Personnel administration in tanker operation is a concern of
increasing magnitude. To recruit, train, assign, and supervise the
performance oflicensed and unlicensed seamen, and to assure that
they receive adequate consideration in handling pay and allot
ments, delivering mail to the ship, granting vacations when due,
and imposing disciplinary measures if necessary, are formidable
undertakings, particularly when the ships are scattered over the
oceans.
The current practice of granting tanker seamen extensive vaca
tions has resulted in the enlargement of company personnel pools
and in the installation of complex record systems. Many owners
have ships under the registry of one nation but staffed with crews
from a different country. A Liberian-flag vessel, for instance, might
have a full crew of Spaniards. By the terms of employment, the
Spanish seamen are entitled to vacation in Spain each year, regard
less of where the ship may be trading. Transportation to Spain and
back to the ship is the responsibility of the owner. Vessels with
multinational personnel have a correspondingly more complex
problem of repatriation. American ships trading along the coast of
the United States, however, are privileged to adopt a comparatively
simple plan of having relief contingents join the vessels periodically
at designated ports, replacing the crew members eligible for vaca
tion. Whatever the method, a program of rotation must be devised
to assure both efficient operation of the tanker and contentment
among the seamen. It is not coincidental that the increasing mech
anization of ships, which facilitates turnaround in a matter of
hours, has created problems of human relations requiring the
exercise of vision and imagination in the search for solutions.
Differing quite markedly from dry cargo ship-operating proce
dures is the significance attached by tanker owners to vessel ac
counts and statistical reports. Ideally, the records of expenditures
for wages, port dues, pilotage fees, tug hire, and the like, should be
in the home office no later than one working day after the vessel's
departure. The practice is somewhat at variance from the ideal, but

for wages, port dues, pilotage fees, tug hire, and the like, should be
in the home office no later than one working day after the vessel's
departure. The practice is somewhat at variance from the ideal, but
every effort is made to transmit these data to the analysts as quickly

as possible. Ships are under orders promptly to provide detailed
information concerning the time used to work cargoes, reasons for
any delays encountered, the effects of weather experienced while in
port, and the conventional operation reports of every completed
voyage. Evaluation of the reports must be accomplished promptly
if they are to have any value, and cognizant supervisors must be
made aware of the findings in every case, whether routine or
exceptional.
It must be emphasized that, from the viewpoint of the oil
companies, tankers are as vital to the industry as are the pumps in
the oil fields and the distillation units at the refinery. Failure of a
tanker to deliver a cargo can range from an annoyance to the cause
of a major shutdown. Until the advent of earth-orbiting communi
cation satellites, the only links between shore staff and the ships at
sea were radiotelegraph and radiotelephone. With the new tech
nology, it is possible for written messages ("telex") to be transmitted
instantaneously and inexpensively from ship to shore and vice
versa. The advantages are obvious, especially in the establishment
of permanent records.
There are additional benefits from the telex system. The ship
can send detailed information concerning repair work to be accom
plished at the next port of call, and can set forth the exact spare or
replacement parts needed and the specialized technicians required
to do the work. Payrolls may be prepared aboard ship and sent by
telex a matter of a few hours before the ship's arrival in port,
permitting full payment of crew wages. The list of additional func
tions that the new system can perform, especially when connected
to a small computer on shipboard, grows almost daily as both
managers ashore and seafarers afloat become accustomed to the
closer relationship that has been made possible.
A most important feature of the telex is the ability it confers
upon the ship's master to report on operating conditions that affect
the efficiency of the ship. If the ship has been delayed in berthing
because of port congestion, and demurrage is payable, the sooner
the chartering staff is aware of this, the sooner steps can be initiated
to collect (or pay) what is owed. If, for any reason, the tanker is
unable to perform to normal standards, a written report of

in these unexpected circumstances. The existence of documentary
records not only facilitates discussions between concerned parties
but also establishes a sound basis for evaluating at-sea and in-port
performance. Increasing numbers of tanker operators, both oil
companies and independents, are installing these satellite com
munication systems as essential tools of management.
There is no substitute for personal contact between the shore
staff and seagoing personnel. When tankers return frequently to
the home port, this contact can be maintained without difficulty. If
the fleet is large, the opportunity is decreased significantly for the
fleet manager to know personally the men aboard his ships. When
the tankers are dispersed worldwide, the problem becomes acute.
Of the possible alternatives to losing contact, the device most fa
vored by oil company management has been the formation of
subsidiary companies to which are assigned responsibility for a
small number of vessels operating in a somewhat restricted geo
graphical area.
For example, Exxon Corporation in 1984 owned nineteen
American flag tankers used to transport petroleum in domestic
coastwise service. Subsidiaries in Denmark, England, France,
Germany, Italy, Norway, and other countries owned and operated
tankers under their respective national registries. Although all
these ships flew the same house-flag, management was delegated to
comparatively small organizations. Worldwide fleet policy was set
by the parent company, but details of operation of the ships were
left to the staffs of the subsidiaries. In this manner, the burden of
operation was divided, and personal touch with the seamen was
more likely to be preserved.
No matter what the range of managerial responsibility, all tank
er owners strive to reduce nonrevenue producing time in port.
Unavoidable delays resulting from weather are accepted for what
they are. The concern is over deficiencies in pumping capabilities
by shore installations, mechanical failures and personnel errors
aboard ship, problems of heating heavy oil to hasten its flow
through the piping systems, lack of proper berthing spaces, and
similar controllable impediments to maximum performance. One
major oil company, in a successful effort to improve overall em

of the responsible supervisors afloat and ashore. Concurrent with
attempts of this nature to achieve optimum results from existing
practices, management must be alert to find new or improved ways
to work the ships when they come into port. As costs of owning and
chartering ships have increased, there has been a corresponding
rise in the pressure placed upon supervisors to better previously
accepted methods and to exercise greater ingenuity and imagina
tion in solving problems.
Gauging exactly the number of barrels of petroleum cargo
pumped into or out of a ship has become an important aspect of
tanker management. In the normal course of operation, a 75,000
tons deadweight tanker may have one or two thousand barrels of oil
remaining in the tanks after discharge. This residue clings to bulk
heads and tank bottoms; it does not flow to pump intakes. Because
the value of the oil is now so great, consignees demand full delivery
of what was loaded, or a compensatory adjustment. It is critical,
therefore, that the number of barrels loaded be determined with
precision, and the outturn be measured equally accurately. This is
accomplished by hiring specialists to monitor both loading and
unloading by use of an assortment of equipment designed for these
purposes.
Modern tankers, especially those built since 1973, are equipped
with very efficient stripping pumps and extra pipelines intended to
suck up the maximum quantity of cargo oil. It is when the pumping
operation stops that the specialists begin their work of determining
the amount of oil that remains in the tanks. The ship owner or
operator has every reason to demand that the specialists perform
competently, that their instruments be calibrated by qualified test
ing laboratories, and that reports be clear and unquestionable. A
major responsibility for overseeing this phase of oil transportation
has been assigned to both shipboard and shoreside supervisors.

Tanker employment is influenced markedly by the characteris
tics of the cargoes the ships transport. Few tankers (excluding the
combination and specialized carriers) participate in anything ex
cept the one-way movement of a given grade of petroleum. Ships
assigned to lift gasoline, kerosene, and other clean products are
restricted to those cargoes which have very nearly the same charac
teristics and never are switched casually to the black oil trade. The

reason is easy to discover: it takes much effort, time, and money to
convert a ship from carrying black oils to the condition requisite to
accept clean products. Prudent management can effect the change
economically and efficiently provided sufficient time is allowed to
make a number of voyages, each one carrying progressively lighter
grades of oil. Once qualified to work clean cargoes, the ship is
retained in that activity as long as possible.
To prepare a black tanker for an immediate shift to clean
service is a very expensive, time-consuming, labor intensive opera
tion. Upwards of two weeks may be required for the extensive
washing (which may involve the use of chemical solvents) of tank
surfaces, and the removal and proper disposal of the sludge and
slops produced. When the ship eventually is made ready to accept
gasoline, she still may not be able to meet the specifications for
carrying exotic liquids like jet fuel. To be acceptable for that type of
cargo may necessitate several successive voyages with gasoline car
goes, each followed by special cleaning action, before the tanks are
given approval for these sensitive cargoes.
Many tankers today have the cargo tank surfaces coated with
special nonferrous compounds that facilitate cleaning and also
neutralize reactions between the metal of the hull and the cargo. If
the ship carrying black cargoes has been treated in this manner, the
shift from black to clean is made less difficult. In these coated ships,
the use of carefully formulated chemical solvents may be appropri
ate as a means of expediting the cleaning process.
Tankers have become so costly, both to acquire and to operate,
that good management dictates that all nonproductive time be
eliminated. One aspect of this effort may be observed in the indus
try-wide standards adopted to control the length of time allowed to
charterers for loading and discharging vessels. Discharge time de
pends upon the tanker's pumps, and significant improvement in
performance can be achieved only by construction of new ships
with pumping systems of greater capacity. For example, the aver
age pumping capacity of the prewar handy-sized tankers was about
200 tons per hour. The T -2 tanker was designed with larger-capaci
ty pumps, and handled approximately 700 tons per hour. Present
day medium-sized tankers are able to discharge about 1,500 tons an

performance can be achieved only by construction of new ships
with pumping systems of greater capacity. For example, the aver
age pumping capacity of the prewar handy-sized tankers was about
200 tons per hour. The T -2 tanker was designed with larger-capaci
ty pumps, and handled approximately 700 tons per hour. Present
day medium-sized tankers are able to discharge about 1,500 tons an
hour, while the giant tankers, especially those over 225,000 tons
deadweight, are moving a minimum of 4,000 tons an hour. Actual

discharge time depends upon the grade of cargo carried, the avail
able shore facilities, and the ambient temperatures: cold weather
slows the flow of oil and imposes heavy burdens upon the ship's
pumps and the booster pumps along the pipeline.
The single greatest cause of loss of time in port is the delay in
placing the tanker alongside its berth. If vessel schedules overlap
and two or more ships, earlier expected to arrive in orderly se
quence and to use the available docking space in turn, converge
upon the port at one time, congestion ("bunching") occurs, and
inevitably there are delays in operation.
Bunching results from an accumulation of minor, unantici
pated troubles afflicting ships in loading, sailing over thousands of
miles of ocean, and discharging. The generic term applied to these
difficulties is "slip." It is caused by late arrivals, mechanical deficien
cies, and many other failures to maintain the established schedule,
regardless of whether they are within or beyond the control of
managerial personnel. Despite a high degree of vessel mainte
nance, efficient personnel, careful management, and watching,
cajoling, checking, praising, criticizing, and the best of intentions,
vessels do not always keep to schedules and therefore present the
operator with a substantial amount of slip. The contributing factors
vary from port to port, company to company, cargo to cargo,
season to season, and only constant attention by operating manage
ment keeps slip from becoming more of a grave problem than it is
already.
The complexity of managing a fleet of world-circling tankers
was brought into appropriate perspective in 1952 by a Norwegian
scholar who analyzed tanker operation in that year. Except that
there are more tankers, and some of the routes are longer, the
patterns delineated by the study remain substantially unchanged.
In 1952, the statistics showed that 2,500 crude oil carriers recorded
1,028,177,000,000 ton-miles and transported 325,106,000 tons of
cargo. There were 290 important routes that fanned out from 18
exporting areas to 43 receiving regions. About 45 percent of the
tanker traffic was assigned to haul oil from Arabian Gulf and
Eastern Mediterranean oil fields to all parts of Europe. These
passages were almost twice as long

cargo. There were 290 important routes that fanned out from 18
exporting areas to 43 receiving regions. About 45 percent of the
tanker traffic was assigned to haul oil from Arabian Gulf and
Eastern Mediterranean oil fields to all parts of Europe. These
passages were almost twice as long as the average worldwide dis
tance of 3,163 miles. Only 53.7 percent of the time spent at sea was
devoted to carrying oil; the remaining 46.3 percent was consumed
in ballast trips.

A somewhat more specialized study of the employment of tank
ers of 200,000 tons deadweight or larger was conducted in 1970 by
an English ship brokerage firm which analyzed a total of 107
voyages. Only 33 of these trips were between one loading port and
one discharging port. Twenty-five sailings had involved loading at
two ports and discharging at two ports, inevitably requiring long
port time. Had it been possible to make all 107 voyages OIl a
one-port-to-one-port basis, the saving to operators in the cost of
port time alone would have amounted to £18,400,000.16
A combination of unfavorable events occurred in the years after
1973. Fuel oil prices were escalated suddenly in that year and have
been maintained at high levels since then. For a variety of reasons, a
surplus of petroleum developed around the world about 1977, with
almost catastrophic effects upon the tanker industry. Charter hire
rates dropped precipitately at the same time that ship operating
expenses rose. To offset these developments, many owners with
ships committed to voyage charters, and time charterers of tankers,
directed masters and chief engineers to cruise their ships at the
speed which would result in optimum mileage per barrel. While the
length of passage was increased, ship time was slightly less costly
than bunker fuel. "Slow steaming" became a pattern of operation,
even though it was admittedly not the most efficient employment of
an expensive resource. Diesel-powered tankers gained noticeably
in popularity with charterers because they used less fuel than did
the ships equipped with steam turbines. At the end of 1981, slow
steaming also was practiced to avoid long waiting periods in the oil
loading ports of the Middle East. Owners considered it was eco
nomically justifiable to take longer on the ballast passage if time at
anchor, always unproductive, could be shortened.
Slow steaming was a worldwide practice in 1980 and 1981 when
the reduction in demand for petroleum created the classic situation
in the tanker chartering market of many ships competing for the
few cargoes available, thereby driving charter rates down to non
compensatory levels. To avoid the great expense oflaying up their
ships, many owners accepted these unprofitable charters. The re

Slow steaming was a worldwide practice in 1980 and 1981 when
the reduction in demand for petroleum created the classic situation
in the tanker chartering market of many ships competing for the
few cargoes available, thereby driving charter rates down to non
compensatory levels. To avoid the great expense oflaying up their
ships, many owners accepted these unprofitable charters. The re
sult was that very large crude carriers were loaded in the Arabian
Gulf and ordered to steam at between six and ten knots throughout
their passage to the United States. Charterers used the big ships for
two purposes: they transported crude petroleum, and simulta
neously provided much needed storage space for the surplus oil.

There are no ports in the United States with sufficient depth of
water to accommodate tankers of greater size than about 225,000
tons deadweight. To obtain the economy of scale from the huge
ships, the oil producers arranged for smaller ships (up to 75,000
tons deadweight) to meet the big ships about sixty miles offshore,
and to transship the cargo into the smaller, shallower-draft vessels.
A complete technique for this operation was developed, and light
erage of petroleum cargoes became standard practice.17

The 263,549-tons deadweight Texaco Japan (built 1975) was 377 meters
long, 53.6 meters wide, with a draft of 20.4 meters. Photo: Foxboro
Company.
To provide a more economical and more permanent method of
using the very large crude carriers, a huge buoy was designed to
serve as the mooring point for the ship as well as the offshore
terminal for a submarine pipeline to shore facilities. The only one
in the United States was put into operation in June 1981. It is
emplaced about eighteen miles off the Louisiana coast, in water at
least one hundred feet deep, and is capable of handling over one
million barrels of petroleum per day. The tanker is moored by a
cable over the bow ("single point mooring"), which permits her
always to face into the prevailing wind and seas. Her cargo is
pumped through a floating hose to the buoy, and there it flows into
the pipeline. A number of these offshore moorings exists world
wide. They are satisfactory devices for delivery by the largest tank
ers afloat to areas where coastal water depths are too shallow to
permit their entry into the harbors.
Tankers of 200,000 tons deadweight capacity and larger have
become numerous in all fleets because they provide transportation

at a lower cost per barrel of petroleum delivered. They are less
expensive to build; crews are only very slightly larger than for ships
lifting 35,000 tons; fuel consumption is much more favorable, per
ton of cargo, than in the smaller ships; and fewer hulls are needed
to transport a given tonnage of petroleum. A 275,000-ton tanker
delivers 28 barrels of oil for each barrel of fuel oil burned. At a
uniform charter rate, a 60,000-ton tanker would earn £500 a day
and have offsetting operating costs of £460. A ship of 100,000 tons
deadweight would earn fl, 120, with costs of £540. The 200,000-
ton tanker would bring revenue of £3,200 per day, but her ex
penses would total £660.18
In actual operation, the very large crude carriers have encoun
tered significant problems. The great draft of these ships, ranging
from 18.29 meters for a 200,000 tonner to the 27.73 meters of the
569,783-ton Seawise Giant, restricts them to trade between a few
ports in the world. Ships drawing over 22.80 meters, when sailing
between the Arabian Gulf and Japan, must be routed via the Straits
of Lombok rather than the thousand-mile shorter passage through
the shallower Straits of Malacca. Dry docks capable of accommodat
ing these very large bottoms are being built in many strategic
locations, but still are not ubiquitous. Tank-cleaning is more haz
ardous than in smaller ships because of the vast size of the cargo
areas and the augmented possibilities of generating static electricity
that could cause an explosion.
Closely related in many respects to the movement of petroleum
and its derivatives is the carriage ofliquefied natural and petroleum
gas. Begun on an experimental basis in 1947, it was not until 1964
that routine transportation of these liquefied gases was available.
Many of the principles of management enunciated earlier in this
chapter are applicable to the management of these specialized
tankers. Certain aspects of operation understandably receive great
er emphasis, especially those related to safety, ship handling, and
the maintenance of equipment. Unceasing attention must be given
to compliance with local rules governing the entry of these ships

Many of the principles of management enunciated earlier in this
chapter are applicable to the management of these specialized
tankers. Certain aspects of operation understandably receive great
er emphasis, especially those related to safety, ship handling, and
the maintenance of equipment. Unceasing attention must be given
to compliance with local rules governing the entry of these ships
into busy ports, their berthing, and the techniques of working
cargo. Adjustments to ship schedules to conform to these regula
tions are normal in this service.

between 1975 and 1980. Representative of these carriers was the

ics at Quincy, Massachusetts. A characteristic of the cargo is that the
gas must be cooled to -160° Celsius (-265° Fahrenheit) before it
becomes liquid. To accommodate this cargo, five tanks, each of
25,000 cubic meters capacity, strengthened and insulated to very
exacting specifications, were installed in the hull. The ship was 285

of 11 meters (36 feet) had a deadweight of 64,620 tons. Turbines of

Whether the ships carry the relatively exotic liquefied natural
gas or the more mundane liquefied petroleum gas of which butane
is typical, the goal of management must be the safe completion of
every voyage. Liquefied natural gas is delivered to public utilities
with large storage tanks, while liquefied petroleum gas is distribut
ed to local vendors with limited storage facilities. Consequently, the
ships which transport "butane" are of much smaller size. Even
granting that butane at - 51 Celsius presents less of a problem in
0
handling than liquefied natural gas at - 1600 Celsius, the burdens
imposed upon management to assure that every voyage will be
completed without incident are almost identical. It is a tribute to the
skill and vigilance of the ship operators that hundreds of voyages
are made each year, and millions of gallons of these exotic liquids
are delivered in what appears superficially to be a completely rou
tine activity. Only the constant exercise of the best supervisory
techniques, coupled with expert ship handling and well-developed
loading and delivery techniques, can produce these results. Those
who are responsible for this transportation take understandable
pride in the fact that they have achieved an unparalleled record of
safety and customer satisfaction.
On January 1, 1984, 47 liquefied natural gas carriers and 448
liquefied petroleum gas transporters were in existence. That the
stringent regulations concerning mandatory safety measures and
precautions in navigation have been worthwhile is borne out by the
fact that this large fleet, over a 17 -year period from 1964 through
1981, incurred only 11 minor accidents, none involving escape of
the gas cargo or a fire.

Shipping Subsidy System
INTERN ATION AL shipping involves not only the
normal rivalry among carriers for the available cargo, but also the
more subtle competition between nations with disparate standards
of living. Often the pattern of trade between two countries reflects
the significant differences in their economic status. Nation A, for
instance, has a well-developed industrial economy with a high stan
dard of living for its citizens. It exports manufactured goods to all
parts of the world, and imports great quantities of raw materials.
Nation B, in contrast, has an agricultural economy, and depends
upon the products of its fields to provide the funds to pay for the
manufactured items it requires. Its standard ofliving, compared to
that of Nation A, is significantly lower, as evidenced by the differ
ences in wages and prices prevailing in that country.
For many sound reasons, Nation A has encouraged its citizens
to own and operate ships to serve its foreign trade, here typified by
the interchange of goods between A and B. The costs of building,
maintaining, and running ships under its registry are well above
those of Nation B, which also has a merchant fleet plying from B to
A and back again. If the principles of pure competition applied
perfectly to this trade, the level of freight rates would be fixed by
what the ships of Nation B must earn to assure an adequate profit.
To remain in business and to obtain any of the cargo, the owner of
Nation A's fleet ::annot charge more than do their rivals.
There are valid reasons why each of the trading partners should
have merchant fleets. One is that money paid to national-flag oper
ators is retained almost entirely in the local economy, in much the
same way that the proceeds of sales of domestic goods to citizens
stay inside national boundaries. Another reason is that the earnings
of the fleet from freights paid by foreign shippers are equivalent to
exports of goods; in fact, they often are referred to as "invisible
exports." Sweden, for instance, considers shipping as a major ex-

goods; in fact, they often are referred to as "invisible
exports." Sweden, for instance, considers shipping as a major ex-

port industry which brings in about eight percent of its revenue
from external sources.l Per contra, money paid to carriers of other
nationalities affects negatively the country's trade balance.
It can be argued that Nation B has greater justification for a
national-flag fleet than does Nation A. With its limited ability to
earn foreign exchange, it must find ways to augment the revenue
from sale of its agricultural produce. A merchant marine partici
pating in world trade offers a means to increase national income.
The money so realized is essential to help pay for the imports
needed by Nation B. In particular, the freight derived from carry
ing goods bought from Nation A reduces the net disbursement
from Nation B's treasury, while the freight collected from Nation A
for transporting its imports from Nation B represents positive
credits. Carried to its logical conclusion, this argument would seem
to justify the elimination of Nation A's merchant fleet in order to
strengthen that country's export sales. The counter to this conclu
sion is that Nation A experiences the same difficulties with its
international balance of payments, and therefore its invisible ex
ports are vital to its economy.
Another purpose of national ownership of a merchant fleet is to
provide service on those trade routes which are of greatest econom
ic importance to the nation. By their presence on a particular route,
the ships of Nation A attract vessels from other countries which are
seeking gainful employment. It is a fact of shipping that no trade
route is so insignificant that there is not at least one competitor of
the principal carrier. Even a small fleet from Nation A will attract
ships from other nations, thereby providing adequate transporta
tion to meet the needs of importer and exporter.
Finally, a corollary to the ability of ships to earn foreign ex
change with which to pay for imports is the employment of vessels
in the "cross trades." That is to say, ships of Nation A may sail
regularly between Nations M and P, rarely returning to a port in
Nation A. Money earned in this manner is a direct and positive
addition to the financial strength of the shipowning nation.
These arguments touch upon the basic rationale for national
flag merchant fleets. They gloss over the problems of disparity of
cost and difficulties of competition which arise out of that inequal
ity. This has been suggested earlier in this chapter in the com
mentary upon differences in national

The freight rates charged by the shipowners of Nation B reflect

that cost of transportation influences the shipper's decision as to
which carrier will be favored with the cargo. Ifs ervice and schedule
are substantially equal, it is almost certain that the lower cost car

The dilemma facing the owner of ships registered under the
flag of high cost Nation A is, to put it very simply, "Where can I
obtain the money I need to bridge the gap between my costs and the
revenue I can earn from carrying cargo at the rates set by my lower
cost competitor?"
There is only so much that efficient and economical manage
ment can do to reduce costs. Once these possibilities have been
exhausted, the most obvious source of the indispensable supple
mentary income is the national treasury. Commercia1 interests will
not pay higher freight rates simply to maintain a national-flag fleet.
There is no patriotism among shippers anywhere; they give their
business universally to the carrier who provides the best service at
the lowest cost, without regard to the flag under which the ship sails.
Philanthropists show no interest in assisting a commercial enter
prise in which some corporation is seeking to make a profit. With no
other avenue open, maritime activities around the world have
turned to their governments for financial help.

Of the maritime nations, the United States has the most com
prehensive, most widely publicized, and most openly administered
subsidy program. It evolved over generations of experience, start
ing in 1847 when the postmaster-general was authorized to enter
into contracts with steamship operators to transport mail destined
to foreign countries. The underlying purpose of this legislation was
to encourage American investment in, and operation of, steam
powered vessels in direct competition with foreign-flag carriers. In
1840, with support from the British government, Samuel Cunard
had inaugurated regular passenger and mail service between En
gland and the United States. To compete with Cunard, some

method had to be devised to offset the higher costs of building ships
in the United States and operating them under American registry.
The mail contract appeared to be a satisfactory method. It called
for lump sum payments for each voyage without regard to the
amount of mail actually carried. A major deficiency in the law was
the absence of a stipulation that the contractor set aside adequate
funds to construct replacement tonnage.
In 1817, the Congress enacted a law which restricted the water
borne trade between the states to ships built and owned in the
United States, and manned by citizens of the United States. Because
California was admitted to the United States in 1850, the well
publicized Gold Rush voyages of the dipper ships from Atlantic
coast ports around Cape Horn to San Francisco were legally inter
state commerce, and therefore limited to ships meeting the criteria
set forth in the 1817 law. Subsequently, an extensive coastwise
trade, especially along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, developed
under this protective legislation and flourished until the advent of
World War II. When the Panama Canal was opened to commercial
traffic on August 15, 1914, it made possible an active intercoastal
trade which prospered for the next quarter century. Aside from
protecting against foreign competition the ships engaged in these
trades, however, there was no government assistance.
This cabotage restriction described above applies today in the
coastwise and intercoastal trade, and in the movement of cargo and
passengers between the forty-eight contiguous states and Alaska,
Hawaii, and the offshore commonwealths and possessions. An
exception exists in the waterborne commerce between the main
land and the Virgin Islands, which were purchased from Denmark
in 1917. Vessels of foreign registry are permitted to transport
goods on this route despite the fact that both origin: and terminus
are on United States soil.
To assure an additional source of revenue to American-flag
ships, which were experiencing difficulty in meeting foreign com
petition, the Congress enacted a law in 1904 which required that all
cargo belonging to the United States military, or consigned to its
overseas installations, be carried in ships either owned by the gov
ernment or registered in the United States. In 1954, the "Fifty-Fifty
