In part it was data drawn from the Atlantic Canada Project that led
to a second major field of research, the market for, and the returns of,
maritime labour. The crew agreements included details on the hiring
of seamen and their rates of pay at ports throughout the world. Skip
had already drawn on this material for ‘The Problem of Desertion',30
which remains the seminal study of this theme, and with Nordvik he
had investigated some of the international aspects of crewing with a
paper on Norwegian sailors in the Canadian mercantile marine.31 But
Skip recognized the wider potential of such data for the study of labour
markets and rates of pay for maritime labour. In the maritime field -
and indeed more generally - labour economics was and still is to some
extent an underdeveloped sub-discipline. Skip (often in collaboration
with Nordvik) sought to rectify this neglect. In some fifteen papers the
issues of labour markets and labour's returns were examined at a variety
of levels. There were studies of these themes in a Norwegian context at
the single port, regional and national levels.32 Outside Norway there
was a study of Antwerp and national studies of the Canadian and
Indian experiences.33 And there were transnational studies embrac-
ing the Baltic grain trade, North Sea ports and international maritime
labour more generally.34 These studies - which merit collection together
in a single volume - stimulated research by others and this was behind
an important International Congress session on ‘The Market for Seamen
in the Age of Sail' in Milan in 1994, although, characteristically, Skip
suggested the impetus had come from elsewhere.35

Skip's studies of maritime wages and labour markets broke new
ground, as did another major area of his research, that of what he
termed ‘maritime middlemen' and in particular the occupation of ship-
broking. The theme of shipbroking was something of a void: not only
were there no serious scholarly studies of the profession but addition-
ally few maritime historians appeared to have any real understanding
of the function of brokers beyond their roles in vessel chartering, selling
freight space and the purchase and sale of vessels. That brokers per-
formed many other functions such as assisting shipowners in acquiring
capital and shipyard space for new vessel construction and, at the other
end of the cycle, played an important role in scrapping was unknown
to many, as was, in more recent times, broker activity in the offshore

Early in his career Skip became a close friend of Gordon Jackson
(author of a seminal study of British ports) and later Adrian Jarvis, the
authority on dock construction and port administration in Liverpool.
Through his interest in their work, port history has become a further
area of Skip's research; a relatively recent paper has examined a previ-
ously little-considered aspect of port operation, warehousing and its
influence on profits in the context of Liverpool docks.39 More gener-
ally he has focused on two themes: one is calculating the efficiency of
ports - a significant issue but highly problematical in terms of criteria
and measurement particularly in a comparative context. The other has
been that of the hierarchy of ports and the influence of seaport plan-
ning within this.40 Both issues are significant today in an era when
technological advances have revolutionized the work of ports and com-
petition between ports is at a transnational regional level rather than
within traditional national boundaries.
Selecting four areas of Fischer's research serves to indicate its impor-
tance and its innovative character. Moreover, the fields briefly surveyed
represent a range of very different themes. Yet this review does not do
full justice to the width of Skip's expertise. Among the many other areas
he has addressed there are papers on information flows,41 government
policies towards shipping,42 migration,43 the integration of the North
Atlantic economy,44 globalization trends and much more. Additionally,
in the field of historiography, there are papers on maritime history as a
sub-discipline, its role and its progress.45
Lewis R. Fischer's career is one of enormous achievement. He has
provided an institutional framework for an important sub-discipline of
history; he (with Helge Nordvik) had the courage to create a significant
academic journal and individually he has devoted twenty-five years to
its editing and enhancing its status; he has been the lynchpin in the
development of a body of maritime history scholars that spans genera-
tions and perhaps uniquely (through his example) is characterized by

and self-interest. Alongside all these, in his research he has pioneered
new approaches to the study of previously unexplored themes in mari-

Such a record is apparent to all associated with maritime history,
yet one suspects that Skip would deny the extent of his achievement.
Perhaps it is worth reminding him of the goals for maritime history
when, back in 1989, he launched the Journal. He enunciated four key
aims.46 These were promoting the recognition that maritime industries
are transnational and hence encouraging a comparative perspective;
emphasizing the social and economic contexts within which maritime
industries operate; encouraging maritime historians to place their stud-
ies within the context of the broader questions being posed by histori-
ans in general; and finally, shifting maritime history from the fringes
to the centre of the historical profession. Viewing mercantile maritime
history today, it must be said that in all such regards great progress
has been made over the past thirty years. One special feature of that
progress that embraces all of the listed aims is the new recognition of
the maritime dimension within the mainstream history focus on global
history. This volume in its overall theme and in the approach, analysis
and subjects of its constituent chapters embodies Skip's vision and,
more so, his achievement of a more international, more truly economic
and more widely recognized role for maritime history.

Shipping and Staple Economies
in the Periphery
C. Knick Harley
Shipping was an important economic activity in various parts of the
periphery during the process of globalization that began with the
European voyages of discovery and lasted until the closing of the con-
tinental frontiers early in the twentieth century. This important ship-
ping activity in the periphery contrasted with the dominance of ocean
shipping in the late nineteenth century that Britain, the dominant core
economy, experienced. Generally globalization before the late twenti-
eth century involved a manufacturing core area trading with a staple
raw material producing periphery. Although India was central to the
imperialism of this period, prototypically, the periphery consisted of
areas of recent settlement where discovery, growing core demand and
falling transportation costs created potential profit opportunities for
staple production (sugar and tobacco in the eighteenth century and
grain, meat and agricultural/industrial raw materials in the nineteenth).
Exploitation of these opportunities involved the mobilization of capital
and labour and its movement to the staple periphery. This process has
been systematized in the staple theory of economic development.1
Although a considerable portion of the recent literature about glo-
balization before the late twentieth century has focused on the late
nineteenth century, I want to go back to the emergence of the Atlantic
economy in the seventeenth century in my discourse. From the early
European empires through to at least World War I, an expanding fron-
tier of settlement was a key element in increasing globalization. The
globalization process has often been fruitfully envisaged as a process
in which the core economies, particularly of Europe, have their influ-
ence over peripheral economies. Often this relationship is analysed in
the framework of imperialism and power relationships; however, as an
economist, I wish to concentrate on market forces.

and Staple Economies in the Periphery
In the frontier economies, quintessentially in the Americas and
Australia but elsewhere as well, the outstanding characteristic of the
periphery has been its land and resource abundance. The economic
history of these regions, although it must encompass power relation-
ships and imperialism, fundamentally involves the process of exploit-
ing this land abundance. In its simplest form - as exemplified by the
slave economies of tropical and sub-tropical America in the seventeenth
and particularly the eighteenth centuries - the process began with the
discovery of resources that were quickly perceived as valuable. If capital
and labour could be applied to exploiting these resources at anything
close to their opportunity cost in the core, there were profits to be
made. Thus European entrepreneurs brought capital to the sugar and
tobacco colonies and organized the supply of labour. It is, of course,
one of economic history's most distressing features that although there
was initially recruitment of European labour utilizing the institution of
indentured service, the entrepreneurs of the periphery found that the
cheapest way to mobilize labour was through the African slave trade.
This resource abundance emerged as the slave-based trading econo-
mies of the eighteenth century that produced sugar and tobacco for
European consumption.
With the coming of the Industrial Revolution technological improve-
ments further extended the prospects for globalization and staple-based
peripheral economies. The first great impact came from the explosion of
demand for raw cotton that arose from the dramatic cost reductions in
textile production following on from Arkwright's discoveries. The rapid
urbanization and population growth that accompanied the Industrial
Revolution also put upward pressure on food prices in the core, increas-
ing prospects for primary production in the periphery. In addition,
and perhaps most importantly, the Industrial Revolution's innovations
in iron and steel and in steam engines radically reduced the cost of
distance. In consequence, grain staple-based expansions occurred dur-
ing the nineteenth century, perhaps most spectacularly in the North
American interior but equally importantly in the northern and western
littoral of the Black Sea.
Distance was an important and inherent part of the core-periphery
globalization from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries. Throughout
this period, frontiers of the global economy existed. Frontiers occurred
at the limits of profitable staple production where the cost of trans-
portation created by distance offset the economies of land abundance

As globalization proceeded the proportion of transportation and other
distribution costs in the final price paid by consumers increased.

In this environment, the demand for shipping grew with the expansion
of globalization.
Most of the involvement of the periphery in the global economy
can fit into a staple-theory framework where raw materials created
opportunities for exports to the metropolitan core. There were impor-
tant exceptions, however. For example, the seventeenth-century New
England and northern mainland American colonies lacked natural
resources to attract settlement. Yet, at least in hindsight, these areas
emerged as the most successful of the regions of European expansion
in the age of discovery. In these regions, there were no export prod-
ucts based on abundant raw materials that initially commanded high
prices in the core, as was the case in the staple economies. Instead,
shipping made up an important part of these colonies' business with
the international economy. Although the availability of shipbuilding
materials played a small part in this success, the fundamental econom-
ics was different from that of staple-induced settlement. Somewhat
later two economies in the European periphery, Greece and Norway,
also entered the globalizing economy as important sellers of shipping
services.
The eighteenth-century British Atlantic economy
Staple-based economies lie at the centre of core-periphery relation-
ships that characterized the rise of globalization. The colonies that the
European powers developed in the Americas are key examples. The
European discovery and subsequent exploitation of the resources of the
western hemisphere was a unique example of a major discontinuity in
economic history. In the Old World there had, of course, been ebbs and
flows of resource development and there were many staple-producing
areas. Discovery of mineral sources, pacification of areas previously sub-
ject to control of rival empires or lawlessness, new trading connections
and the rapid expansion of demand from core areas had created periods
of staple development driven booms. Nonetheless, longstanding shared
knowledge and trading ties implied that the disequilibria that these
booms responded to were of limited magnitude and duration. The New
World was different because it had lacked the centuries-long trading ties
and the shared knowledge of the Old World.2 Consequently, the extent
of the initial disequilibrium was much greater than those that occurred
in resource booms in the Old World. The adjustment to equilibrium,
in which the returns to mobile factors of production equalled their
opportunity costs in the Old World and, if property rights were well

Once the original disequilibrium was overcome, a staple colony
might continue to grow as a result of outward shifts in the demand
curve caused by changing tastes, growing income and population, the
misfortunes of rival producers, shifts in supply caused by technological
change, and so on. The region might also decline as a result of various
forces such as soil exhaustion or pest infestation or the superior for-
tunes of competitors. At this point, however, the economic history of
the region has lost its most of its initial characteristics as an expanding
staple economy.
In the Americas the greatest of the staple expansions occurred in
the West Indies. The islands developed a sugar monoculture econ-
omy between the last decades of the seventeenth century and the
mid-eighteenth century. It was infamously characterized by the devel-
opment of the transatlantic African slave trade as a massive commercial
enterprise that supplied the labour necessary to initially exploit the
islands' potential. The slave trade continued through the eighteenth
century and into the nineteenth in order to maintain a labour force that
failed to maintain itself by natural reproduction. Great fortunes were
made particularly in the early days. By the second half of the eighteenth
century the sugar colonies had become an integral part of the broader
European economy.
Similar development occurred in tobacco production, as European
colonists discovered tobacco smoking from the Native Americans and
undertook its commercial production. Tobacco-based export colo-
nies expanded in the Chesapeake Bay region of the North American
mainland. Tobacco production lacked the economies of scale that
characterized sugar plantations and the economy was less dominated
by large plantations. The demographic regime was less harsh and the
slave population grew by natural increase. The region also continued to
support a white population made up of indentured servants past and
present. It nonetheless exhibited the expansive character of a staple
economy although with the horrors of West Indian slavery somewhat
attenuated.

New England and the middle colonies evolved mainly from the

colonial economy: the rapid and extensive growth of population, of set-

structural change'.3 The involvement of these Malthusian colonies in
Atlantic trade was thus different.

After the United States achieved independence, entrepreneurs in the
former northern mainland colonies found their access to the imperial
economy limited by the Navigation Acts. However, the needs of both
the West Indian staple colonies and the northern mainland ensured
that shipowners in the northern states of the newly independent nation
continued to provide services to the Atlantic economy. When the great
wars in Europe broke out following the French Revolution, the oppor-
tunities expanded for neutral shipping from the United States until war
broke out with Britain in 1812.
The war and the subsequent adoption of the protective tariff by the
United States turned northern entrepreneurs' attention away from
maritime pursuits and inward to the new nation; the Boston Associates,
who set up the integrated cotton mills at Waltham and then Lowell,
Massachusetts and strongly promoted the tariff, had made their for-
tunes from the maritime trades. The effect of the tariff in turning entre-
preneurial attention from maritime activities was only partial, however.
The lure of the national market seems to have been offset by the
opportunities presented by the creation of another of the great staple
trades in a relatively nearby region. Cotton cultivation in the American
South emerged in response to the technological changes that radically
cheapened production of cotton textiles in Britain. During the first half
of the nineteenth century American ships achieved international pre-
eminence in large measure as a consequence of their success in captur-
ing the business of shipping American raw cotton to Europe.
A striking aspect of nineteenth-century maritime history is the rapid
decline of the American merchant marine after the American Civil War.
The Northern merchant marine was hurt by the war and the increased
risks it brought. Beyond the war, however, the 1860s marked a sharp
demarcation between American maritime success and the country's
almost complete abandonment of maritime activity thereafter. There
was a range of causes of which technological change in the form of
iron ships and steam propulsion was paramount. Equally important,
however, was the disappearance of the conditions that had nurtured
shipping from colonial times. Starting with the war of 1812 and rein-
forced by the protective tariff that followed (strongly reinforced during
the Civil War), New England's economic situation changed radically.

The peninsula and the islands had modest resources and low incomes.
Within this environment, however, entrepreneurial groups developed
a vibrant and internationally competitive shipping industry. The
underlying dynamics appear to share important characteristics with
the shipping success of the northern mainland colonies of colonial
British America. The absence of an exportable staple and a fragmented
low-income domestic market provided few opportunities for entrepre-

a potentially expansive market that might be exploited.7 Furthermore,
like the northern mainland colonies Greece proved conveniently situ-
ated to exploit the opportunities that an expanding staple economy
presented for distribution services.
Greeks, with their long indented coastline and myriad islands, of
course, had a long maritime tradition. This had manifested itself within
the Ottoman Empire and also in Venetian Levantine trade.8 The emer-
gence of Greek shipping as a modern success story coincided with the

expansion of a staple frontier whose location enhanced the opportuni-
ties available to Greek shipping entrepreneurs. The staple frontier in
question lay in the grain producing region along the western and north-
ern shores of the Black Sea. The frontier developed after the Russians
acquired the north shore of the Black Sea as a result of victory in the
Russo-Turkish War in the 1770s, the Treaty of Kutchuk-Kainardji in 1774
and subsequent treaties that opened access to the Black Sea. The Ukraine
emerged as a grain frontier and Greek entrepreneurs seized the opportu-
nity to provide shipping and mercantile services. Entrepreneurial mari-
time families from the Greek islands quickly emerged as the mercantile
class in the newly developed ports of southern Russia and developed
connections to the main ports of western Europe. Similar developments
occurred in the Danubian provinces, with Greek entrepreneurial fami-
lies again playing leading roles. As staple-oriented settlement grew in
the grain producing regions and population growth in western Europe
sustained and enhanced demand, so too did Greek shipping.
Greek exploitation of the largely location-free maritime opportuni-
ties that accompanied staple-driven development in a newly opened
resource-abundant region was arguably even more remarkable than the
experience of the northern colonies of British America. Entrepreneurial
Greek shipping families played seminal roles in the creation of the
independent Greek state in the 1830s. Recent estimates of Greek ship-
ping earnings in international trade suggest that they equalled a third
of the land-based income of the country in the years from the mid-
1830s to the mid-1850s and remained above ten per cent of land-based
income for another generation. During these years shipping was the
most dynamic sector of an economy most of whose income was still
dominated by a traditional primary sector.9 Greek shipowners were in
intimate contact with the world economy, competing with the shipping
of the most advanced countries and establishing offices in leading com-
mercial centres in Europe.
Equally remarkably, the Greek shipowners successfully made the
transition to steam shipping during the last decades of the nineteenth
century.10 This involved familiarization with new technologies and
capital investment on a much larger scale than previously. Despite the
potential obstacles, the registered tonnage of steam ships exceeded that
of sailing vessels by the beginning of the twentieth century. The

Norway
Norway provides yet another example of this phenomenon of a
resource-deprived economy successfully exploiting opportunities pro-
vided by maritime connections to the wider global economy, interme-
diated by staple trades. Much of Norway has meagre resources but easy
access to the sea. Again we see the economy's dynamic elements emerg-
ing from the maritime economy. Of course, Norway had long been
involved in the northern fisheries that had provisioned Europe since
medieval times. In the modern period, staple trades developed in the
Baltic to supply the dynamic North Sea economies of the Netherlands
and Britain. Large staple export trades in timber and grain developed on
the northern and southern shores of the Baltic. In the nineteenth cen-
tury this trade was augmented by the export of coal from the coalfields
of the northeast of England. Norwegian shipping entrepreneurs tapped
into this trade which provided much of the dynamics of the economy.

these cases, when suitable entrepreneurship was present, substantial
shipping industries developed, connected to staple-exporting regions.

These periphery shipping centres could become quite large and casual

that accompanied the emergence of the United States not only as a
major staple exporter in grain as well as cotton but also a major indus-

ping as an earner of foreign exchange had disappeared.
Nonetheless, Britain, the world's leading industrial nation, dominated
shipping in the late nineteenth century. In the context of shipping eco-
nomics discussed here this is something of a surprise and merits a few

speculative remarks. British leadership certainly had underlying support
that differed from the simple static comparisons of relative costs that
have been emphasized here. Rather it seems to have rested on features
that we associate with the dynamics of growth. Of course, shipping is a
very capital-intensive business and Britain undoubtedly had the cheap-
est capital in the nineteenth-century world economy. Technological
change enhanced the British shipping position. Relatively cheap iron
and the improvements of the steam engine that were features of the
Industrial Revolution had their origins in Britain and British shipping
reaped first-mover advantages from proximity to these innovations. In
the middle of the nineteenth century, British shipping had been losing
out to American shipping in the Atlantic and to Scandinavian shipping
in the Baltic. However, as iron ships and steam ships became the norm,
the British advantage grew. In addition, British shipowners benefited
from Britain's position at the centre of world trade. Institutions to
finance, insure and manage shipping worldwide developed in Britain
in connection with this centrality to trade. Shipping firms with access
to knowledge present in the shipping districts of London benefited.
However, this knowledge was not exclusive to British firms. Greek ship-
ping firms early set up offices in London and shared the information
available. Ultimately, it is probably not surprising that British shipping
dominance declined and less central economies played major roles in
shipping in the twentieth century. As iron and steam became estab-
lished technologies, Britain's first-mover advantage lost much of its
impact. The information from London's financial, shipping and com-
modity markets became increasingly globalized.

An Appraisal of the Progress
of the Steamship in the
Nineteenth Century
David M. Williams and John Armstrong
The invention and subsequent development of the steamship represents
a great watershed in maritime transport and humankind's relationship
with the sea. For the first time, vessels were not at the mercy of wind
or tide and this, together with the ability to make or leave port at will,
permitted scheduled services. These, to a considerable degree, overcame
the uncertainties that previously had inevitably accompanied maritime
voyages. Over time all elements of shipping - vessels, labour, finance -
were transformed and likewise shipbuilding, the port industry and asso-
ciated shipping services. Steam together with changes in construction
materials - from wood to iron and later steel - along with later advances
in communications and transport technology, the telegraph and the
railway, created a ‘new world of shipping'.1 Such changes contributed
to the integration of the world economy.
The change from a time when steamships did not exist to one where
sail was virtually inconsequential occurred during the long nineteenth
century. To contemporaries it was an exciting transition and histori-
ans have subsequently viewed the process as a remarkable example
of technological change and a vital element in early trends toward a
world economy and globalization. For such reasons there is an exten-
sive literature on the steamboat. Indeed, only recently, Professor Yrjö
Kaukiainen observed, ‘Hardly any other phase in the history of shipping
has received as much scholarly attention as the transition from sail to
steam'.2 This literature, which inevitably focuses on the British experi-
ence, is of considerable interest in historiographical terms as it falls into
two periods, each with their particular characteristics.3
In the nineteenth century, and indeed up until World War II, the rise
of steam was viewed as revolutionary and rapid, a shining example of
technological advance, especially British technology, in the Victorian

the Canadian merchant marine (all sailing vessels) expanded rapidly

not deny the remarkable advance of steam; indeed in a paragraph -

Thus the historiography of the advance of steam comprises the
unqualified accounts of progress from writers up to around 1940 and,
from the 1950s, suggestions that sail more than held its own for much
of the nineteenth century and that steam's advance was a gradual one.
From the latter standpoint it was but a short move to infer that steam's
progress, in the sense of taking over shipping, might be viewed as
slow.
However, almost all those who have written on the shift from sail
to steam have shared a preference for subjective comment rather than
objective analysis. True, there has been some resort to statistics, such as
proportions of sail and steam in registered tonnage, new ship registra-
tions or within shipbuilding returns, but such aggregate measures are
somewhat crude, often misleading and offer nothing in terms of analys-
ing the process of the shift or sectoral analysis by region or commodity.21
Harley perhaps comes closest to this with his chart of when steam
became competitive with sail in the context of bulk trades. However, this
is not the same as when steamactually came to predominateein particular
trades and regions. As far as we can ascertain, Harley never attempted
fully to test his thesis in terms of a statistical analysis, perhaps because
his key interest was that of freight rates and their constituent elements
rather than the technological shift in practice. This study attempts an
examination of the change from sail to steam at aggregate and secto-
ral levels using data on shipping movements. The examination was
embarked upon with no preconceptions as to what might emerge; the
intention was that its outcome would provide scope for analysis and a
firmer basis for the assessment of the progress of steam.

Shipping movements comprise the entrances of vessels into, and the
clearances of vessels from, a particular location. Historians of British
shipping are blessed with a magnificent set of data on shipping move-
ments. These are located in the official record. The first publication of
the Annual Statement of Trade and Navigation in 1853 provided more
detailed and fuller statistics on trade and shipping than ever before. The
first volume contained over 150 tables, 28 of which related to shipping,
including material on shipping movements that distinguished between
vessels entering and clearing with cargoes and in ballast and, of espe-
cial interest in this context, those propelled by sail and those by steam.
Such data on shipping movements was to be continued on a yearly basis
in the Annual Statement of Trade and Navigation until 1870. Thereafter,
when trade and navigation were separated into two volumes, it was
to appear in the Annual Statement of the Navigation and Shipping of the
United Kingdom.22

The data on shipping movements comprised details of entrances and
clearances of vessels with cargo and in ballast (together and separately)
both nationally and for individual ports. Shipping movements ‘coast-
wise' and those ‘with foreign countries and British overseas possessions'
were also presented separately. In the case of foreign and overseas move-
ments, the country of the port of departure of incoming vessels and the

tinguished as was the nationality of vessels - British or ‘foreign' - with

thus represents a remarkable storehouse of data on the growth, pattern
and distribution of British trade, shipping and port activity and, within
this overall picture, the progress of technological change, the relative

Nevertheless, like all great bodies of statistics, the data on shipping
movements requires caution in handling and interpretation. For exam-
ple, if one considers figures of total entrances and clearances of vessels
with cargo and in ballast, the figures, albeit not identical, are remarka-
bly close in both number of vessels and total tonnage terms.23 However,
while overall entrances and clearances correspond, there is a significant
difference between entrances and clearances ‘with cargo only' and ‘with
cargo and in ballast'. There are two important aspects here. First, that
in the definitions used by the compilers, vessels that carried ‘passengers
only' were categorized as in ballast. Second, and this accounts for the
greater discrepancy for entrances than clearances, from the 1860s on,
and especially post-1870, Britain developed a growing coal export trade
(particularly for steamship bunkers). This led to numbers of vessels sail-
ing in ballast from Europe to Britain in order to pick up a coal cargo.
For the same reason vessels from foreign ports arriving in Britain with a
cargo, having once unloaded, then sailed in ballast coastwise to a coal
export port, particularly Cardiff, to acquire an outward cargo.24

The timing and pace of the adoption of steam was an amalgam of a
number of elements. These comprised the efficiency of the steamship
(in terms of coal consumption), the nature of cargo and the distances
involved. These represented the basic constituents of the market for
shipping. Other factors such as the importance of mails and passenger
traffic, the initiative of entrepreneurs and political considerations were
important at various times and in particular regions or trades but the
influences of the market were the prime determinants of the shift.30
Within these was that the steamship had to transport its own fuel: as
has been observed, ‘the factor inputs and costs of steamship transporta-
tion varied inversely with the length of the voyage from the source of

Previous discussions of the shift to steam at a regional level have
eschewed statistical analysis. In terms of a broad sweep of the regional
dimension we have but the comments of Harley made in two papers.
In summary, steamships gradually displaced sail first on the short

took the short trades to the Continent. In the late 1860s and 1870s
they took the North Atlantic. In the 1870s and 1880s, with the aid
of the Suez Canal, the steamship took over the trade to India and
the Far East. But sail still held on to the round-the world trades, the
Australian trade and trades to the west coast of the Americas, into
the twentieth century.33

rightly noted the progress of steam in the home trades. Alone among

in the next decade and a half was surprisingly modest. This might be
explained by the nature of the data - for the French trade extended

the participation of foreign vessels.38 After 1870 the shift to steam was

age. For other regions the picture presented is one of a gradual shift to
steam, with the crucial decades often occurring later than previously
believed. Above all else, it shows how blanket judgements obscure the
regional experience.

existing capital stock, the limitations of the steamship which were only
overcome over several decades, and differences in distance and commod-

Yet the idea of sudden change should not be totally jettisoned and
an examination of the tables reveals that in some regions the timing of
decisive change was short and sharp. For example, the gradual process
of the shift to steam is apparent from 1855 in the following regions:
Western Europe, West and East Mediterranean, Western and South
Africa and South America. But in these regions the decade of the 1870s
was unlike those before or after in terms of the extent and pace of the
shift: it was of a ‘great leap' character. Why this was so deserves more
research at a specialized level. The 1870s were also clearly the decisive
decade for the Far East region, which is perhaps more easily explained
by the opening of the Suez Canal and the explosion of demand for high
quality products from China and Japan which lent themselves to steam-
ship freight. Elsewhere, one could stress the 1880s as the crucial decade
for the North American region. Thus the shift to steam as an ‘event' or
sudden change may have some currency at a regional level and even
more so if individual countries and ports are considered.
But let us return to our basic findings that the process of change was
a gradual one. Two aspects remain to be considered: one, the outcome
of our analysis in the context of the historiography of the shift from sail
to steam; and two, the question of pace: was the process fast or slow?

a gradual process and one that in both aggregate and sectoral terms
occurred later than perhaps has been envisaged. This is particularly so
when one examines the situation as late as 1870 when steam formed
but one-third of tonnage entrances and even in the regions where
steam was most advanced, sail still comprised the majority of tonnage
entrances. Given this, can the view of dramatic and revolutionary
change held by contemporary writers be explained or justified?
Possibly, yes. Obviously contemporaries saw the extension of steam
taking place both generally and in almost all sectors, and this was
sufficient for them. But in addition to this, they viewed the progress
of steam from a different perspective from that of post-World War II
scholars. These different perspectives can be understood if we recognize
that the advance of steam was an advance in both communications and
transport. Contemporaries focused primarily on the communication
dimension, the fact that distance was shortened and information, pas-
sengers and mails could now move with unprecedented speed and regu-
larity. In this respect the steamship had wrought a revolution and had
certainly done so worldwide by 1860 and possibly earlier. By then liner
services covered almost all global routes. This is clear from the Table 4.1
data for 1860, when steam had penetrated virtually all regions, invari-
ably in the form of liner services.46 The steamship had made the world
a smaller place and one in which information and people travelled with
a new speed and certainty. This was progress and, compared with the
situation but a few decades earlier, revolutionary progress.
In contrast, post-1950 commentators have focused on the transport
of goods and, given the nature of world trade in the nineteenth century,
the freighting of bulk commodities. This

a smaller place and one in which information and people travelled with
a new speed and certainty. This was progress and, compared with the
situation but a few decades earlier, revolutionary progress.
In contrast, post-1950 commentators have focused on the transport
of goods and, given the nature of world trade in the nineteenth century,
the freighting of bulk commodities. This was the approach of Graham
and Harley. Their views were taken up by others and seemingly gained
greater weight by the adoption of the mantra (attributed to Robin Craig)
that in shipping it is ‘volumes not values' that are the crucial factor.47
In trade terms this is true, but shipping has always conveyed more than
goods; the sea has also been a highway for the transit of people and
information. It was this - which might be considered the ‘value' dimen-
sion of shipping - that fired the imagination and interpretation of
contemporaries. It also fuelled the development of an integrated world
economy in the second half of the nineteenth century.
Finally, the second issue, the pace of change. Here, although both
contemporaries by implication and recent scholars more specifically
have expressed views, it is hard to see how any clear judgement might
be made. ‘Fast' and ‘slow' are relative terms and are difficult to apply
in an objective fashion. Scholars examining the transition must make

58 The Progress of the Steamship
their own judgement. Our own view, given that the steamship only
came into existence in 1810, and moreover, as is evidenced by the table,
was of very little numerical significance in the overall statistics in 1855,
that the virtual complete replacement of sail by steam within less than
half a century (bearing in mind the millennia of the age of sail), cannot
but be regarded as a rapid process. Certainly, this must be the verdict
in the context of the long run of history. It is this standpoint that most
likely influenced nineteenth-century commentators who, in the brief
span of their own lifetimes, witnessed a transformation of all that had
gone before.

The Advantages of Water
Carriage: Scale Economies
and Shipping Technology,
c. 1870-2000
Yrjö Kaukiainen
… a broad wheeled wagon attended by two men and
drawn by eight horses in about six weeks time car-
ries and brings back between London and Edinburgh
nearly 4 tons weight of goods. In about the same
time a ship navigated by six or eight men, and sailing
between the ports of London and Leith, frequently
carries and brings back 200 tons weight of goods.
Since such, therefore, are the advantages of water car-
riage, it is natural that the first improvements of art
and industry should be made where this conveniency
opens the whole world to a market for the produce of
every sort of labour.
(Adam Smith,The Wealth of Nations)
Adam Smith was one of the first to emphasize the superiority of water
transport for the carriage of goods. Had he lived long enough to see the
rapid development of railways in the mid-nineteenth century he might
have moderated his views slightly. However, the transition from sail to
steam shipping, which gained momentum in the 1870s, produced a
new leap forward for water transport: between 1880 and the First World
War, transport costs in coastal shipping seem to have declined almost
40 per cent faster than on British railways.1 Similar observations have
also been made for the period 1960-1990, and we may, indeed, con-
clude that ‘the advantages of water carriage' have increased even in the
longer term.2 Adam Smith's example suggests that labour productivity
in coastal shipping outpaced that in road transport by the ratio four-
teen to one. In the beginning of the third millennium, the overall cost
64

efficiency (price per ton-mile) of short-sea shipping seems to be some 25
times higher than that of long-trader trucking.3 Thus even after the late
nineteenth century, there have been other technical ‘revolutions' lead-
ing to a continuous, more or less regular, growth of transport efficiency
in both ocean and coastal shipping. A macro-level proof is the fact that
the global merchant tonnage grew about sixtyfold in 150 years, while
the respective growth of output - the physical volume of cargo carried -
grew at least twice as much.4
The long-term growth of technical efficiency, and in particular the
development after World War II, was directly related to an improvement
in the hauling efficiency of typical merchant ships. Table 5.1 shows how
much cargo different ships at different times could load, and how far
they could move this in one day (how many ton-miles they produced
in 24 hours). Such a gauge is, of course, simplistic in disregarding eco-
nomic variables, but all ships included in this eclectic list were (or are)
well established types and, therefore, economically viable in their own
times. Moreover, putting a strong emphasis on physical performance is
by no means irrelevant in our globalized world. Huge quantities of raw
materials and the counter-currents of finished goods are carried across
the oceans all the time.
Table 5.1 shows that even quite modest-sized modern ships are fifty
times more efficient than medium-sized sailing vessels of the 1870s,
or early steamers. A comparison of the biggest ships would show an
even greater difference. While the table cannot pretend any degree of
statistical representativeness, we can still make a few basic propositions.
First, in the long run, improvements in the mechanical efficiency of
shipping have depended on physical size rather than speed through
the water. The average size of merchant ships increased from about
700 to over 24,000 deadweight tons, or thirty-fourfold, between 1880
and 2008, while cruising speeds have hardly grown fourfold.5 This is
explained by hydrodynamics: wave-making resistance, in particular,
limits economical speeds, while there are no absolute upper limits -
apart from water depth - to the size of floating structures.6 Only during
the transition from sail to steam were substantial advantages gained

Thus, liners did not need high deadweight capacity and, travelling
lightly loaded, were able to achieve high speeds - in the 1930s over 30
knots. They also grew bigger than any other ships so far. Not until 1899
was a ship longer than the 211 metres of Brunel's extravagant 1858
giant the Great Eastern launched. However, this was followed by a race
for the biggest ship of the world; in the 1930s, no less than three ships
exceeding an overall length of 300 metres were built.8 The passenger
liner boom started with the rapid growth of emigration to the USA and
it died out with the transatlantic airlines. Recently, however, it has expe-
rienced a rebirth in the guise of modern cruising ships; the biggest ones
have already exceeded the old Atlantic liners in sheer size.9
The real workhorses of the seas, however, remained much smaller
until after World War II. At the beginning of the twentieth century,
cargo ships of over 10,000 tons deadweight (or 150 metres long) were
still rare. While a few cargo liners and oil tankers approaching 15,000
tons and ore carriers of about 20,000 tons deadweight were built in the
interwar period, the Liberty ships (11,000 dwt) and T2 tankers (around
17,000 dwt) still represented the upper end of the size scale for cargo
ships in the early 1950s.10 Soon, however, these were dwarfed by a
‘revolution' that was starting in oil shipping. In the wake of the Korean
War the first tanker exceeding 50,000 dwt was launched. This started
an escalation during which several ‘magical' limits were rapidly passed:
100,000 dwt in 1959, 200,000 in 1966, 300,000 in 1968 and 500,000
in 1976.11

oil was replacing coal as the most important source of energy in rapidly
growing industrialized countries. Actual demand was, however, also
affected by unexpected non-economic factors. First, the Korean War
suddenly boosted the demand for fuel transports across the Pacific and
tanker freights soared dramatically. At the same

ships designed to carry both liquid and dry bulk cargoes, in order to

of ships, compared with their deadweight capacity, were generous, this
was a viable combination. After the 1966 load line revision even dry
cargo ships with tight and strong steel hatches and segmented cargo
spaces were allowed deeper loading. Subsequently, earlier ore-oil carriers
were replaced by the OBOs (ore-bulk-oil) which could fill all holds with
one medium-heavy bulk commodity, or one another (or each third)
with heavy ore. They were often the biggest bulkers afloat but, as long
as the oil boom continued, most of these only carried crude oil, gaining
little from their built-in flexibility.15

At the same time as the two bulk revolutions were in full swing,
another was just brewing. Containers appeared in American coastal
transport at the end of the 1950s and, after international standards
were issued for ‘boxes' (1965), they started to transform liner shipping
all over the world. At first, the strongest impact of this innovation was
felt in ports: it became much faster, in particular if efficient cranes were
available, to load and unload big standard-size steel containers instead
of a large variety of boxes, crates, rolls, bags, bales, and all kinds of par-
cels in which finished goods had so far been brought on board. It has
been estimated that, ton for ton, the handling of container cargo only
required between five and seven per cent of the labour demanded by
traditional general cargo.17
The idea of specialized container ships was, however, only beginning
to develop in the early 1960s. At first, containers were carried as deck
cargo on ordinary dry cargo vessels, Ro-Ro vessels, converted liners and
even tankers. Often, a few container bays were built in existing holds
or a ship was lengthened (‘jumbo-ized') by adding new container sec-
tions. Such semi-container ships suffered from slow turnaround times
in ports because conventional cargoes still had to be handled by the
old methods. Moreover, their sizes remained modest, seldom exceeding
15,000 tons deadweight.18
The first generation of newly built full (‘cellular') container ships in
the late 1960s already had full-width cargo hatches, enabling contain-

These three specific waves have produced the modern shipping
revolution. As a result, the overall weight of the respective shipping
categories was naturally increased: as early as 1986 - even excluding
gas and chemical tankers and oil bulk vessels - they comprised 66 per
cent of the world total gross tonnage, and this increased to no less
than 76 per cent in 2008. In contrast, general cargo ships (traditional
liners and tramp ships) which still around 1970 represented a third of
the tonnage, now only amount to some 7 per cent. Moreover, there
has been hardly any growth of average size in this category. On the
other hand, two special groups, liquid gas tankers and passenger ves-
sels (both conventional and Ro-Ro, and in particular cruising ships)
have recently experienced rapid growth in both total tonnages and
average sizes. Yet these still represent less than 10 per cent of total
global tonnage.24
In addition to a sheer multiplication of ship sizes, shipping efficiency
has also been improved by another crucial long-term development,
increasing specialization. As terms like tanker, bulk carrier and cellu-
lar container ship indicate, ships are presently being designed for an
increasingly narrow range of cargoes. In the late nineteenth century,
most cargo-carrying ships were of very similar general configuration.
For example, if we divide their deadweight tonnage by the volume of
cargo holds in cubic metres, the ratio (corresponding with the specific
gravity of cargo when all cargo spaces are full) generally fluctuated at
around 0.6-0.7, a relationship which, apart from the weight of the
empty ship and basic hydrostatic laws, resulted from contemporary
load line (freeboard) regulations.25 In practice, standard cargo ships
were optimal for carriage of medium-weight goods, such as grain or rice,
which filled the cargo hold without sinking the ship too deep. When
carrying heavy cargo like iron or ores, the ship sank to the ‘marks' long
before the cargo space was full, while with a light cargo the deadweight
capacity could not be fully exploited.

In addition to geographical constraints, ship sizes are also limited in
practice by economic considerations. In the early 1970s, a theory of
optimal ship size was developed to explain such factors, based on the
observation that positive scale economies only applied to ships at sea.
While hauling costs per ton decreased with ship size, costs per ton in
port (loading, unloading, port charges, warehousing, etc.) increased.
Accordingly, the total costs-per-ton function seemed to be U-shaped,
with the relevant optimum size being indicated by its lowest level.33

the dry cargo sector the diseconomies of scale in ports have decreased to
such a degree that theoretical optimum sizes tend to exceed the actual
maximum sizes (as limited by, for example, the depth of water in the
relevant ports) by a substantial margin.34 Finally, it must also be remem-
bered that there is at least one sector of shipping which enjoys full scale
advantages even in port: in tankers the capacity of pipelines and pumps
can be upgraded according to carrying capacity. Big crude carriers can

be loaded and unloaded in the same time - nowadays usually twelve
hours - as smaller product tankers. In this case, it will be impossible to
determine the optimal ship size in the traditional way.
It is obvious that actual ship sizes cannot be explained by economic
functions that only consider the costs of producers (shipowners); the
costs of users (shippers) must also be taken into account. The fact that
different commodities are traded in widely varying quantities is a tan-
gible consequence of the constraints imposed by trade volumes and
the economic interests of shippers. Raw materials and fuels, such as
crude oil, coal and ores, are frequently conveyed by shiploads exceed-
ing 100,000 tons, while the typical parcel sizes for grain or sugar fluc-
tuate around 50,000 and 80,000 tons, those for steel and semi-finished
metal products seldom exceed 10,000 tons, and sawn wood from
Scandinavia is typically sold by shiploads of 4,000 to 5,000 tons.35 In
all cases the volumes are a function of storage and capital costs of the
shippers - not surprisingly, they are higher for cheap than more valu-
able commodities. On the other hand, parcel sizes are also affected
by hauling distances: if these are long enough, the savings in sea
freight (achieved by using bigger vessels) may outweigh the increase
in inventory costs.36 However - remembering that the price elasticities
of many typical bulk products are fairly low - it may be claimed that
the maximum stock size that importers are willing to accept would
be a more important factor than the actual price development of
the relevant commodities. The importance of storage and inventory
costs has recently been increasingly stressed by the ‘just-in/on-time'
principles in industrial logistics. Instead of replenishing stores with
a few big shiploads, many buyers prefer a more continuous flow of
smaller consignments. Such strategies are quite effective in checking
the growth of parcel sizes.

Summing up, it seems that the scope and impact of scale economies
have effectively been restricted - in addition to the more or less inevi-
table geographical factors - by both the relative diseconomies of cargo
handling and inventory costs. Thus, the optimum ship size is closely
related to the actual trade and, in particular, the typical parcel sizes in
the specific sectors. Many shipping companies are therefore faced with
the fact that their customers are demanding ships which, in terms of
voyage costs, would be sub-optimal and, because employing a more
‘size-optimal' ship half empty would involve much worse diseconomies
of scale, they also have to build ships which fit the relevant markets.
Thus, it is no wonder that ‘maxi-size' tankers and bulk carriers still
remain less popular than some thirty or forty years ago. The slowly
growing average sizes in both fleets seem to reflect the fact that scale
economies are still working within a number of niches with medium-
sized ships. On the other hand, at least one major sector, general cargo
carriers, does not present any such trend.

However, the logistic formula of inverse relationships between ship
sizes and the value of cargo no longer holds when we come to the most
valuable end of the commodity scale. While it is true that finished con-
sumer goods are traded in small parcel sizes, rather by containerloads
than shiploads, such ‘general cargo' will normally be loaded on board a
common carrier like (the earlier) cargo liners or modern container ships.
In this case, the size of a single parcel is not important at all because a
vast number of these can be combined on one big ship, thus enjoying
all the scale economies that can be attained within the scope of actual
geographic constraints. Therefore it seems obvious that the rapid esca-
lation of ship sizes which really started in the 1990s will continue for
quite a while. As container ships are carrying light goods this progress
will not, in the short term, be much hampered by draft restrictions in
major ports. The main limiting factor will be the overall size and growth
of markets, which determine how well the increasingly big container
carriers can be filled with paying cargo. However, as the scope of con-
tainerizable goods is still widening, the growth may exceed the general
growth of maritime trade.
Even this coin has a reverse side. Containers are not only carried
from port to port but even from door to door. The overall logistics thus
involve a high number of collection and distribution terminals. In order
to harvest the best profits of size economies on long intercontinental
routes the big ships sailing to ‘hubs' need to be supplemented by feeder
ships cruising to and from the smaller ports. The growth of ocean traffic
therefore results in a proportional increase in short-sea container capac-
ity (see Figure 5.3). The size of feeders, however, may not automatically
rise because ports visited do not always allow that. Moreover, the opti-
mum feeder size has regularly been affected by two other constraints:
the overall size of the respective local markets and the frequency of
services required by customers. Although bigger ships could handle all
cargo by one trip a month a smaller one sailing each week usually sells
better. With the growth of traffic the latter factor will, however, be of
temporary importance, and at least on the major short-sea routes the
size of feeders has already started to grow.

Modern shipping revolutions have resulted from a complex interplay
of technological and economic development. For practical reasons, the
present discussion has focused on the macro-, or industry level, in the
economies of scale of ship sizes, not of firm sizes. Even the develop-
ment of port technology has been dealt with as a backdrop to shipping
technology, rather than as an independent variable affecting the over-
all efficiency of shipping and its different cost components. The basic

Building the Networks of Trade:
Perspectives on Twentieth-Century
Maritime History
Espen Ekberg, Even Lange and Eivind Merok
The development of maritime history as a specialized field of research is
an impressive testament to the founders of the International Maritime
Economic History Association.1 Skip Fischer's own publications, together
with his relentless efforts as editor of theInternational Journal of Maritime
History, have contributed significantly to placing seaborne transport
at the centre of the international economic history of the nineteenth
century. As a result of the collective efforts made in the field since the
1970s, most economists, economic historians and general historians
now recognize the pivotal role played by the maritime sector in foster-
ing a truly global economy before World War One (WWI).
Much of the corresponding literature for the twentieth century,
however, points to a rather different conclusion. In a recent work of
synthesis, Ronald Findlay and Kevin O'Rourke argued that the defining
difference between nineteenth- and twentieth-century globalizations is
a shift in driving forces. According to Findlay and O'Rourke, the glo-
balization process of the nineteenth century had an ‘overwhelmingly
technological ... origin, with falling transportation costs driving com-
modity markets closer together', while the process during the twentieth
century was ‘much more political in origin'.2 Their conclusion - widely
shared - is that the maritime sector had little impact on the globaliza-
tion process characterizing the latter half of the twentieth century. This
view has not been seriously questioned by maritime historians, who
either have ignored the period or been reluctant to link their findings
to broader trends within the international economy of the period.3 The
consequence is that maritime history has been marginalized in ongoing
debates on the factors behind the expansion of the post-1950 interna-
tional economy.

This chapter discusses the role of the maritime sector in the interna-
tional economy during the latter half of the twentieth century. By doing
this we seek to accomplish two things. First, we wish to raise awareness
of the actual importance played by the maritime industry in shaping
the development of the international economy during this period.
Second, we also seek to encourage maritime historians to deal more
eagerly with post-1945 maritime history. Our argument also falls into
two parts. First, we present and discuss recent work in economic history
on the development of ocean transport and its role in the growth of the
international economy after World War Two (WWII). A key issue here
is the adequacy of existing measures of freight costs and their ability
to capture the influence of the maritime sector on the international
economy. While it has been repeatedly claimed that real freight costs
did not decline, we will argue that this interpretation hinges on some
technical assumptions that are debatable.
The second part of the chapter suggests an alternative approach. The
role of maritime transport in the development of the international
economy, we argue, cannot be evaluated on the basis of the price of
ocean transport alone. In this period, the maritime sector went through
dramatic technological, organizational and institutional shifts that
allowed for both rapid expansion of capacity and dramatic improve-
ments in the quality of services provided. To our knowledge, there
exist no studies that attempt to adjust for improvements in the qual-
ity of services in existing freight series. Inference from aggregate data
series may therefore be misleading. To find out how the technological,
organizational and institutional changes in the shipping industry have
affected international trade patterns, we think it is necessary to explore
in more detail how these preconditions for trade came into being. In
such a process, the study of the maritime sector and specifically the
actions of shipping entrepreneurs may provide substantial new insights.
We try to show the fruitfulness of such an approach by way of two case
studies on the post-WWII growth of trade in raw materials, more specifi-
cally coking coal and chemicals.

Shipping and post-WWII freight rate developments
According to the prominent maritime economist Martin Stopford,
the shipping industry of the post-1950 period went through a process
of unparalleled change. By 1980, Stopford argues, ‘there was noth-
ing left of the proud, conservative shipping industry which sailed
confidently into the 1950s'.4 While this is perhaps an overstatement,

90 Building the Networks of Trade
fundamental changes had indeed taken place: The small general cargo
carriers and tramp ships that still dominated merchant shipping in 1950
had gradually been replaced by large bulk carriers, container ships and
ships designed to carry specialized cargoes such as cars, chemicals and
liquefied gas. Scale economies, automation, standardization and spe-
cialization were applied to increase the cargo handling capacity and
the efficiency of the fleet. In addition, institutional changes such as
the increasing use of flags of convenience were introduced to cut costs.
In later years, organizational innovations in the operation of shipping
companies also caused a ‘decomposition of the value chain' within the
industry as a whole. Shipping companies increasingly tended to out-
source many of the operations that traditionally had been a natural part
of their day-to-day operations.5
Despite the compelling organizational, technological and institu-
tional evidence indicating radical changes in the transportation system,
economic historians have been reluctant to ascribe importance to the
maritime sector in the development of the twentieth- century interna-
tional economy. The primary evidence supporting such a stance is the
apparent stability in the cost of ocean transport. The Chicago-based
economist David Hummels has published what is probably the most
referenced analysis of the development of transportation costs in the
latter half of the twentieth century.6 Hummels' conclusion is, simply
put, that ocean freights did not in fact decline in real terms and hence
that the many obvious innovations in shipping during this period did
not play any fundamental role in the growth of world trade. Instead, he
points to the developments in air freight as a main driving force:

The disagreements about the interpretation of freight rates after
WWII, then, boils down to a question of choice of deflators, and more
precisely how one should interpret the freight factor. Compared with
the more traditional GDP deflator, the freight factor, or commodity
deflator, is claimed to be more suitable when estimating the barriers
to trade posed by seaborne transport as the GDP deflator ‘includes
non-tradables and many tradables not carried on all routes'.17 The
basic idea is that when transport costs fall relative to the price of a
given product, the fall will stimulate trade in that product, similarly
to the way a fall inad valorem tariffs stimulates trade. If, on the other
hand, the relative price of transport is stable or increases, it hinders
trade growth. In fact, as Persson argues, ‘transport costs can be seen
as an implicit ad valorem tariff'.18 It is on this basis that Hummels

A second challenge relates to the actual appropriateness of commod-

Kaukiainen, the price of the cargoes that are shipped via tramps and the

fall, the supply of a given product - and hence the price competition -
typically increases, as more distant sources can be effectively brought

commodity prices. In other instances, the cycles of freights and com-
modity prices are not harmonized at all, causing random fluctuations
in the freight factor. An obvious example is the oil price shock of the
mid-1970s. With drastic increases in oil prices, the ratio of oil price to
oil freights increased dramatically, and hence it would seem as if the
real cost of transporting oil decreased much more dramatically than it
actually did.24

Building the networks of trade
Between 1960 and 1990 total transport of industrial raw materials
almost quadrupled.32 This massive growth of trade in industrial raw
materials could not have been accomplished without groundbreaking
transformations in the existing transport system. To be able to carry
all this trade, the total volume of shipping room had to be drastically
enlarged. And indeed, between 1960 and 1975 alone, the total ton-
nage of dry bulk carriers increased more than fivefold, from 15 to 85
million gross tons.33 Completely new types of ships were developed in
this process, such as specialized dry bulk carriers and various types of
combination carriers. And, of course, the average size of these ships was
substantially enlarged. While Liberty ships at about 10,000 tons dead-
weight (dwt) carried most of the dry bulk shipments in 1950, by the mid
1970s, the size of an average dry bulk carrier was about 30,000 dwt. By
2006 it had reached 56,000 dwt.34
All in all, the growth of the post-war raw materials trade rested on a
series of transformations and improvements in the existing seaborne
transport system. When explaining international trade growth, such
processes are, however, seldom recognized as important and instead
taken as given. But, by neglecting to investigate how technological and
institutional preconditions for trade are in fact developed, one only
gets part of the story of international trade growth. Individuals have to
establish the conditions necessary for that trade to actually take place.
An adequate historical understanding of trade growth should put these
processes at centre stage.

A good place to start such an enquiry is to study the actions of ship-
ping entrepreneurs, and their role in the growth of a specific trade.
Take as a first example the growth of trade in coking coal. Coking coal
is a major raw material in the steel industry and the increasing trade
reflected the growth of steel production both in Europe and in Japan.
The leading suppliers of coal were the North Americans and later
Australia and Indonesia. In 1950 general purpose carriers such as the
Liberty ships still handled most of the coal trade. In fact, so dominant
was the Liberty ship in this trade that coal (as well as iron ore, grain
and bauxite) was traded in standard ‘Liberty ship loads'. The increasing
demand for long-haul transport of coal implied that much could be
gained by increasing the size of the ships. Steelworks were increasingly
moved to the seaside to eliminate the need for landward transport of
incoming coal and ores. However, the most substantial savings could be
accomplished by making the seaborne leg less costly. Shipping entrepre-
neurs came to play a vital role in this process.
The price of steel was relevant to shipowners. If the price of steel
could be reduced, ships would be cheaper to build. This was the main
idea behind the New York-based Norwegian shipowner Erling Dekke
Næss' initial interest in the coal trade. When Næss became interested
in how coal was transported, he had already developed a substantial
tanker business, with a total of 20 new buildings on order by 1957.35
When developing the tanker fleet, his principal strategy had been
to invest in larger vessels in order to reap economies of scale in ship
design. When first learning about the coal trade, Næss found that there
had been few attempts at introducing similar strategies, and came to

double motivation for shipowners. The operation would be profitable,

economically advantageous.

The simple point to be made from these examples is that the expansion
of international trade - in our examples the coal and the chemical trades -
was not an automatic process. It required people to take action and trans-
form the whole transport system on which the trade was based. Shipowners
stood at the centre of these processes. They were central in developing new
ship designs, in linking together the producers and receivers of raw materi-
als, and in organizing new and innovative ways of financing and building
the ships needed to take care of the growing trade. As Næss puts it: ‘The
job was to tie up the links in the chain. The steel companies would buy
the coking coal to produce the steel which the shipyards would use to
build the ships which I would order to carry the coal.'50 Historical analysis
of these trends in the development of shipping provides us with important
new insights into how the expansion of the international economy during
the post-war years unfolded and was accomplished.

stick to the conclusion that as long as the commodity-deflated price of

of the twentieth century, the contribution from the maritime sector
in increasing the level of international trade must have been limited.
Maritime historians have only shown limited interest in post-1945
development trends, and to the extent that they have dealt with such
issues, they have largely refrained from linking their findings to more
general aspects of the international economy. As a consequence, the
prevalent interpretation remains that while the shipping sector pro-
vided a crucial stimulus for the integration of the world economy before
1914, the same role is ascribed after 1945 to trade liberalization, and
shipping is largely left out of the equation.
In this chapter we have questioned the viability of this interpretation
and, as an attempt to bypass it, argued the need for maritime historians
to engage more eagerly with twentieth-century development trends.
First we discussed existing interpretations of freight rate developments.
While data supporting a substantial decline in freight rates for crucial
commodities during the post-war period have been widely published,
the usual practice of deflating the freight rate with the price of the
transported commodity has led scholars to conclude that real freight
rates have not declined. As suggested above, we believe that it is equally
reasonable to argue that the fall in prices of industrial raw materials
and freight rates were related processes, as lowered transportation costs
increased availability and price competition for key industrial raw mate-
rials. Using such a deflator may therefore yield misleading results.
The dual process of decline in freight rates and the falling price of key
industrial raw materials had substantial consequences. The location of
industrial production had, since the industrial revolution, been heavily
determined by the availability of industrial raw materials, and this was
still very much the case in the early 1950s. In the following decades,
however, new industrial centres relying on importation of such materi-
als emerged (most notably Japan), and industrial production economies
spread to new geographical destinations. The establishment of an inter-
national market for key industrial raw materials thus removed a critical
limitation for emerging industrial centres and served as a preamble to
later developments of geographically dispersed production regimes.

and geographically scattered industrial centres, is, of course, highly
dependent on the development of modern transportation systems. The
demand for increasingly complex shipping services was met by a mas-
sive expansion of capacity as well as crucial changes in quality, not eas-

difficult to envisage that the transportation needs of the industrial sec-
tor at the outset of the twenty-first century could have been served by
Liberty ships and manual loading of goods. In the absence of massive
technological and organizational improvements, it is more realistic to
expect increased transportation costs, and severe difficulties in sustain-
ing the global industrial economy that has emerged since WWII.
The adoption of new organizational models and technologies is often
described in a manner that conveys the impression that these strategies
faced few challenges. As an alternative hypothesis, we would suggest
that the development and adoption of certain aspects of modern bulk
handling system was a very complicated and challenging process for
the participants. While the advantages of adopting new technologies
are obvious with the benefit of hindsight, participants were faced with
several risks when committing resources to such projects. First of all,
the development of specialized bulk handling vessels demanded invest-
ments in new ships where the cost could not be recouped by the ship-
owner if the deal went sour. Second, the development of new loading
arrangements demanded coordinated commitment of investments in
specialized equipment, and represented high risks for participants not
knowing who would reap the economic gains of such investments. The
technologies adopted in the shipping sector thus shared characteristics
that tend to predetermine market failure and prompt vertical integra-
tion, but only rarely do we find this pattern adopted in the sector.

of how maritime historians can illuminate these processes. In these sec

arrangements demanded coordinated commitment of investments in

that tend to predetermine market failure and prompt vertical integra-

Our examples from the coal and chemical trades provide some hints
of how maritime historians can illuminate these processes. In these sec-

from participants outside the shipping industry. It is exactly this ability
to transgress the shipping sector - in coordinating the interests of par-
ties across the value chain - that gave the shipping entrepreneurs in
our examples their central position. Identifying such transnational and
trans-sectoral entrepreneurial networks may allow us to understand more
fully the innovation processes at work in the international transporta-
tion sector after WWII. Placing shipping entrepreneurs at the centre of
such frameworks may also serve as a complement to research focusing
on individual shipowners or on the rise and fall of merchant fleets. This,

The Development of Commercial
Infrastructure for World Shipping
Gordon Boyce
The chapter examines the development of elements that in combination
provided vital commercial infrastructure for the global shipping
industry. Specifically, it discusses the roles of key institutions, such as
the Baltic Mercantile and Shipping Exchange,Lloyd's Register of Shippinggg,
the Lloyd's of London insurance market and various commodity
and financial markets, in facilitating exchanges needed to sustain
oceanic transport. In addition to these institutions' formal attributes,
for example, their constitutions and rules, the discussion considers
their informal characteristics, including the customs, routines and
behavioural patterns observed by participants. Together, these formal
and informal institutional arrangements have supported shipping by
disseminating information, reducing uncertainty and mitigating trans-
action costs associated with this volatile industry.1 The chapter also
pursues a secondary, somewhat abstract aim; it explores how markets
operate and attempts to show how various mechanisms have generated
efficiencies.
Context
Historians have long recognized that Britain underwent a commercial
‘revolution' long before it experienced the first industrial revolution. The
former phenomenon entailed the development of institutions that facil-
itated growing trade. C.H. Lee argued that as early as the eighteenth cen-
tury, Britain possessed a strong, London-based service sector that proved
to be an enduring cornerstone of the economy.2 Cain and Hopkins used
the term ‘gentlemanly capitalism' to describe financial and social links
along with codes of conduct that emerged in the seventeenth century
and supported transaction-facilitating bonds of trust.3 These behavioural
106

patterns, based on the expectation that one's word was their bond,
shaped the operations of the institutions examined below.
Although regional centres developed local institutions that encouraged
trade, London was the centre of the nation's commercial infrastructure.
(Indeed, from the seventeenth century, the capital was the nation's most
significant port and generated two-thirds of all customs revenue.)4 Many
of the key elements within this construct grew out of a seemingly quaint
venue: the coffee house. The first of these establishments appeared in
London about 1650, and their number increased to over 80 within a
decade as coffee drinking became fashionable. Individual coffee houses
attracted specific occupational groups. Medical men congregated at Child's
in St Paul's Churchyard, while writers attended Will's house in Covent
Garden. In the City, traders conducted business on the Royal Exchange
but after hours they gathered at coffee houses. Edward Lloyd's venue
attracted shipowners and merchants, as did Garrway's, while Jonathan's
catered to security dealers. Commodity traders frequented the Virginia
and Maryland, and metal dealers visited the Jerusalem coffee house.5
Eventually, all of these groups removed to purpose-built facilities which
only subscribing members could enter. The original coffee houses arose
from the need for information and the face-to-face contact so vital in
building the trust required for exchange. The shift to dedicated buildings
reflected demand for rules and regulated admittance - information was
valuable and needed to be protected - but all the new venues remained
concentrated within the City.
Regional centres developed compact districts where businessmen
gathered. Graeme Milne found that ‘old street layouts and spatial rela-
tionships between the focal points of business life - offices, exchanges,
banks, bars - were often maintained' despite rapid urban growth.6
Traders walked between these venues to gather intelligence and meet
clients, suppliers, and specialist intermediaries. Maritime business
was highly service-oriented, and it required a ‘hands on, face-to-face'
approach to respond swiftly to changing customer needs. A writer in
1881 observed of merchants that ‘half of their life seems to be spent
out of doors', and Bertie Bates [shipowners] intimated that informa-
tion emanated from the ‘flags[tones]'.7 Provincial worthies built grand
exchanges for the same reasons that actuated their

for a place where the feeling of the trade could be ascertained'.9
Those attending the floor of the Stock Exchange could detect
