market direction by the quality of the sound arising from open cry
trading.10 Moreover, this system of exchange gave rise to a floating
price known to all but unattainable when pairs of bargainers trans-
acted in private.11
A measure of price convergence occurred on a national scale as
regional markets were linked more closely to London by improved
communication.12 Kaukiainen found that the speed of information
transfer increased more rapidly before the advent of the telegraph
than it did afterwards due to more efficient land and sea transport.13
Nevertheless, the telegraph did provide the first near-instantaneous
communication mode. It is significant that by 1914 Britain controlled
the largest part of the global telegraphic network (281,828 km versus
100,831 for the USA and over 43,000 each for Germany and France).14
As Scholl points out, the cable system contributed ‘decisively to the
pre-eminence of the City of London as the mercantile-financial capital
of the world'.15 The radio had less of an integrating effect perhaps, but
its capacity to provide immediate information regarding incidents at sea
induced Lloyd's to involve itself in the system's extension.

Lloyd's of London
Lloyd's of London (an insurance market, distinct from Lloyd's Register
of Shipping - see below) originated in a coffee house that Edward Lloyd
(c. 1688-1726) ran in Tower Street and later Lombard Street. The estab-
lishment attracted merchants and shipowners who conducted marine
insurance business or commodity trading as an adjunct to their main
line of trade. By 1771, unfettered speculation and ‘shameful practices'
induced the leading figures at Lloyd's to restrict entry to respectable
businessmen who paid an annual subscription and to form a committee
to provide governance.16 These developments, which marked the formal
beginnings of the modern Lloyd's insurance market, were underscored
by removal three years later to the Royal Exchange Building. After a
sojourn at South Seas House between 1838 and 1844 while the Exchange
was being rebuilt after a disastrous fire, Lloyd's returned there. In 1928,
Lloyd's moved to a purpose-built venue in Leadenhall Street, and thirty
years later took up residence in Lime Street.17
The legislative foundations of Lloyd's developed slowly. In an effort
to enhance competition, in 1720 Parliament passed an Act that gave
Lloyd's and two chartered fire insurance companies authority to write
marine policies. However, in practice these organizations kept to their
main sphere of operation. Four years later, the Marine Insurance Act

allowed other organizations to enter the business, and more companies
(mostly new joint-stock enterprises) appeared during the US civil war to
become enduring players in the industry. Nevertheless, the provisions
laid down by Lloyd's Committee provided a regulatory framework by
common consent. This situation was formalized by the Lloyd's Act of
1870 which incorporated the Society and gave its rules the force of law.
Under this legislation, Lloyd's was confined to the marine business,
but innovators like Cuthbert Heath and Frederick Martin introduced
non-marine policies (burglary, loss of jewellery and motors) outside
the scope of the Act.18 Further legislation in 1911 permitted Lloyd's to
provide all types of non-marine cover.
Within both sectors different figures working at Lloyd's carried out
specific functions and employed an esoteric terminology. Underwriters
covered risks; they derived their title from the practice of signing their
initials under the information laid out on an insurance ‘slip'.19 This
document disclosed particulars of the cover sought and related condi-
tions but did not constitute a contract enforceable at law. Nevertheless,
no underwriter would ever repudiate a slip he had initialled for fear of
completely destroying his reputation and being expelled from Lloyd's.
Underwriting agents solicited business for underwriters who often gave
these agents a ‘binder' that described the type of insurance they wished
to cover and the general conditions they found acceptable. People
seeking insurance engaged an underwriting broker who laid the business
before underwriters or their agents.
To spread risk,syndicateswere formed; partnerships and firms i nitially
were not allowed to underwrite insurance. Syndicates consisted of sev-
eral names (another term for underwriter) who were so called because
they were well-known figures of substantial means and because they
initialled slips. In return for a premium, the amount of which reflected
the probability of loss, each name accepted a ‘line', that is a portion of
the total risk. For example, ‘FAA' took up £150,000 on Titanic's £1 mil-
lion policy. However, the name would be liable only for the figure he
nominated (viz. £150,000) since the risk entailedseveralnotjoint liabil-
ity. Moreover, names' liabilities were not limited; their personal assets
could be claimed

and its standardization facilitated rapid and accurate consideration,
thereby reducing transaction costs. The wording and form of policies
also arose from usage as implicit understanding unfolded over time.

The physical layout of Lloyd's, along with the routines and informal
rules observed by participants, enhanced the efficiency of the market.
Each venue occupied by Lloyd's consisted of a public area and a sub-
scription room open only to fee paying members. The latter space in
the new building had a glass domed ceiling and a stone floor both of
which echoed the sound of conversations and thereby gave members
an indication of the state of trade, even though open cry bidding was
not used, as it was at most other markets. Around the edges of the trad-
ing room were a series of ‘boxes', much like the booths in the original
coffee house, where underwriters held shop. To an extent, the location
of boxes relative to each other shaped network formation and, subject
to unwritten rules (see below), generated flows of preferential informa-
tion.22 At one end of the room were placed volumes containing public
information about ship movements, safe arrivals and losses. In the
same location there was a rostrum attended, as in the old coffee house,
by a crier who called out fresh news for all to hear. In addition, the

movement of brokers and agents around the room and congregations
at specific boxes conveyed information to knowledgeable participants
who recognized major figures by sight.
Such movement was initiated when a broker with a blank slip sought
out an underwriter who was a ‘good lead'. This name would be widely
known as a person of stature and as an expert in assessing the type of
risk being offered. The premium he quoted and the size of the line he
took conveyed powerful signals to other underwriters whom the broker
subsequently approached to place the rest of the slip. For example, one
highly regarded nineteenth-century name was John Julius Angerstein,
and such was his renown that slips he led were called ‘Julians', the
Roman connotation perhaps conveying imperial solidity. Moreover,
some syndicates continued to use the initials of a deceased member
who was revered as the lead name because it was widely recognized as
a strong inducement for others to follow.
Brokers did not, however, deal exclusively with a select number of
underwriters; that is, their networks were not ‘tight'. Instead, they
operated across the market seeking out names who had the expertise
required to assess a specific type of risk they might be called up to cover
for their clients. Underwriters specialized in handling risks related to
hulls, cargo types or particular trade routes. Thus, brokers needed to
know who to approach for a particular type of risk in order to complete
a slip quickly and efficiently.
As brokers moved among boxes they observed unwritten rules that
smoothed exchange and safeguarded preferential information. For
instance, brokers queued at boxes -never did one push himself before
others - and it was understood that eavesdropping while others trans-
acted was not acceptable. Thus, knowledge flowed across the market
to varying degrees; in important respects comprehensive transfer was
impeded by artificial constraints and working relationships that pre-
served sensitive details.

Lloyd's provided the required facilities. The Underwriters' Claim Office
investigated losses and responded to incidents with the aid of Lloyd's
Salvage Association which developed contacts with surveyors, salvors,
and repairers across the world. The Claims Office also acted as adjustor
and compiled data to inform the evolution of underwriting practice.23

Lloyd's collected data on claims and other operating matters to
develop feedback that informed risk assessment and the refinement
of systems. In 1850, it set up an Intelligence Section followed by a
Statistical Committee in 1867. It also compiled a Captains' Register
that noted the service performance of masters: their records were an
important variable in determining risk. Various underwriters' associa-
tions working within the Lloyd's umbrella refined contract wording and
policy clauses in response to unfolding developments.
From Napoleonic times Lloyd's acted as an intermediary between
underwriters and government branches.25 It mediated on such matters
as convoy discipline and the treatment of prizes and captured cargo.
Lloyd's successfully lobbied for reductions in the stamp duty levied on
policies and undertook legal actions to safeguard the interests of under-
writers. By the early nineteenth century, Lloyd's had established itself as
‘a great national institution'.26
Indeed, Lloyd's became recognized as the centre of the world insur-
ance industry because it harnessed the information flows and learning
effects needed to support efficient market mechanisms. It developed
channels needed to assess risk and attract coverage while building
feedback loops that promoted the refinement of practice. Lloyd's also
established sound procedures for claims handling in order to maintain
customer confidence. These information lines and processes safe-
guarded the interests of both insured and insurer, and thereby enabled
these parties to arrange mutually beneficial transactions. Edward Lloyd's

Lloyd's Registerr of British and Foreign Shipping
Since 1833, when it appeared in its modern form, Lloyd's Register
has performed a function essential to the maritime community by
recording details of the command, construction and condition of
ships. These data were valuable to merchants who entrusted their
goods to shipowners and their captains, to underwriters who assessed
risks and set premiums, and to shipowners who bought and sold ves-
sels. The Register recorded in a standard form technical details (type
of machinery, design, construction material) as well as information
regarding any repairs effected, and classified a ship's overall condition,
A1 being the highest ranking. Each vessel entry also noted the date of

the most recent inspection (or survey). The information embodied in
the Register provided decision-makers with accurate and verified data,
thereby saving them an incalculable amount of time, especially when
conducting transactions involving ships that operated far from home
and could not be readily examined.
The origin of the Registry can be traced to a news sheet provided by
Lloyd's coffee house to attract clients. Publication of the paper was sus-
pended for a time as a result of political controversy, but it reappeared
as Lloyd's Listtin 1726. In 1800, disagreement between shipowners and
insurance brokers resulted in the formation of a second paper, but
by about 1833 reconciliation led to merger and the Register assumed
in its modern form. The publication was supported by subscriptions
paid by individuals and firms as well as by fees charged for surveying
vessels.
The Register's headquarters were located in Sun Court, then in Castle
Court, and ultimately in Fenchurch Street in the heart of the City. The
offices accommodated clerical staff and a committee that over time
increased in size and expanded in its occupational and geographic
composition in response to changes in maritime business. For example,
in the 1860s, the shifting locus of shipbuilding from the Thames to
the northeast and Scotland led to increased representation for regional
ports.27 By 1913, Committee members numbered 72, with 26 coming
from London, ten from Liverpool, eight from Glasgow and eighteen
from other centres. That year, the Registry listed over ten thousand
ships aggregating more than 22.5 million grt.28 To qualify for regis-
tration, a ship had to be built in accordance with Lloyd's rules and
inspected regularly by Lloyd-appointed surveyors.
In formulating its construction regulations the Society (as the Lloyd's
organization was called) sought to accommodate rapid technical
change and the interests of a range of occupational constituents. 1855
saw the articulation of provisions for iron ships in consultation with
shipbuilders, but these rules were general in form and a rigid approach
was not taken in their application.29 The regulations were revised ten
years later after much experience had been gained. Rules for manufac-
turing anchors and chains were developed in 1853, and later the Board
of Trade delegated to Lloyd's responsibility for testing these items

In developing and enforcing its rules, Lloyds did not have any f ormal
statutory power. Rather, the Society operated as a quasi-regulatory
agency because the maritime occupations recognized the necessity of
sustaining the organization. Indeed, Kirkaldy saw it as ‘an illustration
of the advantages of co-operative effort'.30 Blake recorded that ‘the strict
legal position of the Society is nearly indefinable, its constitution beau-
tifully vague'; it was ‘the product of a national genius for compromise …
and for technical excellence'.31 Lloyd's motto, Sine Praejudicio (without
prejudice), reflected its desired ethos.
Nevertheless, it is not clear whether the Society was sufficiently
responsive and flexible. Kirkaldy argued that it effectively accommo-
dated technical and commercial developments, but it appears that the
formulation of some sets of rules (for example those for refrigerated
ships) was slow. Moreover, disagreement over load line regulations
induced Glasgow shipowners and builders to set up a rival registry, the
British Corporation for the Survey and Registry of Shipping, in 1890.
This competing entity attracted only about fifteen per cent of the ton-
nage listed in Lloyd's in 1913, but it was not until 1949 that the two
registers merged. Lloyd's attracted support from overseas. By 1913, it
was recognized by twelve countries, and Blake described it as having a
supranational presence.32 Over time, other registers

The Baltic Mercantile and Shipping Exchange (the Baltic)
This City institution originated at the Virginia and Maryland coffee
house which, in 1744, was renamed the Virginia and Baltick [sicc] to
reflect more accurately the growing importance of the latter trade to the
merchants and shipowners who congregated there. The Baltic region
was becoming a vital source of strategic naval stores, including hemp
and timber, as well as civilian goods such as tallow, seeds, and oils.
While shipping services were arranged at this venue, commodity trad-
ing was the main activity conducted there; to an extent, the Baltic com-
peted with the Royal Exchange and other coffee houses.
In 1823, frenzied speculation at the coffee house led a group of
respectable merchants who feared that their collective reputation
would be tarnished by such wanton gambling, to restrict entry to the
venue to those who paid subscriptions (4 guineas for individuals and
6 to 8 guineas to firms depending on their size). Membership was
limited to three hundred persons; new entrants were admitted after

attracting six supporting recommendations from existing members.
These d evelopments led to the creation of the modern Baltic, and from
this point onwards its composition was highly cosmopolitan.
By 1857, larger quarters were required and traders moved to the South
Seas Company's old headquarters. The Baltic Co. Ltd was formed to
buy the lease on this building which was in turn rented to the Baltic
Society. Overcrowding had become a problem again by the early 1890s;
a group of traders formed the London Shipping Exchange and another
faction removed to the old Jerusalem coffee house. In 1903, all three
bodies merged and took up residence at a new, purpose-built exchange
in St. Mary's Axe. This building was destroyed by an Irish Republican
Army bomb in 1992, and the Baltic moved to a venue further down the
same street.
Since their first articulation, the Baltic's rules were refined progres-
sively in response to changes in business, but their overarching aim was
to protect the exchange's standing. Controlling entry to ensure that
members were creditworthy and honest was the governing Committee's
‘"most important function'.33 In addition to requiring references for
prospective entrants, this body independently conducted investigations
into their affairs.
The Committee ejected defaulters and bankrupts, although the latter
could be readmitted after meeting specified conditions.34 Over time,
regulations governing dealing on private account, making firm offers
and confirming representation were enunciated. More generally, and in
keeping with the basic tenet of gentlemanly capitalism, the Committee
enjoined that members must not engage in ‘conduct derogatory to a
man of business', and the exchange took as its motto ‘our word our
bond'. Such ethical prescriptions were vital to the functioning of a
market where members concluded deals verbally and later confirmed
arrangements in writing.35
Many trading contracts stipulated that if arbitration was required a
member of the Baltic Committee would provide this service. Dispute
resolution processes called for arbitration first, and in the event
that a solution was not reached an umpire would be appointed and
his decision would be final.36 This efficient process economized on
time costs and financial expenses associated with legal proceedings.
Through its rules and processes, the Baltic acted as the unofficial
regulator of the shipping business and significant segments of com-

Indeed, one historian suggested that the Baltic was ‘the clearing house
for the cereal produce of the world'.37 Complementing the operations

of the London Corn Exchange, where London and regional merchants
transacted, the Baltic was for an extended period larger than other
centres of world commodity trading, including the New York and
Chicago exchanges. In the 1920s, it handled 250,000 tons of grain
worth over £2.5 million each day. Trends at the Baltic influenced and
were shaped by those at US wheat exchanges as well as centres in Russia,
Argentina and India. The same interdependence typified operations
between the Baltic and foreign markets specializing in other commodi-
ties: Calcutta and Bombay for linseed, Egypt for cotton seed, and Cairo,
Smyrna and Morocco for beans. From the 1850s the Baltic was linked
to these centres by the telegraph and from 1880 by telephone. Thus, by
the mid-nineteenth century, the Baltic was the centrepiece of a global
commodity market.
The nature of the operations conducted at the institution did
change over time. During the 1930s, when commodity prices col-
lapsed and trading patterns were dislocated, the Baltic's principal
business shifted from trading in grains to ship chartering. Moreover,
within the commodity sector the dealing process changed as brokers
were increasing marginalized. These figures had provided valuable
services, such as financing transactions, reconciling buyers and sellers
who often could not agree to a price through face-to-face negotiation,
and supporting reasonable levels of futures speculation which facili-
tated hedging. However, by the 1920s mergers among merchants and
processors created large companies, such as Hovis, Rank and Unilever,
which could finance their operations and increasingly bought direct
from sellers.

The efficiency of the latter sector was enhanced by the London Grain

contracts. This organization also streamlined operations by establishing
five annual trading positions, setting a uniform unit of exchange and
installing a benchmark (No. 3 Manitoba) against which other grades

The manner in which trade was conducted and the physical char-
acteristics of the buildings occupied by the exchange generated effi-
ciency effects. Dealing was done by open cry as it was at all markets
except Lloyd's, and noise levels were prodigious. A visitor to the Royal

Exchange, for example, wrote in 1818: ‘the clamor of voices, to an
ear unaccustomed as mine was to such confusing sounds was almost
deafening; and though no doubt perfectly intelligible to one another,
yet seemed to remind me of what I read of Babel'.38 In 1896,Chambers'
Journal reported that ‘the hum of voices [at the Baltic] is suggestive of
a large beehive'.39 No doubt, like traders on the Stock Exchange, those
working at the Baltic could determine the direction of the market by
the quality of the noise generated by open cry.40 The architecture of
the buildings that housed both of these markets - high domed ceilings,
stone floors and walls - enhanced the nuances of such valuable, inform-
ing noise.
Above the clamour came calls from ‘waiters', a title preserved from
coffee house days, who, situated at a rostrum, informed individuals
that messages awaited them. Everyday specific commodities were traded
on the same recognized position on the floor. On the Royal Exchange,
these locations were called ‘walks', and at the Stock Exchange individu-
als occupied their own jealously guarded ‘pitches' within a walk, where
proximity to a large operator brought valuable information.41 In the
1920s, the Baltic freight market was situated near the main door, linseed
was traded in the centre of the room, and wheat dealing occurred at the
far end of the room. This positioning reduced the time costs of those
intending to deal in particular types of business and provided forums
for observing and listening.

Lloyd's to take up insurance, the trader could buy financial securities at
the Baltic. Stockbrokers were admitted to the exchange, and the number
of them present at any time was a barometer of business conditions.

The Baltic arranged occasions for members to socialize and thereby
acquire the interpersonal knowledge that smoothed dealing processes.
One could meet colleagues in the lunch room, or join the rifle, rowing
or musical clubs. Dinners marking salient events promoted goodwill,
but their seating plans revealed a hierarchy of members.45 This pecking
order reflected peer rating - an activity that facilitated safe transacting -
and functional specializations that generated efficiency effects. In 1895,
an observer noted the following hierarchy in descending order: ship-
owner/brokers, shipowners, and brokers in the shipping sector; and in
commodity trading merchants offering full cargoes, chartering agents,
dealers in seeds, timber and oils, and finally share brokers.46
In his manual on shipbroking, Cufley emphasized the importance of
maintaining reputation and business connections by means of firm but
flexible dealing which was enhanced by interpersonal knowledge.47 Barty-
King suggested that through social and business intercourse ‘the tightness
of this community, and the familiarity of its members the one with the
other had the effect of stabilizing rates'.48 In his view, these interpersonal
links also ensured that all participants got the bestmarket price. It is likely
that similar bonds had the same effect at other places of exchange.
The City itself constituted an emporium of specialized markets, and
businessmen observed a routine of visiting several venues each day or
each week at specific times when calls occurred. This pattern of movement

The London Metal Exchange
In the seventeenth century, metal traders gravitated to the Jerusalem
coffee house off Cornhill. In 1876, the London Metal Exchange moved
to rooms in Lombard Court and began restricting entry to subscrip-
tion payers. Whether this development, like similar ones that occurred
at Lloyd's and the Baltic, was prompted by the desire to restrain
speculation is not known. Eventually, the LME occupied premises in
Whittington Avenue in 1882 and remained there until 1978.49
The Exchange shaped trade and supporting lines of communication
through its rules of conduct and governing regulations. In order to
economize on transaction costs, it introduced standardized contracts,
quality benchmarks, and uniform units of exchange. Like the Baltic, the
LME established dispute resolution procedures that saved time and miti-
gated legal expenses. Members were carefully vetted, and their financial
standing was rigorously assessed. Severe penalties, including expulsion,
were levied on defaulters.
The LME conducted open cry trading which was made possible after
quality standards were set and uniform units of exchange were estab-
lished. Initially, transacting took place in a ‘ring', so-called because
merchants drew a circle in chalk on the floor to provide a reference
point for parties interested in a particular metal. Eventually, these rings
became permanent locations.50
Trading times crystallized into two sessions, also called rings. The first
took place between 12.30 and 1.15, and the second ran from 4.00 to
4.30. During each ring two blocks of five minutes each were allocated
to the trading of a particular metal. Prices established at the end of the
second session became the world price for the next twenty-four hours,
reflecting the global influence of this trading centre.

Other markets and other infrastructure elements
The City accommodated many other markets. Exchanges for wool,
furs, other textiles and other commodities arose within the precinct.52
A number of these markets had international connections and were
therefore relevant to the shipping industry. For example, the reach of
London meat markets was extended by the installation of landward
refrigeration plant that facilitated the handling of frozen meat cargoes
from Australia, New Zealand and Argentina. Other food markets oper-
ated across the metropolis, but most served as distribution points for
products sent from regional Britain.
Other UK ports developed important exchanges and markets, and
many of these venues await historical investigation. These centres also
gave rise to industry associations relevant to shipping because they too
served information gathering and disseminating functions. Chambers
of shipping promoted local interests and interacted with each other
and their London counterpart when issues of broad concern arose. Port
authorities facilitated communication across the local mercantile and
shipping communities, in addition to maintaining and extending phys-
ical infrastructure. Organizations like the Protection and Indemnity
Clubs that were based on co-operative principles provided important
services and often had extra-regional connections. All of these entities
built up valuable knowledge bases.
Industry-specific expertise was compiled and preserved in numerous
manuals and reference works. Cufley's Ocean Freights and Chartering
helped newcomers into the broking industry. Thomas' 1928 book on
Stowagee in 1923 disseminated knowledge that protected goods during
shipment to the benefit of merchant, shipowner and insurer alike. Scrutton
on Charterparties educated generations of brokers and shipowners as it
passed through at least thirteen editions following its appearance in 1886.

essential for the efficient operation of an integrated world market.
Conclusion
From the seventeenth century, England developed and refined an inte-
grated commercial infrastructure centred on London. The fundamental

strength of this construct and that of each constituent element lay in
their ability to harness and disseminate information. Interpersonal
knowledge generated trust to support transactions, commercial intel-
ligence sustained flows of goods and the provision of services, while
essential expertise was preserved and conveyed through a library of doc-
uments. It was London's information-related advantages that enabled it
to become the centre of the global shipping industry.
Cultural forces provided a complementary source of comparative
advantage. The basic tenets of gentlemanly capitalism permeated all
London markets and transacting arenas. Without the assurance implicit
in the underlying codes of behaviour, information flows would have been
disrupted and markets subject to failure, or at least diminished efficiency.
Each trading centre developed its own formal rules and informal con-
ventions that shaped behaviour and transmissions in complementary
ways. In addition, the efficiency of exchange was enhanced by the rise
of specialized terminology and terms of reference that saved time and
improved precision. The physical construction of trading places and the
organization of space also shaped communication and enabled partici-
pants to ‘feel' the state of trade.
The longevity of London's commercial infrastructure can be explained
by the flexibility exhibited by its interlinked elements. Trading venues
remained open to all qualified participants, and from their first appear-
ance cosmopolitanism was a distinguishing and highly beneficial char-
acteristic. Markets evolved over time to accommodate new conditions
within the global economic system. Yet change unfolded in a way that
preserved a solid core of expectations shaped by precedent and estab-
lished practice. The gradual nature of institutional evolution prevented
dislocation, provided sustaining certainty and maintained business
confidence.

Introduction
From the vantage point of the twenty-first century the history of
Britain's shipping over the previous century may seem one of a long
process of decline - ‘ebb tide' in the words of one historian.1 In 1900
approaching half of the world's tonnage was under the British flag.
In 2000 British owners' share of world shipping, whether vessels were
registered in the UK or elsewhere, was 2.58%, putting it in tenth place.2
This change in Britain's maritime status was not, however, a gradual
process. In 1967 the UK flagged fleet was still the third largest in the
world and continuing to grow, albeit more slowly than its major com-
petitors. It then went into free fall, shrinking from its historic peak of
1,682 vessels in 1975 to 693 vessels ten years later. By 1995 there were
just 365 vessels of over 500 tons flying the British flag.
The reasons for Britain's diminution as a maritime economic power
have been covered in a number of academic studies.3 They were also
the subject of two major contemporary investigations: the ‘Inquiry into
British Shipping', known as the Rochdale Committee, which reported
in 1970 and the ‘Decline in the UK-Registered Merchant Fleet' by the
House of Commons Transport Committee, which reported in 1987 and
1988.4 The particular vulnerability of Britain's shipping to changes in
world conditions features strongly in the range of responsible factors
identified by the Rochdale Committee. Six developments were seen
then as having had a ‘profound effect on the UK industry': disruption
caused by the two world wars, particularly the First World War; decolo-
nization; slow growth in the types of trade in which British owners spe-
cialized; relatively slow growth of Britain's own trade; competition from
shipping of developing countries; and competition from air transport

126 Government and British Shipping in the Later Twentieth Century
The aim of this article is not to debate the relative weights of exter-
nal and internal reasons for decline, but to consider some aspects of
the response by the British government. How did politicians and civil
servants react to the striking change, over a relatively short period,
in Britain's international status as a shipping nation? What were the
arguments employed to justify or to oppose assistance? To what extent
did international considerations feature here? Such questions are more
appropriate than they might be in the case of land-based industries
because of the special status that national merchant fleets have com-
monly been accorded in matters of public policy. Navigation Acts,
cabotage, subsidies and subventions have resulted from a belief in the
value to a country of its shipping, with such worth estimated in many
cases as greater than a simple calculation of economic contribution
would suggest. In the inter-war years virtually every maritime nation,
including Britain, supported its shipping industry in some way and
internationally such assistance continued to be prevalent in the later
twentieth century.10 Yet, as shall be shown, over a period of growing
crisis the British state's relationship with the shipping industry altered.
(For reasons of space, the discussion which follows concentrates on
the domestic rather than the international element of British maritime
policy.) Domestically directed shipping policy moved from traditionally
supportive in the 1950s, to subordinate to the needs of shipbuilding in
the 1960s and 1970s, to non-supportive in the 1980s and for much of
the 1990s, until a major reversal of approach led to a high degree of
intervention from 2000.
How far does the literature deal with these developments? All of the
general studies of shipping already cited necessarily touch on this, but
there is nothing that compares in scope and use of primary sources
with Johnman and Murphy's outstanding British Shipbuilding and the
State.11 Davies's Belief in the Sea: State Encouragement of British Merchant
Shipping and Shipbuildingg (1992) deals in detail with developments in the
later twentieth century.12 Davies, a lawyer, brought to this authoritative
study professional links with the maritime world.

In contrast, former civil servant Richard Goss in a recent article provides

Shipping policy cannot of course be isolated from the wider policy
context. Later twentieth-century British industrial policy has received
some attention from mainstream economic historians, though ship-
ping barely features in this literature.16 The 1964-70 Labour govern-
ments had high hopes that the performance of British industry could
be changed by intervention.Belief in the efficacy of planning was also
a feature of the last years of Conservative government, 1959-64. The
Conservatives, however, began their term in government in 1970 with
a strong preference for the market but rapidly reversed this position,
beginning with the rescue of Rolls-Royce and Upper Clyde Shipbuilders
in 1971, followed by the 1972 Industry Act. Industrial policy in the
next period of Labour Government (1974-79) was reactive rather than
proactive, but there was no question that government had a central
role. In contrast, under the Conservatives led by anti-statist Margaret
Thatcher, that role was questioned and in due course replaced by trust
in the efficacy of market forces. New Labour electoral victory in 1997
under Tony Blair did not reverse the now generally non-interventionist
tenor of industrial policy though, as shall be shown, shipping was a
notable exception.
The industry in the 1950s and 1960s
In 1960 the British shipping industry comprised 270 companies
together owning 20 million gross tons - 14.4 million gross tons of dry
cargo and passenger vessels and the remainder tankers. With half of
tonnage owned by ten constituent groups of companies, the industry
was concentrated. In the tanker sector BP and Shell were the largest
players, while P&O, Furness, British and Commonwealth, and Cunard
dominated the non-oil sector, though the P&O group at 2.1 million gt
dwarfed the other three.17

(1962)
British shipowners in the 1950s made much of their lack of reliance
on government support, contrasting this with the ‘unfair' subsidies
and subventions enjoyed by their competitors in other national fleets.
In recent memory was the assistance the industry had received in the
1930s, including the loans provided to Cunard to enable them to build
the twoQueens.19 In fact shipping benefited from special fiscal status in
the form of investment allowances, which in 1957 they succeeded in
getting increased. The description of this concession by the Chancellor
as ‘a unique step for a unique industry which is the lifeline of our coun-
try' indicates the basis of shipping's claim for assistance.20

In the late 1950s British shipping, along with the rest of the world
shipping industry, was in the grip of a freight rate depression, resulting
from an oversupply of tonnage. Tramp freight rates, which had tumbled
in April 1957 with the re-opening of the Suez Canal and showed no
sign of recovery, and liner freights were also depressed. In these adverse
conditions world shipbuilding orders also fell, but British yards suffered
disproportionately. In 1958 the order book of British yards was 16.6 per
cent of the world total but by 1962 it was 11 per cent.21
With both the shipbuilding and shipping interests urging some action
by government, in the summer of 1959 separate departmental investi-
gations into both industries began. A note of a meeting of Ministry of
Transport civil servants set out the shipping issue:
as the prospect of a subsidy for shipping comes nearer, it becomes
more important for us to be certain in our own minds what would be
the future of the shipping industry. Since the Treasury could not be
expected to make available an unlimited subsidy or even one to main-
tain the merchant marine at its present size, it was essential to decide
how large, in our view, the shipping industry should ideally be.22
The final confidential document, ‘The Prospects of British Shipping',
which emerged from this internal review accompanied a memorandum

from the Minister of Transport, Ernest Marples, which was considered
by the Conservative Cabinet in July 1962. It dismissed the suggestion
that it was possible to fix a figure for a reduced shipping industry size,
on both practical and political grounds: ‘the Government would attract
to itself both odium for reducing the industry and responsibility for
maintaining it thereafter at the planned figure'. Strikingly pessimistic
in tone, in the short term this saw little prospect for any improvement
for British shipping ‘whatever anyone does' and in the longer term
judged that ‘it is difficult to avoid the impression that some decline
not merely in the British share of world shipping but in the size of
the British fleet is inevitable.' It identified Britain's long dominance of
many trades, protected by conferences, and its large seaborne trade as
advantages. British shipping was, however, disadvantaged as a large user
of British ports, the subsidies and protection enjoyed by competitors
and weak management of some firms - ‘the industry as a whole tends
to be old-fashioned'.23
The Cabinet was invited to note ‘that the shipping industry, and in
consequence the British shipbuilding industry also, face serious diffi-
culties'. In response it was agreed that the government should ‘pursue
energetically' proposals for giving British shipping ‘a fair field interna-
tionally' and also introduce various measures to ‘develop managerial and
technical efficiency'. These twin policy directions - the first an aspect
of international relations involving the Foreign Office and the second
an attempt to influence the performance of the industry - also under-
pinned the approach of the Wilson governments of the 1960s. External
policy efforts directed against ‘unfair competition' and attempts of
other powers to weaken the conference system were in fact to persist
until the 1980s, by which time changes in the global maritime busi-
ness environment, as also the much diminished UK flag fleet, finally
confirmed their futility.
The domestic proposals were pretty feeble - the most important was
setting up (in 1962) a Shipping Advisory Panel - but the memorandum
hinted at an important and persistent policy dimension: difficulties
in the relationship between government and the shipping industry.
Unsurprisingly shipowners disliked external inspection of their affairs
and could be uncooperative.24 The Rochdale Committee was later to

The Cunard case
Behind this distrust was the issue of the Cunard Queen liners. In the
late 1950s the Macmillan government was confronted with the prob-
lem of the replacement of the liners, Queen Maryy and Queen Elizabeth.
The possibility that Cunard might look to government for assistance
with financing the replacement of the two liners had been raised as
early as 1954 in confidential correspondence between the combative
then Cunard Chairman, Colonel Percy Bates, and Gilmour Jenkins,
Permanent Secretary at the Ministry of Transport.26 In 1959 Cunard
made it clear to the government that unless assisted it would be unable
to replace the two Queens, bringing an end to over a century of British
transatlantic shipping. With an election looming, and the reaction of
other companies to consider, the Cabinet's dilemma is neatly summed
up by the Minister of Transport's minuted comment at a Cabinet meet-
ing on 7 July 1959:
Chairman of Cunard is diff. to handle, has upset the industry, and
can't be trusted to handle this tactfully…
We shd. protect ourselves by seeking independent advice. W'd help
to get industry happy: wd help on when ship shd, be built etc., And
wd. give us time.27
In the event a commitment, ‘we intend to support the replacement

Then unexpectedly in October 1961 ministers learned that Cunard,
with no consultation with government, had decided in the face of dete-

politically embarrassing development was much resented by ministers.
Once again the Cabinet found itself considering the future of Cunard
passenger services, this time looking at arguments for and against the
subsidy now being asked for.33 It decided to take no action, but in 1963
Cunard obtained a loan of £17.6 million for the building of Q4 (Queen
Elizabeth IIII) by John Brown's of Clydebank under the Shipbuilding
Credit Scheme.34
The financial problems were not over, however, and in September
1967 and in 1968 - this time under a Labour government - Cunard
received further loans to finance vessel completion. Unsurprisingly
such taxpayer assistance to one company created hard feelings, both
among other companies and in Parliament. ‘There were some who felt
that, after more than a century of favoured treatment, it was time that
Cunard should cease to be regarded as a sacred cow; as one member of
the Commons remarked, a sacred cow is an object of great veneration
but is generally of very little economic use.'35 The government neverthe-
less considered that it had no alternative, not least because the ‘ship had
become an object of some national significance'.36

The impact of government support in the 1960s
and 1970s
As far the maritime sector in general was concerned, there is a contrast
between the focus of government policy in the 1960s and 1970s. The
later 1960s were marked by a remarkable number of public inquiries,
a reflection of concern about the balance of payments. There was Geddes
(1966) into shipbuilding.39 There was Pearson (1966-67) which fol-
lowed the seamen's strike, plus two into the port industry, as well as the
Rochdale Inquiry into Shipping.40 While commentators have sometimes
assumed that the problems of shipbuilding dominated the agenda in
both decades, the subjects of these inquiries, as also the initial rationale
for assisting Cunard's North Atlantic service, show that this was not
entirely the case. Not until the 1970s, with unemployment now the
major issue, did support for shipbuilding come absolutely to the fore.

Taxpayer support for Cunard earned for government the ire of other
companies and, as we have seen, no particular gratitude from the recipi-
ent. No other company was singled out in this way, but the industry as
a whole could not complain that it did not benefit from taxation and
fiscal policies. Indeed shipping companies were treated more favourably
than other UK companies. There was ‘a national interest in creating
conditions [which are] conducive to maintaining a larger national fleet
than would exist without such policies'.41
Between 1967 and 1975 the industry also benefited from support not
available to any other service industry, in the form of investment grants
and loans. Such assistance was motivated by the problems of shipbuild-
ing, rather than a concern to support shipping. ‘There was a clear policy
of attracting vessels to the United Kingdom register, not … so much
from the point of view of enlarging the British merchant fleet for its
own sake, but in order to secure the additional shipbuilding business.'42
Eligibility was restricted to vessels remaining on the UK flag register for
a minimum of five years and, since registration was open to ‘resident'
shipping companies, it was possible for foreign ‘brass plate' owners to
qualify.

Such measures did not halt the decline of the UK-owned merchant
fleet relative to other fleets. Indeed, from the Marples Memorandum
onwards, it is clear that it was not anticipated in government circles that
it could reverse the trend. The Rochdale Inquiry made 1,697 recommen-
dations to improve performance, but looked to the industry itself, not
government, to respond to these. In the event, only changes relating
to manpower and training were implemented, but most commentators
take the view that these were already underway.43
Loans and grants for shipping investment did have an impact on the
size of the UK-flagged fleet and once these came to an end, total regis-
tered tonnage plummeted. A third of the tonnage on the UK register in
1975 was, however, foreign owned. Indeed, foreign ownership masked
the extent to which national interest in merchant shipping had already
declined before the downward plunge after 1975.44
Shipping policy in the 1980s and 1990s
Against the background of a world shipping recession the downward
trend in the UK fleet continued. Recession also affected other maritime
nations, encouraging protectionist measures.45 By then three-quarters
of the tonnage owned by UK companies was not UK registered, but ‘the
resort of British shipowners to foreign lower cost registries was unable
to halt the process of a substantial UK withdrawal from the industry'.46
Flagging out and the shrinking size of the UK fleet were accompanied by
a reduction in the numbers of British seafarers, which fell from 57,923
in 1980 to 16,445 in 1995.47
Decline prompted the cross-party Parliamentary Transport Committee
to investigate. The policy context was now different from that in the
past. No longer was the condition of merchant shipping a matter of
interest mainly to those directly involved. We can, indeed, see in the
long list of those individuals and organizations responding to the call
to give evidence a sign of the widening concern as to what this might
mean for Britain, economically and politically.48 There were echoes
of the traditional case for maritime support on grounds of national
interest.49 Among bodies pressing for interference was the British
Maritime Charitable Foundation which commissioned academic studies
to provide an authoritative counterpoint to the official Department of

support for UK shipping. This was encapsulated in the statement: ‘any

corporate taxation under the Finance Act had ended shipping's 100 per
cent first year investment allowances and, although this had perhaps
been an unintended consequence of a comprehensive fiscal measure,
the industry had failed to get this concession reinstated.54 The govern-
ment did, however, accept that the industry needed to be ‘capable of
meeting the essential needs of the nation in emergency and war' and
in this context introduced some assistance with training and crew relief
costs as well as setting up a merchant navy reserve scheme.55 This was
a small departure from an otherwise strict policy of non-intervention.
Indeed the rationale for providing no direct encouragement to UK flag
registration was that:
any initial adverse economic effects on the shipping sector result-
ing from the transfer of vessels away from the UK register will be

offset by economic adjustments elsewhere in the economy which
leave the overall level of employment and output largely unaffected.
Indeed, the sale of loss-making vessels to overseas interests and the
redeployment of resources into more profitable industries will help
to improve the overall performance of the economy.56
The apparent insouciance of this approach in the face of the decline in
the UK fleet is striking but, as we have seen from shipping policy discus-
sions in the early 1960s, it was actually not unique to government in
the 1980s. It was also the case that the Thatcher government's laissez-
faire approach did not extend to activity on the international maritime
scene, which continued as in the past.57 In 1980, for example, the
Department of Transport described its current concerns as: ‘the impli-
cations for the British shipping industry of the world shipping reces-
sion and the reduction in the size of the UK merchant fleet'; UNCTAD
issues, including ‘implementation of the UN Code of Conduct for
Liner Conferences'; European Economic Community shipping policy;
‘problems with the USA over our different approaches to the regulation
of liner conferences'; and ‘concern over the expansion of the Soviet
Merchant Marine'.58
Policy reversal
Although the 1980s offered little by way of government support for
shipping, change was in the air. The Transport Committee's recom-
mendation for government action substantially remained just this, but
its long investigation and the mass of evidence it had accumulated
brought the decline in the UK fleet to public attention.59 The Defence
Committee also entered the debate, concluding in a 1988 report that:
The ready availability of adequate merchant shipping resources rep-
resents a very significant element in the make-up of deterrence. The
lack of such resources represents a grave deficiency in our ability to
deter. The availability of merchant shipping for defence purpose is
governed by three key factors - the number of UK flagged ships, their
accessibility when they are needed and the availability of a pool of
British seafarers to man them. There are grounds for concern on all
three counts.60

Committee, weighed in by investigating the future of maritime skills

the Conservatives in their last years of government bore no compari-

Under the enthusiastic lead of Prescott, now Deputy Prime Minister,

Conclusion
Political twists and turns necessarily had implications for support or
otherwise for British shipping. The UK government archives suggest,
however, that for the first half of our fifty-year period, three factors were
more significant for shipping policy than changes in the attitudes of
politicians to the functions of the state. These were: a pessimistic official
assessment of the long-term economic prospects of the industry, a loss
of belief in shipping as a source of national prestige and, together with
these, the mutual mistrust of companies and government. Towards the
end of the century, with the total annihilation of a British shipping
presence threatened, some traditional ‘nursery of seamen' considera-
tions of national interest in maintaining the flagged fleet resurfaced.
One further influence was a revised view of economic contribution;
a shipowning presence was seen as important for the UK's role as a lead-
ing international maritime cluster. A transparent, seemingly harmoni-
ous, relationship between industry and government, which contrasted
with the previous situation, facilitated an historic reversal in British
maritime policy.

Why They are Tall and We are
Small! Competition between
Antwerp and Rotterdam in the
Twentieth Century
Stephan Vanfraechem
This chapter considers the results of micro-economic and political-in-
stitutional research that has been carried out into the ports of Antwerp
and Rotterdam and investigates whether it can help to understand
why the two ports have made quite different choices as regards labour
organization on the docks.1 Despite the fact that ports like Antwerp,
Hamburg, Bremen, Le Havre and Rotterdam all share the same hin-
terland and therefore compete with each other for market share, com-
petition between specifically Antwerp and Rotterdam has become an
important focus of attention in previous research projects.2
Citius, altius, fortius: from sail to steam
From the mid-nineteenth century the steamship gradually came into
service. The steam engine and the iron ships were stronger, more pow-
erful and more flexible. More power led to higher speed and greater
capacity. The considerably higher running-cost of those steamships
forced shipping companies, port authorities and cargo handlers to adapt
and change the organization both on board the ships and also on shore.
Because of the higher running costs of the steam vessels, the ‘dead'
time in the port had to be reduced to more realistic, economic terms, so
the loading and unloading of cargo needed to be speeded up. Because
of the volumes and the need for a faster turnaround, cargo handling
became a more specialized business.
In Antwerp cargo handling and especially the transport and storage
of the goods had traditionally been dominated by the naties. The crew
of the ship took care of the actual loading or unloading of the ship and
delivered or received the goods to and from the naties who brought the
142

goods under the crane or transported the goods from under the crane to a
warehouse or shed.Naties had been active in the port since the thirteenth
century. Originally they were no more than a group of labourers working
together in a co-operative structure, and initially this meant little more
than working together and afterwards sharing profits. Gradually, the
expansion of the port led to a more formal structure of naties with their
own rules and procedures. As a consequence of this formalization, from
the fifteenth century onwards people who wanted to enter this business
had to buy a share of the natiee and thus became formal shareholders of
their company. As from then various companies of naties emerged and
the members of the naties gradually started buying the necessary equip-
ment as a group. As the port and hence the cargo handling business grew
further, this core group of natiee companies with ‘natie-men' became too
rigid to cope with all the work, so from the seventeenth century the
naties started hiring casual labourers. Unlike the natie-men, these casual
workers were not formal shareholders of the company but were hired on
a daily basis and were paid a formal wage for the service they rendered
that day. They could work for variousnatiee companies.3
In Rotterdam the vemen offered more or less the same services as the
naties did in Antwerp.4 The vemen were active in transport, distribution
and warehousing. As in Antwerp - and in other ports - they worked
together with the crew to load and unload ships.
With the introduction of the steam vessel, the need for a faster turna-
round of the vessel, combined with the larger volumes, transformed cargo
handling in most (European) ports into a more specialized business. The
ship's crew were no longer able to load or unload their vessel themselves.
In both Antwerp and in Rotterdam specialized stevedoring companies
developed during the last quarter of the nineteenth century, in Antwerp
at least often founded and owned by former captains.5 These stevedores
made exclusive use of casual labour. An ‘army' of casual labourers was
formed in both ports. In 1899 the Arbeidsbladd - the official bulletin of the
Belgian Ministry of Labour - estimated the number of dockers in Antwerp

In both Antwerp and in Rotterdam specialized stevedoring companies
developed during the last quarter of the nineteenth century, in Antwerp
at least often founded and owned by former captains.5 These stevedores
made exclusive use of casual labour. An ‘army' of casual labourers was
formed in both ports. In 1899 the Arbeidsbladd - the official bulletin of the
Belgian Ministry of Labour - estimated the number of dockers in Antwerp
at around 25,000.6 In Rotterdam an equal figure is mentioned.7
In Rotterdam, the difference between the traditional vemen and the
new stevedoring companies was to fade very soon. Veem and steve-
doring activities were combined in vertical integrated companies. In
Antwerp, however, a clear distinction between the traditional naties and
the stevedoring companies remained. Both types of companies stayed
within their own territory: the naties remained active in transport, dis-
tribution and warehousing, whereas the actual loading and unloading
of the vessels was the sole terrain of the stevedores.8

This clear division of labour between thenaties and the stevedores in
the Antwerp port had both long- and short-term effects. In the short
term, shipping companies complained about this unnecessary compli-
cation of the cargo handling and also the lack of transparency: it led to
situations where the natie had to wait for the stevedore to unload the
ship, or vice versa where the stevedore had to wait for thenatie to bring
the goods under the crane.
In the longer term, and unlike the port of Rotterdam where vertical
integration led to bigger (and more substantial) companies, the small
and medium-sized companies also remained dominant in Antwerp.
The naties in particular remained very small companies, mostly family
businesses and most of the time undercapitalized. Most of the naties
were still organized on a co-operative basis: people who wanted to
enter the companies had to buy shares and thus became co-owners of
the company. In practice most naties became family businesses where
the son inherited or took over the shares of his father. These com-
panies did not have a broad or solid financial base: at the end of the

year the profits were split up and distributed amongst the sharehold-

to the shareholders there was no surplus that could be re-invested.
There was also little need for investment. For instance, investment
in the port infrastructure was the sole responsibility of the city: the
city authorities were responsible for and financed the construction
of the docks, quays, canals, cranes, warehouses, etc.9 The stevedores
and naties hired quays, warehouses and cranes from the authorities
and did not have to invest themselves in their infrastructure. The
city council was also very reluctant to grant long-term concessions to
private operators for fear of monopolies. This fear of monopoly was
shared by maritime circles also. Furthermore, the city council, in a
bid to avoid specialization, opted for a general cargo port where all
facilities (warehouses, cranes, etc.) were as universal as possible. The
exception to this rule was the grain and oil business where the city
council, though unwilling to invest in specialized warehouses and
tanks, was forced to do so by trading companies. It was forced, for
example, to grant a long-term concession to the Magasins à Grains
d'Anvers (SAMGA) in 1891 to build a grain silo at their own expense.
Long-term concessions, however, were very rare prior to World War I.
As a consequence the majority of naties and stevedores invested very
little in infrastructure and depended on the investments made by the
city council; they all seemed happy with this arrangement. For the
naties and stevedores the hiring of infrastructure such as warehouses

little in infrastructure and depended on the investments made by the
city council; they all seemed happy with this arrangement. For the
naties and stevedores the hiring of infrastructure such as warehouses

and cranes from the city council seemed the best guarantee of
keeping large foreign companies out of the port of Antwerp.10
This hanseatic tradition, where the local municipality played a very
active role in the development of the port - mainly as a financer of
infrastructure - would remain until World War II. In the long term this
aloofness or absence of the cargo handlers from investment in port
infrastructure led to conservatism. Thenatieswere not aware of techno-
logical innovations and were not willing to invest in new technologies
and specialized terminals. The same was true of the stevedoring com-
panies: though not organized on a co-operative basis, they too were
mostly under-capitalized and were slow to invest in their own installa-
tions for specific cargo.
Nor did the organization of labour and dominant use of casual labour
force thenaties and the stevedores into investments. Although the turn
of the century confronted the employers with trade unions and strikes
and subsequently the demand for permanent employment instead
of casual labour, naties and stevedores remained assured of a stable,
large army of casual labourers.11 The introduction of a National Joint
Committee established a more or less formal procedure of collective
bargaining, wage agreements and, at the beginning of the 1920s, even
a link with the consumer prices index. The employers' permanent wage
bill remained very low: if they needed dock workers they hired them on
a daily basis without any further financial obligation for the future.
In Rotterdam we see a different picture. In the first place the division
of labour was not as strict as in Antwerp. Thevemen and stevedores were
more integrated, looking after the whole supply chain from the berthing
of the ship to the storage of the goods in the warehouses and vice versa.
This prevented loss of time and also made things more transparent.
Secondly, the cargo handlers took a more proactive approach towards
technological innovation and were supported in this - but also de facto
forced - by the city council.12 Unlike their colleagues in Antwerp, the
Rotterdam city council and the Rotterdam port authority opted for spe-
cialization. Dedicated facilities and technology received much greater
stimulation than in Antwerp. There was also a bigger incentive or
necessity for private companies to be more proactive. In Rotterdam the
national government invested in the maritime

technological innovation and were supported in this - but also de facto
forced - by the city council.12 Unlike their colleagues in Antwerp, the
Rotterdam city council and the Rotterdam port authority opted for spe-

stimulation than in Antwerp. There was also a bigger incentive or
necessity for private companies to be more proactive. In Rotterdam the
national government invested in the maritime and continental access
to the port while the city council focused on maritime infrastructure
within the port, such as docks and quays. Investment in infrastructure
was left entirely to the private sector as from the beginning of the twen-

etc., so private companies had no choice but to invest in their own

infrastructure. In Rotterdam companies were also given the opportunity
to take long-term leases. Stevedoring companies obtained their own
terminals. The city invested in the docks and quay walls but all super-
structure was built and paid for by private companies. In Antwerp, until
World War II, the naties and stevedores could not - but also seemed
reluctant to - get long-term leases; they made use of public superstruc-
ture which was equipped mainly for general cargo.
In Rotterdam the trend towards specialization led, from the end of
the nineteenth century, to the introduction of modern technology like
floating grain elevators and floating/shore based grab cranes. Rotterdam
now gained a clear technological advantage over Antwerp in bulk han-
dling technology. Rotterdam cargo handling companies were much
more flexible, service-oriented and innovative than their Antwerp col-
leagues. This gave the Rotterdam port a competitive advantage.
The fact that in Rotterdam the port authority and the municipal
and national authorities - stepped aside much earlier, compared to
Antwerp, where investments in superstructure were concerned, led to
different kinds of companies in the two ports. Since the Rotterdam
stevedores were - at least to a much larger extent than in Antwerp -
financially involved in the development of their ‘own' port and had
to invest in their own cranes, warehouses and terminals, they needed
a much sounder financial basis. In Rotterdam profits were re-invested

World War II: short- and long-term effects on port
infrastructure, labour costs and labour organization
The effects of World War II on North Sea ports were enormous.
Both Antwerp and Rotterdam were used by the German occupying
forces to supply their troops.13 Once the Allied troops had landed in
Normandy and the Allied victory seemed inevitable, German troops
started preparing to destroy port infrastructure in Belgium and the
Netherlands to prevent the use of both ports as a supply centre by
the Allied troops. The swift Allied advance and the Belgian resistance
surprised the German troops in the port of Antwerp: they had to flee
before they could finish their preparations, leaving the port almost
untouched.

In Rotterdam, however, the destruction of the port was almost com-
plete. Quays had been bombed, cranes and other superstructure had
been transported to Germany, the Nieuwe Waterweg been blocked by
the sinking of ships. Once the Allied troops had arrived in the port
they could hardly fail to see the damage done: 42 per cent of the total
quay length had been blown away, 35 per cent of the warehouses were
destroyed and the storage capacity for bulk-goods was reduced by 90
per cent.14
Antwerp benefited in the short term: since its main competitor lay
in ruins, the Allies had to use Antwerp as the main supply centre for
their troops. Very shortly after liberation the Antwerp port was used to
almost full capacity by the Allied forces. Meanwhile the Dutch govern-
ment had been re-installed and quickly understood that the reconstruc-
tion of the Rotterdam port was of national importance, essential for the
full economic recovery of the whole country, hence a financial priority.
With the help of the Marshall funds a completely new port rose out of
its ashes. The Rotterdam port became partially operational from 1946,
reaching almost full capacity in 1948.
Antwerp was now confronted with the downside of escaping the war
almost intact. It would struggle until the mid-1960s to overcome the
long-term effects of this immediate post-war period. In sharp contrast
with the short-term effects, the long-term effects of the fact that the
port was relatively intact after the war were very negative: the port of
Antwerp entered the post-war period with exactly the same port infra-
and super-structure as during the interwar period. In 1950 most cranes
in Antwerp were over 30 years old.15 Now that Rotterdam had been
completely rebuilt and was equipped with the most modern cranes
and other equipment it became painfully clear that the Antwerp port
was simply outdated: the superstructure was no match for Rotterdam.
In 1948 Rotterdam overtook Antwerp and would leave it (far) behind
forever.

and national authorities. The local authorities however lacked financial
means and budgetary scope to invest in the port. The large investments
that were made by the city council in the 1930s in order to make the

In 1948 Rotterdam overtook Antwerp and would leave it (far) behind
forever.
For solutions the port companies looked directly to the municipal
and national authorities. The local authorities however lacked financial
means and budgetary scope to invest in the port. The large investments
that were made by the city council in the 1930s in order to make the
port more competitive and ready for the expected economic recovery
had clipped the council's wings. After World War II the council was still
paying for the investments of the 1930s and was simply not able to
launch a new wave of investments. This was an irreversible evolution:
the city council would no longer be able to play the active role of the
port builder or port architect that they had played since the beginning

148 The Evolution of Antwerp and Rotterdam
of the ‘modern' port in the 1870s and 1880s. The council would now
put more responsibility in the hands of the cargo handlers themselves.
The city did continue, together with the national government, to invest
in the docks and the construction of the quays but left everything
concerning superstructure to the companies themselves. They were
expected to invest in cranes, specialized handling equipment and the
construction of warehouses.
Most likely because of their conservatism and small scale, and lacking
good forward-looking management, it was quite some time before the
cargo handlers actually realized that they would have to play a more active
role and could no longer wait until the ripe fruits would come falling off
the trees. The overall figures of inward- and outward-bound goods for the
period 1948-55 show that Antwerp was simply outplayed by Rotterdam.
The gap between the two ports became wider every year.
It was ten years before action was finally taken. The Belgian govern-
ment gave financial support to the Antwerp port authority's Ten Year
Plan, which anticipated a doubling of the Antwerp port capacity. This
multi-million dollar project was finished in 1965. In the 1960s the
world fleet almost doubled in size from 172 million dwt (deadweight
tons) to 338 million dwt. During that same period seagoing trade grew

still quite vulnerable in some areas. Port expenses had been a constant
worry for both Antwerp and Rotterdam since World War I. Piloting
costs, port taxes and handling costs were constantly compared by ship-

The biggest port expense, which also influences freight rates to a
considerable extent, is the actual cost of handling. Both ports and
their employers' federations always kept their tariffs somewhat obscure
and were reluctant to publish official tariffs since that might encour-
age the competitor to take another look at his own tariffs in order to
present a better - that is cheaper - tariff to a potential client. It is and
was also common practice to give considerable reductions on the offi-
cial tariffs in order to entice shipping companies to come to a certain
port.17Handling costs - especially for labour-intensive cargo like general
cargo - are mostly determined by the cost of labour. This meant that
port authorities and port employers were extremely sensitive to a rise
in labour costs because this would normally have a negative effect on
handling and terminal costs and could harm the position of the port.

Before World War II the port of Antwerp had little to fear from
Rotterdam as far as labour costs were concerned. Dockers' wages were
considerably lower in Antwerp than in Rotterdam, resulting in lower
handling tariffs. The Antwerp port promoted itself during the interwar
period as the ‘quickest and cheapest port of Europe'.18 The Rotterdam
port authority could not compete with this low cost of labour. Rotterdam
tried to make itself more competitive by offering reductions on official
port tariffs but these efforts could not compensate for the considerably
higher labour costs, compared with Antwerp.
The period 1944-48 was of enormous and decisive importance for
the way in which labour costs evolved in both ports. After liberation
both the Dutch and Belgian governments came up with a plan to keep
prices and wages under control in order not to create an unstoppable
spiral of wage rises leading to price increases. Both governments devel-
oped similar solutions: the free (that is, free from government interfer-
ence) initiative between trade unions and employers' organizations
was temporarily shelved - although this system would not be officially
abolished in the Netherlands until 1964 - and replaced by a central,
government-led incomes policy. The government would decide how
prices and wages evolved in order to prevent massive inflation.19
Although the medicine was the same, the patients reacted in different
ways. In the Netherlands the central incomes policy was very successful.
Several institutions saw to it that the different sectors and industries
did not exceed the margins that were set by the government. This led
to wage and price movement that was in almost perfect balance and
control. The Rotterdam port profited from this situation: although there
was some friction between trade unions over the control over the port,
generally speaking wages in the Rotterdam port increased in a moderate
way which had positive consequences for the handling costs.
In Belgium, on the other hand, wages and prices were at no point
under the control of the national government. The central incomes
policy was a disaster and had already been abandoned by 1946. After
only a few months the different sectors and industries started exceeding
the margins imposed by the government and institutions such as the
National Labour Council where government, trade union and employ-
ers sat around the table. The Antwerp port reflected this situation: after
liberation one wage increase followed another, which made Antwerp

put Antwerp in 1948 - so only 4 years after liberation - in an extremely

Combined with the hopeless sight of the outdated port infrastructure,
this placed the Antwerp port until the mid-1950s in an extremely vul-

cial trade unions got a grip on the communist nucleus in the port and
were now able to follow a more realistic course where wages and work-
ing conditions were concerned. In order to make the port more compet-
itive the trade unions now even supported the employers' federations
in their demand for more flexibility and especially more realism and
pragmatism. The wage gap between Antwerp and Rotterdam, however,
was only gradually to diminish: only after the central incomes policy
was completely abandoned in the Netherlands in 1964 did labour costs
in Antwerp and Rotterdam evolve at the same pace.

a daily basis which left these casual dockers with almost no financial

further decasualization of dock labour.21 As
shown above, the Rotterdam port and its employers mainly made use of
casual labour at the beginning of the twentieth century. Trade unions,
however, quickly began opposing the practice of hiring labourers on
a daily basis which left these casual dockers with almost no financial
security. As from the beginning of the twentieth century a new category
of dockers appeared. With agrarian roots and Orthodox-Protestant back-
ground these dockers showed ambitions to become respectable and dis-
ciplined workers. They showed little or no affinity with the stereotypical
docker who favoured the freedom and flexibility of choosing for himself
which employer he would work for that day. This new category of dock-
ers wanted a steady job with some formal rules and regulations. This
tendency was also seen among some enlightened employers who were
influenced by social issues and hoped to stabilize the social climate in
the port by introducing proper rules and better working conditions.
This combination had led to the introduction in 1918 of a Labour
Pool which guaranteed work (and income) to some 2,000 dockers.
Fluctuating with the business cycle this number could rise to 6,000. A
large proportion of the Rotterdam dockers however remained casual
labourers during the interwar period.
In the immediate post-war period (1945-46), the unemployed dockers
were active in the rebuilding of their port and were mobilized to restore
the cargo handling activities in the port. From 1947 on, however, there
was a shortage of casual labour. Dockers who used to work in the port
now found employment in construction or metallurgy. From 1959

employers in the port of Rotterdam were confronted with a structural
shortage of casual labour. The port tried to attract commuters from
other parts of the country and in the 1960s a bonus was given to dock-
ers who could persuade workers to become dockworkers. In 1961 the
Rotterdam employers launched an offical sociological survey to find out
why they were not successful in attracting new labourers for the port.
The conclusion showed that dock work was perceived as a temporary,
dirty job and not as a job for the long term.22
Rotterdam now took a step forward by consciously choosing the path
of decasualization. All companies in the port raised the numbers of
regular workers at the expense of casual labourers. In 1965 the number
of regulars reached 80 per cent. The remaining casuals were all offered
a contract by the Labour Pool and were granted holiday benefits, health
insurance, formal rules of dismissal, and so on. No longer hired on
a daily basis, these casual workers were in practice hired for a consider-
able period of time and worked longer periods for the same employer.
In Antwerp quite the opposite happened and casual labour remained
the cornerstone of labour organization in the docks. A system of unem-
ployment insurance was introduced - the ‘Compensatiefonds voor
bestaanszekerheid' which guaranteed dockers 66 per cent of their nor-
mal income in case of involuntary unemployment. The majority of the
Antwerp dockers however remained casual labourers who were hired on
a daily basis. In 1964 a formal proposition by the employers to decasual-
ize and introduce a guaranteed weekly income was rejected, with most
dockers referring to the loss of independence and freedom.23 So unlike
their Rotterdam comrades the Antwerp dockers did not see casual dock
labour as an ‘improper' occupation.

the necessary re-structuring. The official inauguration of the last docks
and lock in 1965 marked the end of the Ten Year Plan, doubling the
port's capacity with new docks and locks. With containerization in the
