Towards the end of the 1960s the Antwerp port had finally undergone
the necessary re-structuring. The official inauguration of the last docks
and lock in 1965 marked the end of the Ten Year Plan, doubling the
port's capacity with new docks and locks. With containerization in the
offing, however, this would not prove to be the correct or complete
remedy for the Antwerp port.
In 1966 both Antwerp and Rotterdam welcomed their first container
vessel.24 At the end of that year Antwerp had received 43,000 TEU while
Rotterdam did slightly better with 60,000 TEU. In the following years
however the Antwerp port was once again no match for the Dutch

152 The Evolution of Antwerp and Rotterdam
competitor. In 1971 the Rotterdam port was already handling 1 million
TEU annually. The Antwerp port would only reach that level in 1978.
In 1980 Rotterdam broke the barrier of 2 million TEU. Antwerp would
reach that level 13 years later. So after a somewhat comparable start in
1966, the Rotterdam port had once again outclassed its major competi-
tor. Why did Rotterdam once again adjust better to the challenges of
containerization? The fact is that the standardization of the cargo - with
the container as the symbol for this evolution - made speed the key
factor in the cargo handling business. The eventual loading and unload-
ing of the cargo had to be speeded up because of the capital-intensive
nature of container ships. Since container ships were three or four times
more expensive - both in building and in exploitation - than a regular
liner, the shipping companies wanted to further reduce dead time in the
ports. Where the sea:land ratio for the average liner was about 1:4, this
changed to 1:1 for the container ships. This quest for more speed could
not be met exclusively by an additional labour force.
Given the physical challenges of container handling, the only way to
really increase speed was clearly to invest in new technologies specific
to the container handling business. The shipping companies required
specialized terminals with specialized large capacity cranes. Antwerp
and Rotterdam responded in totally different ways to these market
demands. In Rotterdam the large stevedore companies

changed to 1:1 for the container ships. This quest for more speed could

really increase speed was clearly to invest in new technologies specific
to the container handling business. The shipping companies required
specialized terminals with specialized large capacity cranes. Antwerp
and Rotterdam responded in totally different ways to these market
demands. In Rotterdam the large stevedore companies, correctly inter-
preting the implications of those boxes, started investing in specialized
terminals constructed solely for container handling, encouraged by
the Rotterdam port authority.25 The result was that after a few years
Rotterdam was the undisputed leader in container handling in the
triangle Antwerp-Rotterdam-Hamburg, with Antwerp remaining in
second and sometimes third place. Antwerp responded much too late
to the challenges of containerization. In the 1960s the overall picture
of cargo handling in the port of Antwerp was remarkably similar to
the situation in the interwar years, with the clear division between ste-
vedores and naties continuing to affect the actual handling. Although
some firms had disappeared, there were still several dozen small cargo
handling companies. The cornerstone of the naties remained their
co-operative structure. This limited the investment options for too
long. Compared with their Rotterdam opponents, the Antwerp port
companies were simply unable to meet the financial challenges of con-
tainerization; with their co-operative structure, they could not generate
the necessary capital for large investments. The Antwerp port also had
no tradition of specialized terminals. As long as the port authority had
been responsible for the construction of the docks, warehouses and

quays, it had been mainly a multifunctional general cargo part, so that
all kinds of general cargo could be handled in most of the installations.
After the port authority's withdrawal, the stevedores andnaties had fol-
lowed that same policy: the quays were installed for general cargo and
had to be multifunctional.
It took the Antwerp cargo handling companies too long to realize
that they needed only specialized cargo terminals if they wanted to
play an important role in container handling. More than just a change
of mentality was required, however. The cargo handling companies also
needed to change their organization and structures if they wanted to
cope successfully with the challenges of containerization. In the 1970s
and 1980s the Antwerp cargo handling companies abandoned their co-
operative structures and reorganized as normal enterprises with a sound
and transparent financial base and structure. A process of vertical and
horizontal integration started: naties offered stevedoring services and
vice versa. Fewer but larger companies invested in specialized terminals
from the early to mid-1980s.26 The real breakthrough of containers
and increased market share for the Antwerp port did not, however,
arrive until 1992. In that year the first specialized container terminal
upstream was opened. Previously all container terminals had been situ-
ated downstream of the locks, resulting in considerable loss of time for
the container vessels. In Rotterdam, however, container terminals had
long since been situated upstream.
Some conclusions
At the end of the nineteenth century both Antwerp and Rotterdam
were confronted with the need for a faster turnaround for the vessels
that docked in their ports. The higher running costs of the steam ves-
sel made speed more important for ship-owners. In both ports we have
seen that specialized stevedoring companies started offering their serv-
ices and made use of mainly casual labour, with dockers being hired on
a daily basis.
In Antwerp, however, we have seen that these stevedoring companies
worked separately from the traditionalnaties. Stevedores were in charge
of the actual loading and unloading, while thenaties took care of distri-
bution, transport and warehousing. In Antwerp the small, undercapital-
ized company remained dominant. In Rotterdam the traditionalvemen
started offering stevedoring services. By the end of the nineteenth

154 The Evolution of Antwerp and Rotterdam
Because of the limited role of the city council in the port's
superstructure, the Rotterdam companies were pushed into a more
pro-active role than their Antwerp colleagues. In Antwerp the com-
panies could rely on warehouses, cranes, etc. that were built and
financed by the city council. In Rotterdam the city council limited
itself to the building of the maritime infrastructure (docks, quays).
All superstructure needed was financed by the private companies.
This pushed the Rotterdam companies into technological innova-
tion in a bid to increase the return on their investments. In Antwerp
this factor was absent: the city paid for all superstructure, and the
financial risks, consequently the potential benefits, for the private
companies were limited. The Antwerp naties and stevedores seemed
happy with this. In Antwerp the city council and the private com-
panies opted for an ‘all-round' port. All facilities were designed for
the broadest possible types of cargo. In Rotterdam the city council
encouraged specialized terminals and facilities.
How has all this had an impact on labour organization? The choice of
a general cargo port combined with the limited financial involvement
in their port meant that an ‘all-round' labour organization with a large
pool of casual labourers seemed the best deal for the Antwerp employ-
ers. Supported by the fact that, apart from some labour shortages in
the 1960s, there was an abundant supply of casual labour and thus no
pressure to take steps towards decasualization, cheap casual labour and
a pool of all-round dockers remained the cornerstone of dock labour in
the port of Antwerp. The financial risks for the Antwerp employers were
limited: if they needed dockers, the supply was more

the best deal for the Antwerp employ-
ers. Supported by the fact that, apart from some labour shortages in
the 1960s, there was an abundant supply of casual labour and thus no
pressure to take steps towards decasualization, cheap casual labour and
a pool of all-round dockers remained the cornerstone of dock labour in
the port of Antwerp. The financial risks for the Antwerp employers were
limited: if they needed dockers, the supply was more than adequate. If
not, they had no financial obligations towards this large army of casual
labourers. Permanent labour costs for the Antwerp employers remained
limited. For the majority of small companies casual labour and leasing
superstructure was the only way of doing business. In Rotterdam, on the
contrary, from the end of the 1940s the supply of casual labourers will-
ing to work in the port dried up. The Rotterdam employers were forced
to rethink their labour organization and took decisive steps towards
decasualization from the 1950s. I believe that in the long run this
forward-looking approach definitely proved to be the best strategy. To
protect their own large investments but also to make labour organiza-
tion on their own terminals as tailor-made or specialized as they wanted
to, the Rotterdam employers fell back on their own core of permanent
labourers. Although further research needs to be done, I believe that this
company rather than port-wide approach (as was the case in Antwerp)
made the Rotterdam employers better prepared for the challenges of the

future. Once it became apparent that the introduction of the container,
for instance, would fundamentally change cargo handling (techniques
but also the composition of the gangs),the Rotterdam employers were
faster to adapt. In Antwerp, for example, it took difficult negotiations
with a pool of several thousand casual dockers before there was any
movement towards a reduction of the gangs. For too long the Antwerp
port and its employers maintained a strategy of ‘one size fits all' with a
large pool of all-round dockers. The fact that the Rotterdam stevedores
were pushed towards a more substantial financial involvement in their
own superstructure and made definite choices of certain types of cargo
also made them more aware of the most appropriate labour organiza-
tion for their own terminal. In Antwerp, the employers had been think-
ing that they needed to do everything and therefore needed a pool of
labourers who were as all-round as possible. Choosing to maintain a
very large pool of casual labourers at community level (in 2011 there are
still 10,000 labourers in the pool, 5,000 of whom remain casual) made
it very difficult to adapt to market changes. In Rotterdam the choice of
permanent labourers made this easier.

Institutional Path Dependence
in Port Regulation: A Comparison
of New Zealand and Australia
James Reveley and Malcolm Tull
Introduction
The Australian and New Zealand port industries in the post-World
War II period exhibit strong elements of path dependence. Simply
put, economic and political actors' purposive decisions pushed the
development of port institutions down a pathway which became hard
to step off: institutional lock-ins impeded strategic flexibility and
the growth of port productivity; inefficient macro- and micro-level
institutional arrangements reduced Australian and New Zealand port
efficiency. Given this experience, our chapter uses path dependence
as a method to explain institutional stability and change within
New Zealand's and Australia's respective port systems. While port
institutions in both countries were slow to adapt to shifts in the wider
industry environment, they eventually succumbed to reformist change.
As we explain, this occurred more strongly in New Zealand through
pathbreaking institutional transformation in 1989, the pressures for
which mounted over several decades. In Australia, by contrast, there
were many false starts and change was slower even after the ports
were caught up in the federal government's late 1980s economy-wide
programme of microeconomic reform.
Applying path dependence to port history
Despite its cross-disciplinary appeal, the path dependence concept has
only recently been utilized by historians who study ports.1 In line with a
social science trend, moreover, they use path dependence not to explain
how technical progress occurs, but rather to investigate institutional
and organizational stability and change.2 This approach follows

Not infrequently, New Zealand's ports were chokepoints that slowed
the movement of the staple commodity exports on which its economic
development relied. Waterside workers repeatedly demonstrated their
capacity to hold up stevedoring work. Countrywide strikes shut ports
down in 1890 and 1913.17 A thorn in the side of governments of various
political stripes thereafter, port-level labour disputes impeded trade
flows.18 Spurred by a crisis moment in 1940, as the country prepared

This scheme regularized port hiring and provided greater employment
and income security to waterside workers.20 Worker selection and

administered by a specialized government agency, the Waterfront
Control Commission.
Trying to prevent costly hold-ups at the country's ports, legislators
amended the institutional rules of New Zealand's port ILMs no fewer
than four times between 1946 and 1948.21 During this time the labour
bureau control agency, renamed the Waterfront Industry Commission
(WIC), maintained the port-based ILMs. Irritated by militant port

endorsed the decision by port employers to confront the national
Waterside Workers' Union (WWU).22 In 1951, during a landmark 151-

it with twenty-six new port unions. Path dependence was initiated by
this government's answer to the logical next question: should port-level
ILMs and the WIC be abandoned in favour of a different labour market
arrangement, such as a return to firm-based hiring?

Appointed in 1950 to consider alternatives, a Royal Commission of

The returns to this port labour market institutional arrangement
increased throughout the 1950s as the fortunes of both the unions
and many firms became entwined with it. First and foremost, the
ILM institutions empowered the new port unions, which quickly
organized themselves into a North Island and a South Island Federation.
By providing job security and regular pay to registered waterside
workers and giving them a legal monopoly over stevedoring, the WIC
inadvertently supplied a stable base for union organizing. Principally,
it maintained an exclusive port-level register of legally licensed
waterside workers (known in local parlance as watersiders) available
to be allocated to shipping and stevedoring companies. All registered
watersiders were required by law to join their local port union, with
casual hiring permitted only in cases of extreme labour shortage. While
it was never the policymakers' intention, the WIC quickly became the
cornerstone of post-1951 union strength at the country's ports.25

firms. Principally, firms were guaranteed a supply of skilled labour with

Institutional lock-in also stemmed from the ILMs' advantages for
firms. Principally, firms were guaranteed a supply of skilled labour with
which to meet their fluctuating labour needs. A national levy spread
the cost of maintaining the stevedoring workforce across the industry;
firms contributed in direct proportion to hours worked by the registered
watersiders they drew from the Commission. Not having to employ a
permanent workforce sustained an array of independent stevedoring
firms operating on short-term contracts with shipping companies; they
held around 20 per cent market share until the late 1960s.26 But it was
not just the independents that benefited from this set-up. Given that
firms did not need to permanently hire a workforce, relying instead
on the WIC's labour supply, the use of ‘cost-plus' contracts meant
that there was money to be made from stevedoring. This contracting
system displaced labour costs elsewhere in the transport chain, as the
stevedoring operator simply charged the shipper a percentage on top of

stevedoring company subsidiaries, notably the British-owned New
Zealand Overseas (Conference) Lines, used an equivalent of cost-plus
contracting: they simply built into their freight rates a high margin for
anticipated stevedoring - especially labour - costs.28

decreasing uncertainty about the quality of labour inputs and worker

they elicited sustained work effort by tapping into elaborate informal
routines that evolved within this institutional environment to govern

Institutional path dependence in Australia
As an island nation with a coastline of 36,735 km and widely separated
centres of population, Australia has always depended on shipping and
ports to handle its trade. Australia's 42 major ports include specialized
bulk ports and mixed cargo ports handling both bulk and container
cargoes. In 2009-10 total trade at Australian ports was about 922 million
tonnes, 94 per cent of which was accounted for by bulk cargoes. This
reflects Australia's longstanding comparative advantage as an exporter
of primary products to world markets. Australia has been a major
beneficiary of industrialization in Asia: in the 1960s Japan's ‘growth
miracle' led to a major increase in demand for mineral exports and saw
it replace the UK as Australia's major trading partner. Since the 1980s
double-digit growth of the Chinese economy has led to unprecedented
growth in demand

world economy. However, as in New Zealand, ports have sometimes been
chokepoints rather than gateways for shipping and trade, especially for
high-value general cargoes. This is mainly because for much of its history
the Australian waterfront has been characterized by rigid institutions that
have been slow to change as the maritime industry has changed. The
primary institutional features are the monopoly power and job control
exercised by the waterfront unions; the concentrated market structure
and high level of vertical integration in the cargo handling industry; and
the management practices of public port authorities. These combined to
produce a classic pattern of self-reinforcing path dependence. Waterfront
crises - ranging from major strikes to cargo bottlenecks - have led to
episodic intervention by both state and federal governments but until the
1980s most governmental attempts to overcome institutional lock-in met
with only limited success.
Regulating the waterfront
Until the 1990s, when a limited number of ports were privatized, all of
Australia's major ports were directly controlled by state governments.
The federal government, however, has the constitutional power to
intervene due to its responsibility for interstate trade and commerce.
Historically its role has been limited to industrial relations (the
Commonwealth Court of Conciliation and Arbitration provided the
first award for the industry in 1914), defence, quarantine and national
security.

the world over - has been notoriously strike-prone.47 This was originally

improvements in labour productivity.54 Just like New Zealand, the rules
and procedures of the internal labour market continued to suppress the
pressures of the outside labour market.

Shifting to reactive path dependence
In the early years of the twentieth century government policy
was dominated by the creation of ‘protective' strategies to help
preserve living standards: the White Australia Policy (1901); arbitration
(1904) and the basic wage (1907); tariff protection (the first clearly
protectionist tariff was the Lyne tariff of 1908); and the government-
owned Commonwealth Bank (1911).60 While in the first half of the
twentieth century these policies and institutions helped boost Australia's
population and economic progress, by the 1960s there were indications
that institutional rigidity was reducing the competitiveness of the
economy. In the 1970s economic slowdown and globalization forced

and the creation of a more competitive commercial environment. The
size of the workforce was to be reduced by 3,000 voluntary redundancies
but 1,000 younger workers were to be recruited to improve the age

Conclusion
The durability of inefficient port regulatory institutions in New Zealand
and Australia is only explicable by reference to path dependence.
Comparing the reform process in each country, clearly the institutional
change trigger points had different timings and effects. In New Zealand
containerization functioned as a trigger event, ushering in a process of
reactive path dependence that ultimately exposed waterside workers to
competition in the external labour market. Once initiated, institutional
change occurred in a lockstep manner. Stemming from a backlash effect,
the change was decisive, transformative and long-lasting. By contrast,
pressures for change in Australian ports were more diffuse, coalescing
only under the wider process of microeconomic reform. Unlike New
Zealand, where the roots of frame-breaking port labour market change
can be dated to containerization spreading across the country's ports
in the early 1970s, the Australian waterfront industry's shift to reactive
path dependence coincides with the economy-wide reforms of the
1980s. New Zealand's reactive path dependence culminated in an earlier
regulatory decision, to lock the WIC in place, being unambiguously
reversed. Arguably in Australia, however, port regulatory reform
was but the first step down a path that is still being travelled. It is
replete with obstacles. The economists' solution to problems of path
dependence and institutional rigidity is usually to recommend a ‘good
dose of competition', but

Since adopting the Open Door Policy as its strategic development
direction in 1978, China has enjoyed decades of substantial economic
growth. By the 1990s, China had already become the second largest
recipient of foreign direct investment (FDI) after the United States.
Throughout the early Open Door Policy period, China persistently
achieved a highly impressive annual GDP growth rate.
Such achievements, however, were the outcomes of considerable
painstaking side effects of reforms. Indeed, during the early Open
Door Policy period, the government struggled to overcome a number
of challenges, notably: (1) to improve the rural economy; (2) to secure
infrastructure and basic industrial development; (3) to acquire the latest
innovations in science and technology; (4) to upgrade key industries;
(5) to improve education and training; and (6) to reform the CCP and its
institutional system, while continuing strictly to control political and
military power. Moreover, economic development could be sustained
only if the country was supported by good transport systems, well-built
infrastructures, technological and managerial innovations. Acting as
the interaction point between land and sea, ports were critical nodes
in the establishment of efficient multimodal supply chains, especially
since maritime transportation was (and still is) the most cost-effective
and popular way to move cargoes and raw materials around the world.3
Nevertheless, in China, construction and upgrading of transport infra-
structure often lagged behind economic growth, thus forming bottle-
necks along the supply chains.
Various authors investigated the problems of developing a good trans-
portation system in China,4 and identified several problems, including:
(1) inadequate physical infrastructure; (2) insufficient deep water ports;
(3) poor bureaucratic structures; (4) an imperfect legal framework,
especially for supporting international trade; (5) the lack of a healthy
competitive environment for the port and shipping industries; and (6)
uncoordinated, if not conflicting, central and local government respon-
sibilities in these industries. Given that these problems would seriously

Successful institutional reform was critical to achieve good port gov-

be allowed to operate in important economic sectors, with the govern-

With increasing FDI and contacts with the global market, China's port
industry became more complex, with intensified inter-port competition
in the international arena. Inefficient institutional structure was one
of the most problematic obstacles to further economic development.
Therefore, during the early Open Door Policy period, the government
carried out four phases of institutional reform (1982, 1988, 1993 and
1998) to improve the economic structure. The first phase took place
in 1982 after Deng Xiaoping's speech entitled ‘Institutional Reform
is a Revolution'. To achieve the ‘modernization of socialism' and to
complement economic development, the State Council abolished some
overlapping ministries or integrated departments with similar responsi-
bilities.5Moreover, in view of the increase in foreign trade, the Ministry
of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation was established through
the merger of several committees and ministries.
This phase succeeded in resolving some urgent economic problems.
However, it mainly focused on the rural economy. With increased FDI
and private sector participation, new problems related to centralized
decision-making and the merging of administration and operations
arose. This exposed the need for another phase of reform. The concept of
separation of government and enterprise was first proposed in the CCP's
On Reform of Economic Structures (1984). This idea was accepted during the
Thirteenth CCP Congress and the Seventh National People's Congress in
1987 and 1988 respectively. The objective was to create an institutional
structure which could complement demands for modernization, includ-

tion and considerable investment by multinational corporations.
In this respect, we argue that this fourth phase was a watershed for
the genuine separation of administration and management. For the first
time, the responsibilities of government and the private sector were
clearly defined in ways that could be generally understood. The govern-
ment's responsibility was to levy taxes on enterprise owners according
to their investments and profitability, to regulate the operation and
financial arrangements of enterprises, and to appoint major officials of
enterprises. The enterprises were responsible for the autonomy of man-
agement, profits or losses, the maintenance (or increase) of the value of
public assets, as well as defending the rights of enterprise owners. Such
clear-cut definitions aimed at accurately identifying the relationship
between the state and the market, allowing each to fulfil their appropri-
ate roles. Therefore it was clear that the government was attempting to
alter its ruling ideology from ‘multi-faceted government' to ‘govern-
ment with limitations'.7 This reformed system was also an answer to
the changing demands of new economic development. What then are
the implications of these reforms for the Chinese ports during the early
Open Door Policy period?

Institutional reforms
Accountability was what was required of officials; they were responsible
for their actions and must explain to the public both reasons and antici-
pated consequences. China's institutional structure faced problems of
overlapping ministries, irresponsible behaviour by officials (in both
senior and junior ranks), poor efficiency and sweeping government
intervention. As a consequence, institutional reforms were urgently
required to allow China to achieve sustainable economic development.
This was especially important for the port industry, which was one of
the frontiers to the outside world.

Public sector management
With a coastline of more than 14,500 km, and nearly 30 ports with
international connections, China has substantial potential in develop-
ing maritime transportation, as can be seen through the long history of
overseas trade in traditional China. Nevertheless, modern port develop-
ment in China got off to a slow start. Although the container revolution
started in the 1960s, the first container did not appear in China until
1973,8 and it was not until 1978 that the first regular container service
between Shanghai and Sydney was launched by COSCO, the country's
flagship container shipping line.
Such backwardness started to change with the implementation of
the Open Door Policy. With intensified economic development, the
demands for shipping services in China boomed. The government
recognized that ports and their infrastructures were the basic tenet of
China's economic development, and thus ports were assigned priority
for further investments.
Article 7 of the Sino-Foreign Equity Joint Venture Law stated that
an equity joint venture might enjoy preferential treatment, notably
tax reduction and tax holidays.9 This law applied to the ports. The
crucial document revealing that port development was given priority
by the government was probably the Interim Regulations of the State
Council of the PRC on Preferential Treatment to Sino-Foreign Joint Ventures
on Harbour and Wharf Construction (hereinafter ‘Interim Regulations').10
Recognizing that modern and efficient ports were necessary for China's
‘socialist modernization' (Article 1), while understanding the fact that
port-related projects were often capital-intensive and time-consuming
with low returns (Article 2), joint ventures in port projects and opera-
tions were given preferential treatment in terms of time period and
financial arrangements. These efforts were reflected in subsequent

Public financial management
Finance shortage was a major barrier hindering Chinese port develop-
ment. The government recognized that its budget was inadequate to
finance ambitious port projects, implying that it was impossible to
dominate port affairs completely. Thus some financial concessions were
required.

encouraged to raise funds through the levy of port construction fees.
Another source of income was international financial institutions.

China to develop ten container depots in the port of Tianjin. Finally,

and the political perception that ports were regarded as strategic assets.

a certain fixed amount of income was given by the port administration
to port enterprises to pay for port expenditure. In other words, enterprises
were paying ‘fees' rather than ‘taxes' to the government. Recognizing the
disadvantages of annual rental payment, as well as the need to comple-
ment Chinese economic development, the payment method for conces-
sion fees changed

been up to the enterprises themselves to determine the prices.
Other financial concessions
Under the Interim Regulations, tax concessions were introduced to
encourage port investment. There were exemptions from custom duties
and other consolidated commercial-industrial taxes on raw material
imports, facilities, transport equipment and other devices used for termi-
nal construction. Moreover, tax exemptions were introduced for newly
established port joint ventures with 15 years or more of operation.
Legal reforms
With shrinking public and national planning and support, the govern-
ment could no longer govern solely through executive means. Indeed,
discussions to improve the Chinese legal system had been taking place
since the 1970s. However, the objective of legal reforms was largely
complementary to the direction of the country's economic develop-
ment. As Zheng pointed out, most of the laws and regulations passed
since 1978 mainly concerned economic development, commercial
activities and foreign investments.26
Being part of the economic development package, maritime trans-
portation also underwent legal reforms. As in other industries, purely

TheMaritime Code
China began to construct a legal framework for maritime policy after the
formation of the PRC in 1949. However, the legal structure of the mari-
time sector was not laid down until 1992 when the Open Door Policy
triggered such a need. As mentioned earlier, before 2004, there were
no laws specifically addressing the management of the port industry.
Previously, the Maritime Code, adopted in 1992, had served as the major
legal framework for China's maritime development (including ports).
Within the Code, there were two major port-related points. First, the
MOC was responsible for land (except rail) and maritime transporta-
tion, including maritime strategy and policymaking. For the manage-
ment of ports, MOC granted permits to foreign firms to engage in the
operation of Chinese ports, while the MOC was responsible for national
port planning, strategies and policies. Second, the Code introduced
exceptions in various areas. Before its adoption, no foreign firms were
allowed to engage in any activities within Chinese ports. After the adop-
tion of theMaritime Code, exceptions were granted in four situations: (1)
if there was a joint venture with a foreign partner; (2) if special technol-
ogy and skills not available among domestic companies were needed;
(3) if the principal base of the joint ventures was located in China; and
(4) if the registered capital contributed by the foreign partner(s) did not
exceed 49 per cent. Hence, several points that significantly contributed
to the evolution of Chinese port development during the early Open
Door Policy period were present. First, the Code laid the foundations
of China's strategy in port reform and development during this period.
Second, it endorsed the necessity of introducing foreign capital in port
development projects through the establishment of equity joint ven-
tures with domestic partners. Third, it enabled the transfer of new (

Second, it endorsed the necessity of introducing foreign capital in port

Other laws, regulations and guidelines
In addition to the Code, many other maritime-related regulations were
also approved and promulgated during this period. Partly to com-
plement maritime-related laws and regulations, other more general

Adolf K. Y. Ng and Ka-chai Tam 191
commercial laws were also drafted, approved and published. These
aimed to protect the economic rights of both foreign and domestic
investors. For example, Article 2 of the Sino-Foreign Equity Joint
Venture Law prohibited nationalization or requisitioning by the state of
any equity joint ventures under normal circumstances. Even under very
special circumstances where public interest required the requisitioning
of such joint ventures, the document required the state to strictly follow
legal procedures and compensate the affected investors. Under certain
circumstances, the State Council also issued ad hocc regulations and
guidelines facilitating port development whenever necessary. Due to
decentralization, local guidelines were also provided which gave advice
on how local port authorities should implement administrative duties.
All these laws, regulations and guidelines were efforts to standardize and
systematize the development of China's maritime industries, including
ports. In general, the definitions and statements in these documents
were reasonably clear and well-defined. The government clearly showed
its determination to create a market-friendly environment.

Decentralization
The participation of non-government interests was necessary to act as
watchdogs and to provide services which could not be effectively pro-
vided by the public sector. Within the Chinese port industry, the partici-
pation of the private sector was two-fold: first, the national government
decentralized power to local authorities; second, the private sector was
involved through investing terminals and facilities in these decentral-
ized ports. During the Mao era (1949-76), all Chinese ports were under
strict national control. Indeed, even until 2002, the maritime transport
sector was still directly guided by the State Council, together with the
Maritime Bureau under the MOC, which de facto was responsible for
almost every single maritime activity within ports, including human
resource management, financial planning, infrastructure building and
production. The relevant port authorities and local government played
only subordinate roles.
Despite such direct leadership, some changes had been made. The
centrally controlled system had exposed obvious disadvantages for
contemporary port development, including: (1) inconsistency between
port and city development; (2) lack of attention paid by local authori-
ties to port development; and (3) distance from the national authority,
based in Beijing and mainly staffed by people with little understanding
of port operations, often imposing inappropriate policies and strategic

Adolf K. Y. Ng and Ka-chai Tam 193
Port authorities in different cities or regions had different levels of
autonomy and strategic priorities. There were several reasons for this,
including history and government ranking, as well as the port and its
corresponding city's status and importance. With reference to Shanghai
Port Authority and Shenzhen Port Authority, these differences will be
analysed here. First, it was about history. Shanghai had been a major
port even before the establishment of the PRC in 1949, and thus unsur-
prisingly, the city had an established tradition. Shenzhen Port Authority,
by contrast, was created in 1994 after the establishment of Yantian
International Container Terminals (1992). Hence, the port authority was
new and did not experience the (rather painful) re-structuring process
of the public sector and state enterprises which took place in the 1980s.
Also, while there were a number of domestic port enterprises under
the Shanghai Port Authority (for example, Shanghai Port

new and did not experience the (rather painful) re-structuring process

Also, while there were a number of domestic port enterprises under
the Shanghai Port Authority (for example, Shanghai Port Container
Co. Ltd.), no similar enterprises were affiliated to the Shenzhen Port
Authority.30 The Shanghai Port Authority was therefore often far more
authoritative and insistent when dealing with the private sector.
The second factor affecting local authorities' power and planning
concerned the hierarchies within the Chinese institutional system.
Vertically, Shanghai was a municipal city, that is, a ‘provincial level'
authority. On the other hand, Shenzhen was a city under the Guangdong
Province, that is, a ‘city level' authority. Horizontally, the port author-
ity was a department under its respective government. Under such
an arrangement, the Shanghai Port Authority was de facto one grade
higher than its Shenzhen counterpart within the institutional system.
As illustrated in Figure 11.1, the Shanghai Port Authority and Shenzhen
Port Authorities were situated in Grades III and IV respectively within
the institutional system. Hence their interests could be channelled to
the government much more easily, a notable example being their par-
tial (but also critical) role in the government's decision to accept their
proposal to construct SISC, rather than other alternatives proposed by
nearby Zhejiang and Jiangsu Provinces.
The last factor was the status and importance of the port and its city.
Shanghai had been perceived as China's commercial city since the nine-
teenth century. After the adoption of the Open Door Policy, the govern-
ment still largely regarded Shanghai as the main gateway for foreign
investments. This gave Shanghai a rather special status, which in turn
generated self-esteem for the city and its citizens. Unsurprisingly, the
vision of Shanghai Port Authority, which aimed to restore its previous
role as a core player within the global shipping industry, was far more
ambitious than all other port authorities in China. On the other hand,

Challenges and discussions
We have analysed how China attempted to reform its port govern-
ance and development during the early Open Door Policy period.
Nevertheless, the existence of a reform framework did not guarantee the
process and its outcomes. We argue that although port governance was

recognized and the framework of meta-governance already established,
there were still substantial challenges. Indeed, with an improving finan-
cial situation, hardware deficiency was largely resolved through mass
infrastructure, technological improvements and education. But a more
problematic factor that prevented effective governance was the ‘softer'
aspects which could not be settled without painstaking efforts. As Jessop
has noted:
the state reserves to itself the right to open, close, juggle and
re-articulate governance not only in terms of particular functions but
also from the viewpoint of partisan and global political advantage...31

Throughout this period, it was not difficult to see that the government
was still suspicious of investment by multinational terminal operators.
Although ideological issues still existed, the Chinese authorities were
not unwilling to give up certain rights. Indeed, the government was
eager to reform port management systems, but its major problem was
the difficulty of defining the public sector's new responsibilities.32
With the lack of clear vision and allocation of responsibilities, the
Chinese authorities struggled to fulfil accountability in good port
governance during this period. Moreover, despite China being the
developing country which introduced the largest number of laws and
regulations during this period, the guidelines to local authorities did
not impose real constraints on their actions.As Zheng pointed out, the
Chinese legal system had struggled to transit from the ‘rule by law' to
the ‘rule of law' during the early Open Door Policy period.33 The gov-
ernment was often unwilling to improve existing laws and regulations
which further complicated the modes of conduct of investors. Even if
certain laws had been approved and promulgated, it was questionable
whether or not such laws would be comprehensively implemented due
to the country's fragmented legal structure. Possible government inter-
vention so as to protect ‘national' and/or ‘public' interests further com-
plicated matters. As Huchet and Richet argued, during this period, the
application of laws in China was far from being generally respected by
political and economic players.34 The lack of an effective framework to
promote transparency and predictability adversely affected confidence
and hence private participation in ports and other business.

In addition, the port, as a strategic asset, was especially vulnerable to
excessive government intervention. Indeed, one of the main difficul-
ties of doing business in China was excessive government interference
in strategies and operations. This was often driven by non-economic
motives and inhibited efforts to create a reliable and trustworthy legal
framework, therefore undermining effective promotion of good transpar-
ent and predictable port governance. Furthermore, the unwelcome hand
of government also inhibited the development of a healthy market envi-

ports. Before the 49 per cent ceiling for equity joint ventures was waived
in 2002 most Chinese port companies (usually directly affiliated to port
authorities) had a majority stake and their decisions were not always
made on grounds of economic benefits. As Dickens has argued, states
tend to be nervous about the impact of multinational corporations on
autonomy and stability within their national boundaries, as well as being
concerned about the leakage of tax revenues.36 Such fears were particu-
larly significant in China during the early Open Door Policy period.
A good example can be found in the Catalogue for the Guidance of
Industries for Foreign Investment.37 In it the government tried on the one
hand to create an attractive investment environment, while on the
other imposing restrictions

in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
Nevertheless, since the turn of the century, it has become clear that
China has entered a new phase in port governance and development. In
2002, China was admitted to the World Trade Organization (WTO), thus

opening a completely new era for the country's economic development,

28 June 2003, the Government approved the Port Law (promulgated on

development, as they finally ended the rather chaotic, non-legalized,
and very much executive methods that dominated Chinese port gov-

become the two busiest ports in China and the Asia-Pacific region, if

stage of development provides a meaningful lesson for other developing
countries and emerging economies considering their own approaches

Skip Fischer has suggested that maritime historians often fail to situate
their studies ‘within the broader debates that animate discussion and
research in the larger [historical] profession'.1 While this may be true
of many branches of the history discipline - Fischer cites Atlantic and
gender history as examples - it is not so applicable to business history, a
vibrant field that has long had an important maritime dimension. This
is evident in the contributions of Francis Hyde, Peter Davies and Sheila
Marriner - the Liverpool School of maritime business history - to our
understanding of the role that companies play in the process of eco-
nomic development.2 It is also apparent in works relating to the develop-
ment and regulation of shipowning as a specialist activity in particular
localities during the early stages of industrialization in Britain.3 Building
on, and combining, these two perspectives on the business of shipping,
Gordon Boyce devised a ‘complementary yet alternative framework to
Alfred D. Chandler's transaction cost approach'.4 This alternative lay in
Boyce's focus on British shipping, which introduced a non-American,
service sector element to the literature on patterns and processes of
economic growth, which had hitherto been dominated by discussions
relating to manufacturing industries in the USA. Others have followed
in Boyce's wake, with the work of Gelina Harlaftis and John Theotokas
on family enterprise in the British and Greek shipping industries offer-
ing a notable European insight into the field as it has moved beyond
the Harvard School and Chandler's paradigm.5
This chapter seeks to enhance the maritime contribution to the
business history of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

The private limited company: a ‘typical
British compromise'
The significance of a favourable legal framework for the development
of shipowning in Britain has been widely recognized. Building on
Ralph Davis's seminal analysis of early modern shipping,7 Simon Ville's
study of Henley and Son, and his broader appraisal of the growth of
specialization in shipping, contend that as shipping was governed by
Admiralty law it was afforded critical advantages in the late eighteenth
and nineteenth centuries when demand for sea transport rose sharply
due to the pressures of war and industrialization.8 Similar contentions are
advanced in Sarah Palmer's overview of British shipping between 1815 and
the repeal of the Navigation Laws in 1850, in Philip Cottrell's discussion
of steamship concerns in Liverpool during the mid-Victorian era, and in
Boyce's analysis of

liability companies propelled the industry forwards from the 1850s.

growth was limited, the broad extension of markets after 1850 encour-
aged business expansion.12 This was accompanied by changes in the
law relating to company formation. The Bubble Act of 1720 had made
the formation of a joint-stock limited liability company prohibitively
time-consuming and expensive for most business enterprises. After
1720, according to John F. Wilson, ‘it would cost at least £600 in legal
expenses to form a joint stock company ... and (even in the early nine-
teenth century) as average fixed investment in industry would probably
not have exceeded a few thousand pounds few were willing to pay so
much for the privilege of incorporation'. Although the Act was repealed
in 1825, this ‘was actually only a nominal breakthrough in extending
the availability of joint stock company status, because firms still required
an Act of Parliament before limited liability could be granted'. However,
increased pressure for further relaxation of the laws governing com-
pany formation - especially from the banking and utility industries -
led to the enactment of increasingly permissive legislation. The 1844
Joint Stock Companies Act enabled firms to incorporate through a
relatively simple registration procedure, and limited liability became
widely accessible following the 1856 Limited Liability Act. This process
of reform culminated in the 1862 Consolidating Act,13 which unleashed
‘a veritable flood of applications' that witnessed 24,002 companies reg-
istered in the United Kingdom between the passage of the Act and 31
December 1885.14 As the company differed from the proprietorship and
partnership in that its equity could be sold to professional shareholders
with no managerial role, it is reasonable to expect that the rise in com-
pany formation would foster the separation of ownership and control.
But this did not occur to any significant degree. Rather, as Peter Payne
observes, ‘in contrast with the expectations of the statesmen respon-
sible for the early company acts, there developed a private company'.15
Distinguishing a private limited company from a public concern was
difficult before 1907, when the former attained legal recognition as a
company in which ‘all equity was retained by those who signed the arti-

Hull's private business mentalité
Hull was a major, multi-faceted maritime centre in the early twentieth
century. As contemporary Hullenesians were keen to point out, theirs
was the UK's third largest port in terms of the volume of cargoes han-
dled by its nine docks. This ‘gateway to the great manufacturing centres
of England' was home to a shipping interest that had turned to steam
power and metal hulls much earlier and more comprehensively than
its counterparts in other major ports, and in 1913 it ranked as the UK's
ninth largest shipowning port.22 Although Hull was not a naval base,
it possessed a shipbuilding industry and was unique among Britain's
principal ports in that it boasted a substantial interest in the fisheries.

as the covert proliferation of the private limited company demon-
strated. Accordingly, in Britain's third port, the spirit of the ‘typical
British compromise' imbued the maritime business sector to such an

1860-1914 period.

Business behaviour and culture in an ‘isolate city'
It has been alleged that Britain's family firms engaged in non-expansion-
ary strategies so that founding families could maintain control over their
enterprises. Chandler, in particular, criticizes British business leaders for
perceiving companies ‘in personal rather than organizational terms, as
family estates to be nurtured and passed on to heirs'.46 This, it is centered,
encouraged founders to remain in power for longer than they were able
to perform satisfactorily, and to bequeath the running of firms to heirs
who lacked the necessary competencies for such a role. But the notion
advanced by Chandler that British business leaders ‘failed' by not follow-
ing the American example of ‘managerial capitalism' has been challenged
on various grounds. Roy Church, for instance, highlights the fact that
family firms deployed contrasting strategies in different countries, while
others argue that family firms and non-family firms engaged in similar
behaviours.47 So, as Wilson concludes, ‘one cannot say that the family
firm per see was a problem'.48 This highlights the limitations inherent in
what Philip Scranton describes as ‘organizational determinism', with
Chandler's focus on the internal workings of the firm yielding ‘a field of
vision so constrained that little other than the desired objects and proc-
esses can be seen'.49 In other words, insufficient attention is afforded to
the impact that factors external to the firm had upon business behaviour.
Locating business behaviour within the environment in which it oper-
ates has therefore emerged as a key research theme. This is especially true

esses can be seen'.49 In other words, insufficient attention is afforded to
the impact that factors external to the firm had upon business behaviour.
Locating business behaviour within the environment in which it oper-
ates has therefore emerged as a key research theme. This is especially true
with regard to the cultural context. As Jonathon Brown and Mary B. Rose
assert: ‘[e]asily the most important influence on [business] behaviour is
shown to be "culture", as reflected in the value systems in society, locali-
ties, religious groupings, or firms'.50
Hull's experience emphasizes the weakness of analyses that err
towards ‘organizational determinism'. Strategies routinely associated
with family firms - especially those held to have impacted negatively on

in point, as Thomas Wilson - according to his sons and heirs - remained
at the helm of TWSC for too long, while 40 years later the progeny of
Charles Henry and Arthur Wilson took over the management of TWSC
(and Earle's) despite doubts about their ability and aptitude for such
positions.51 There is also evidence to support the contention that fam-
ily firms were vulnerable to ‘the extraction of excessive resources from
a firm to support family lifestyles'.52 When, for instance, the nominal
capital of TWSC was halved from £2 million to £1 million in 1895,
£500,000 of this was transferred to the depreciation fund, with the
remainder used to create debentures for the family at an interest rate of
5 per cent per annum, which guaranteed a yearly income of £25,000.53

in the firm, even when profits were low. Accordingly, in 1883, the

may devolve, by reason of death of a Member may hold such share or
shares during a period not exceeding 12 months, nevertheless such
persons shall not be entitled to participate in the dividend declared by
the Company'.55

obvious flaw in the notion that principals pursue extramural interests

these external, often costly, interests is largely reliant upon their firms
remaining profitable. Moreover, in the case of the Wilsons, like many
other entrepreneurs, it was demonstrably not the case that the pursuit
of ‘aristocratic' and business interests was incompatible. As theNew York

businessmen merely fell prey to a set of nationally determined social

It would be an exaggeration, however, to say that the relative remote-
ness of the locality prevented external influences from penetrating
Hull's maritime business community, which, given the very nature
of sea-related activity, had vital overseas connections. But it is highly
probable that the relative isolation of Hull meant that the fortunes of
individual firms had a greater resonance in this ‘lonely daughter' than
they would have done in other towns and cities of comparable size. This
accounts for the close correlation between ownership and control in
the maritime sector, and its relative immunity from outside influences.
As Brown and Rose observe, ‘depending upon the relative importance
of a business group, the culture of the firms helped to mould that of
the surrounding society'.69 The shipping concern of TWSC was funda-
mental to this process. The monopoly enjoyed by the company in Hull
was not only captured in a local adage - ‘Hull is Wilson's, Wilson's is
Hull' - but also explicitly recognized in a report prepared by a branch
of MI5 regarding the 1914-18 war in which ‘the strength of the Wilson
influence at Hull' was noted.70 The sheer size and commercial power
of this private limited company meant that it exerted an extraordinary
influence on the behaviour of the local maritime business commu-
nity, an influence that was enhanced by the diversification of Wilson
family members from shipping into other sea-related industries. By

Culture matters
Three threads are interwoven to form the fabric of this chapter. First,
examination of the legal framework within which the organization of
British firms evolved indicates that shipowners were not especially priv-
ileged with regard to limited liability before 1850, a finding that tem-
pers the conclusions of earlier works on shipowning. This discussion
further suggests that a large proportion of companies remained largely
unchanged even after they incorporated under the terms of legislation

Michaela G. Barnard and David J. Starkey 215
passed in 1862, with many continuing, in effect, to operate as private
limited companies. The second thread offers empirical evidence relat-
ing to Hull's maritime businesses to assess the extent to which a private
mentalité prevailed in the port's business community, an assessment
that revises conventional wisdom regarding the significance of joint-
stock organization in the local maritime sector, notably the steam trawl
fishery. The importance of people and place in shaping commercial
strategies and organizational structures is appraised in the third element
of the chapter. Here, it is evident that business behaviour is not merely
dictated by profit levels, with culture paramount in conditioning the
way entrepreneurs organize, develop and conduct their firms. As Wilson
observes, ‘one must state boldly that Culture matters'.72 The national
culture system is important in this respect but, as evidenced by Hull's
maritime business sector, it is at the local level, or within the context of
‘place', that culture is honed.
This tripartite approach sheds lights on wider themes. For instance,

This tripartite approach sheds lights on wider themes. For instance,
in condemning the ‘cultural critique', Rubenstein notes that one of the
most objectionable features of the criticism levelled at ‘Britain's economic
performance during the past generation is its obsession for manufactur-
ing industry, its manufacturing fetishism. Tacitly, only manufacturing
counts as "legitimate" business activity.'73 Comprising a range of service
and extractive activities, as well as manufacturing, the maritime business
sector should be afforded particular attention if a comprehensive under-
standing of the relationship between culture and business behaviour is to
be attained. As this chapter demonstrates, moreover, invaluable insights
into business evolution can be gained from comparative analyses of mari-
time industries in particular spatial contexts. Such analyses, in turn, have
the capacity to inform broader debates about economic performance over
the long term. Accordingly, to address the criticism voiced by Skip Fischer
that opens this chapter, further research into sea-related enterprise will
enable maritime historians to contribute effectively to scholarly debates
in business-facing fields of historical enquiry.

Risks and Rewards: The Business
of Norwegian Shipping
Stig Tenold
Due to the volatility of freight rates and vessel values, shipping is gen-
erally considered an industry in which the risks of doing business are
substantial.1 One reflection of this riskiness is the fact that fortunes can
be made, and lost, extremely quickly in the shipping sector. This chap-
ter discusses how shipowners in Norway, which for more than a century
has been one of the world's leading maritime nations, have dealt with
the question of business risk in a historical perspective.
Four time-specific cases are presented. The first is the traditional
business model that facilitated the expansion of Norwegian shipping
in the sailing ship era. Second, the advent of tanker shipping in the
interwar period saw high levels of Norwegian participation, and the
owners' willingness to take on new types of risks bore fruit. In the third
case, the first postwar decades, the most common Norwegian strate-
gies involved a substantial overall increase of risk. The hazards of this
approach became evident when shipping markets collapsed in the early
1970s. Finally, Norwegian owners' retreat towards less volatile market
segments during the last few decades is briefly presented.
The chapter deals specifically with the two most important aspects
of business risk within shipping: what I have decided to call ‘the activ-
ity risk' and ‘the asset risk'. The activity risk refers to the volatility of
profits from the sale of transport services, while the asset risk refers to
the effects of fluctuations in asset values on the companies' balance
sheets. Through a very simple analytical framework, it is shown how
the manner in which Norwegian shipowners have been exposed to, and
dealt with, these risks has changed over time. Some of these changes
have been related to the transformation of the shipping market, while
others have been the result of conscious or unconscious adaptation
by Norwegian owners. While these risks, at least to some extent, are

An introduction to business risk: the shipowners'
perspective
Shipping is often considered a high-risk industry. According to the
leading textbook in maritime economics, shipping sounds ‘more like a
gambling game than a sober transport business. Itisa gambling game.'2
In their book on risk management in shipping, Kavussanos and Visvikis
refer to eight broad risk categories, before pointing out that their list ‘is
certainly not exhaustive'.3 Today, shipping companies are well aware
of the different types of risks, and of the importance of communicat-
ing the manner in which these risks are managed. For instance, the
Norwegian shipping company Odfjell presents their approaches to
six different risks in their annual report, while the Danish company
Norden discusses their handling of seven specific risks.4
From a financial and economic point of view, the most important
risks are the ones related to the two tasks at the core of the shipping
companies' business; indeed, the two tasks that determine success or
failure in the shipping industry. The first task is the production and
sale of transport services. The second task is the investment in the
ships necessary to produce such services. Thus, it might be convenient
to use an uncomplicated analytical framework to isolate these parts of
the shipowners' business. Figure 13.1 presents this framework graphi-
cally. The left hand side - representing supply - refers to the factors
that are largely controlled by the shipowner, while the right-hand
side - depicting demand - refers to elements over which the owner
has less influence.
In the case of an individual ship, the activity risk is directly related
to the day-to-day operation of the vessel. Transport activities generate
profits; the freight income that the owner is able to obtain in the mar-
ket, minus the costs of providing the service. The costs refer not only
to operating costs, but also voyage and cargo handling costs, periodic
maintenance costs and capital costs. Dividends - or other forms of
remuneration to the owners - can be considered part of the capital cost
element. However, one can also think of the remuneration to the own-

Insurance will be touched upon briefly where it is relevant to discuss

Case 1: The sailing ship era - limited capital, limited risk
In the second half of the nineteenth century, Norwegian ship-
ping expanded rapidly; according to calculations by the statistician
A.N. Kiær, the value of the Norwegian merchant marine multiplied by
a factor of more than four from 1850 to 1870.5 The basis of the growth
was a combination of beneficial domestic and international conditions.
In 1860 revenues from third-country shipping - transport between for-
eign ports - for the first time exceeded the revenues from transporting
Norwegian imports and exports.6
The main form of organization in Norwegian shipping was the part own-
ership system, as in many other maritime nations.7 This was a system that
facilitated capital accumulation, but also enabled investors to spread risks.
Ship investments were organized on what would, in current ‘management
speak', be called ‘a project basis'. Individual investors bought shares of a
vessel and received remuneration if the ship traded profitably. When the
ship was sold, or for other reasons ended its trading life, remaining funds
were paid out to the investors, and the partnership was dissolved.
Although profits from shipping in the sailing ship era fluctuated in
close relationship with general business cycles, the activity risk appears
to have been limited. One of the most thorough analyses of a ship-
ping business in the last part of the nineteenth century is Fischer and
Nordvik's account of the investments of the shipowner Peter Jebsen.
The activity risk, in Jebsen's case, was clearly limited. Close scrutiny of
the accounts proves that ‘it was indeed hard to lose money operating
sailing vessels in the early 1870s' and Jebsen's ‘high rates of return cast
doubts on the reliability of the traditional arguments about the [low]
profitability of sail' in the late 1880s.8
The low activity risks were matched by relatively limited asset risk.
Due to the part-ownership system, the financial resources that an inves-
tor needed to enter the shipping industry were small; the size of the
balance sheet was limited. The initial expansion in the first half of the
nineteenth century was mainly based on cheap resources (wood and
labour) used to build ships locally. However, even when Norwegian
owners expanded through investments in second-hand sailing vessels,

The apparently low activity and asset risks in the sailing ship era have
one important caveat: it is primarily valid for ships that sailed without seri-
ous incidents. This was not the case for all ships, however: in the ten years
after 1890, more than 2,000 Norwegian ships were wrecked.10 On average,

224 Risks and Rewards: The Business of Norwegian Shipping
more than 4.75 per cent of the Norwegian sailing fleet was wrecked annu-
ally in the period from 1851 to 1914. Before 1880 around 3.1 per cent of
the sailing fleet suffered this fate every year. However, from 1881 to 1914,
with the average age of Norwegian sailing vessels getting markedly higher,
the share increased to more than 5.6 per cent annually.11
The wreckage figures illustrate that though shipping investments
appeared to be low-risk, they were far from risk-free. In fact, marine
accidents created a two-way trade-off between activity and asset risk.
Some owners refrained from insuring their vessels; this led to lower
costs and higher profits (lower activity risk), but implied the total loss of
the investment if the ship were wrecked (higher asset risk). Other own-
ers chose to over-insure the vessels, particularly in years with a bad mar-
ket (and correspondingly low vessel values). One Norwegian shipowner,
Fredrik Smith Petersen, claimed that this could explain the increasing
losses in bad years; owners speculated on the ship being lost, the crew
being saved and the insurance premium being paid out.12
Even with the transformation towards more expensive steamships,
the Norwegian ownership system enabled the limitation of asset risks.

Case 2: Interwar tanker shipping - high rewards
for new risks
The transformation of Norwegian shipping in the interwar period has
been succinctly characterized by Haakon With-Andersen as the develop-
ment from laggards to leaders.15 The basis was the rapid modernization
of the fleet, specifically the focus on modern motorships and tankers.
The Norwegian foray into the tanker segment stood out in an interna-
tional perspective. This new strategy enabled many owners to weather
the storms in what was generally a difficult period for shipping.
The tanker ventures also involved a new way of conducting business.
While many Norwegian owners still operated along traditional lines,
the tanker investments provide a good illustration of an ‘investment
choice' that totally transformed the approach to and question of risk.
The purchase of a series of second-hand tankers from Anglo-Saxon
Petroleum, the transport arm of Royal Dutch Shell, has often been
described as the breakthrough for Norwegian owners in the oil tanker
industry. While the direct long-term importance of these purchases is
debatable, the ‘Anglo-Saxon business model' became the fundament for
most tanker owners.16 The oil company chartered the ships for a period
of ten years and also arranged long-term financing for 75 to 80 per
cent of the purchase price. This business model - with a steady income
stream from long charters and substantial external financing - became
a blueprint for most expanding Norwegian tanker owners.17
What characterized the risk aspect of this business model? The long-
term time-charters with the oil companies reduced the activity risk.
The owners knew what their annual income would be throughout the
charter period, and the activity risk would then be reduced to the ques-
tion of the ability to keep costs down and the effects of currency fluc-
tuations. Moreover, in the case of the Anglo-Saxon ships, the financing
provided by the oil company implied that the demand for equity from
the owner was relatively low, varying between £10,000 and £20,000

The Anglo-Saxon purchases were but a small part of the Norwegian
tanker expansion. From the mid-1920s onwards, a number of owners
began to order new-built tankers, particularly from yards in Sweden and
Denmark. Usually, but not always, these ships were committed to long-
term charters. The depressed world economy and the massive competition
in the shipbuilding industry meant that the yards established a system of
relatively generous financing for new-buildings, on a scale similar to the
80 per cent offered by Anglo-Saxon. Both the activity risk and the asset risk
therefore remained low in the initial period of the ships' economic life,
enabling entrepreneurs with limited capital to amass funds for expansion.
Again, however, there is a caveat. The Norwegian tanker tale ended well
at the outbreak of World War II, and the tankers played a crucial role dur-
ing the war. This happy ending reflected the fact that oil transports were
the only rapidly increasing segment of international seaborne transports
in the interwar period. The investments were undoubtedly a gamble, but
a gamble that paid off because the stakes were placed on the right horse.
Indeed, if tanker demand had developed differently, the fact that tankers
were inflexible and purpose-built for one market would have changed the
outcome significantly. Indeed, as Sturmey has pointed out: ‘For the inde-
pendent shipowner tanker ownership entails some special risks in that
he is completely dependent for his livelihood on a few large companies
whose residual requirements only he satisfies'.18
Investments in tanker tonnage, financially backed by long-term char-

However, the remuneration from the time-charters was lower than that
which the owners in good years could reap in the spot market, where
transport services are sold on a voyage-by-voyage basis. Shipowners paid
a premium, in the case of foregone earnings, to get the security of a long-
term charter. Consequently, just as risk-prone owners in the sailing ship
era sailed without insurance in order to improve profits, an increasing
share of the tanker community sought the added incomes available in
the spot market. As long as the market was good, this was a beneficial
choice. When the tanker market turned sour, it proved to be disastrous.
Case 3: The first post-war decades - becoming ‘the
gamblers among the gamblers'
Michael Porter refers to the Scandinavian tanker owners in the early
1970s as ‘gamblers among the gamblers of the shipping industry'.19
While this impression is partly a result of misinterpretation and based

on faulty empirics, there is an element of truth in it. By the early 1970s
there is little doubt that the Norwegian shipowners in general, and
tanker owners in particular, were more exposed in the event of a market
downturn than their foreign competitors.20 Thus, when the shipping
market collapsed, few nations were as hard hit by the crisis as Norway.
How can we account for the massive vulnerability - or risk exposure - of
Norwegian owners?
The demand for seaborne transport increased rapidly from 1950
to 1973. A number of factors worked together to push up shipping
demand: transport-dependent industrialization in Europe and Japan,
the continuing growth of oil consumption, which was largely filled by
supply from the Middle East, and changes in sea lanes, in particularly
during the two closures of the Suez canal. As a result of these beneficial
demand developments, the world fleet grew rapidly, with economies of
scale as an important ingredient of the expansion (see Chapter 5 by Yrjö
Kaukiainen in this volume).
From the early 1960s the Norwegian fleet developed differently from
the fleets of most other countries. There was still a predilection for tanker
investments, but the ships now became both larger and, as a result of fre-
quent renewal, younger than the world average. This development, which
can be explained by the relative price of capital and labour in Norway,
implied that the asset risk increased substantially. While external financing
was still extremely important, the sheer size of the units led to a problem
of divisibility. The owners put all their eggs in one basket, not only by
operating relatively inflexible ships that could transport a limited number
of cargoes, but by operating fleets of few large vessels, rather than many
small vessels. In gambling terms, they went ‘all in' on a number of large
positions, rather than hedging their bets. The asset risk became substantial.
However, in a market characterized by demand growth this was not prob-
lematic; as a result of the development of ship values, good timing of sales
and purchases meant that the value reduction of the vessels was limited.
At the same time, many shipowners purposely increased their activ-
ity risk. The duration of the time-charters was reduced, and an increas-
ing proportion of the fleet was operated in the

The discussion of risk within shipping also received academic atten-
tion. In 1970, two young economists, Peter Lorange and Victor Norman,
presented seventeen Scandinavian tanker owners with a number of
hypothetical investment alternatives in order to gauge their attitudes
towards risk. The owners systematically disregarded the safe alterna-
tives, preferring instead risky investments with identical expected
returns.23 Indeed as the expected return in real life was higher in the rel-
atively risky spot market, it should come as no surprise that Norwegian
shipowners, if this risk-prone group were representative, would shun
long-term charters.
Furthermore, the joint movement of freight rates and vessel values
put the owners in a very difficult position. Revenues dissipated as a
result of the freight rate reduction, and the overcapacity in the shipping
market reduced the value of some ship types by as much as two-thirds.
The significant external financing implied that this was a problem the
shipowners shared with the banks. However, the mortgage conditions
usually included a ‘minimum value clause'; if the value of the ship fell
below a certain threshold, the owner was forced to put up additional
collateral or sell the vessel. As a result, the banks would often force the
vessel. As a result, the banks would often force the

disposal of vessels in a depressed market - ‘selling chicken in the rain',
as it became known in Norwegian shipping circles - securing some pay-
back on the mortgage, but leaving the owners without assets.24
When the market collapsed, the perils of the ‘typical' Norwegian
strategy became obvious. Vessels in the spot market were laid up, while
those trading on short time-charters failed to find profitable employ-
ment when the charters expired. The strategy of frequent renewal of
ships also implied that Norwegian owners had large amounts of new-
buildings on order. Some relented and paid heavy cancellation fees,
while others took delivery of vessels that were worth only a fraction of
the original investment. In one way there is a parallel to the situation in
the sailing ship era; just as the Norwegian strategy then was beneficial as
long as the ships sailed without accident, the post-war decade strategy
was eminently suited to a market with growing demand. When vessels
were wrecked, and when the market collapsed, the results were cata-
strophic. It is tempting to reduce the most extreme strategies to a binary
or ‘black-and-white' outcome. When things went well, all was good.
When disaster struck, all was lost. For most Norwegian owners there was
no alternative strategy if the vessels were wrecked or the market growth
declined - such incidents led to an exit from shipping.
The shipping crisis led to haemorrhaging of the sector in Norway. The
number of companies and the size of the fleet were drastically reduced.
Too many shipowners had assumed activity and asset risks that were
unsustainable when the market collapsed. The problems were of course
a result of the demand side of the business risk framework presented in
Figure 13.1: the low freight rates and vessel values. However, increas-
ingly uncompetitive Norwegian costs and extremely unfortunate invest-
ment choices made the situation even worse. Indeed, the fact that some
Norwegian companies survived indicates that the basis for the problems
was not only exogenous. There were successful companies, those that
had chosen a strategy with less spectacular short-term profits than the
spot tanker market, but which proved sustainable in the longer term.

Case 4: After the crisis - once bitten…
The majority of the companies that survived the shipping crisis had
diversified their investments, primarily through investment in new and
innovative specialized vessel types such as car carriers, chemical tankers
or gas carriers. To follow Sturmey's argument above, these ships were
extremely specialized, usually suitable only for a specific cargo, and as
such apparently increased both the activity and the asset risk. However,

230 Risks and Rewards: The Business of Norwegian Shipping
the specialized market segments are characterized by long-term rela-
tionships between shipping companies and their customers. Specialized
markets, often referred to as ‘industrial shipping', are not characterized
by the same cut-throat competition and flexible price-setting as the
main dry and liquid bulk markets. This feature improved the predict-
ability of the revenues, which again was helped by institutional changes
that reduced the costs of providing transport.
The 1987 introduction of the Norwegian International Ship Register
led to a substantial reduction of operating costs for vessels flying the
Norwegian flag. The strong growth of the Norwegian fleet in subse-
quent years was partly a result of asset play strategies by companies
speculating on an improvement in vessel values. In the longer term,
however, the importance of such strategies has been reduced. The
majority of the current Norwegian shipping companies are involved
in the highly specialized markets of industrial shipping, where one of
their competitive advantages is a reputation for solidity and competent
handling of risks.
The Norwegian expansion within specialized shipping was far from
risk-free. The case was rather the opposite; it involved the launching
and nurturing of non-existent markets and also hinged upon new, and

synthesis
The Norwegian exposure to business risk in shipping has changed over
time. The scheme presented initially, dividing the business risk into an
‘activity risk' and an ‘asset risk', enables the evaluation of the relative
importance of various types of risks, as seen in Figure 13.2.
In Case 1, referring to the sailing ship era, the most important risk
was related to the perils of the sea: would the vessel be able to safely sail
from one destination to the next? The capital investment was relatively
meagre, and through the part ownership system, investors were able
to spread their risks by holding minority shares in a number of vessels.
